# Introduction

The intellectual journal that Carl Schmitt kept under the title *Glossarium* from 1947 to 1958 survives among his papers in the State Archive of North Rhine-Westphalia, Rhineland Department. It consists of five notebooks, which Schmitt called “books,” bound in black board and light-grey half-cloth (RW 0265, Nos. 19607–19611). Books II, III, and V have title labels written by Schmitt himself. Books I–III measure 17 × 21.5 cm, Book IV 13.5 × 20.5 cm, and Book V 15 × 21 cm. Each cloth spine bears a large “G,” the Roman numeral of the volume, and the period it covers. The notebooks were probably first used as household account books by Schmitt’s wife Duška, as a few isolated entries by her suggest.

*Glossarium* was first published by Duncker & Humblot in 1991, edited by Schmitt’s former student and assistant Eberhard von Medem. The book attracted a great deal of attention because it contains, in concentrated form, the world of thought of the later Carl Schmitt. These thoughts also appear almost completely unfiltered: spontaneous, written down in rough form, and expressed with all the peculiarities and resentments of an author who had been excluded from academic life but remained fully aware of his own importance.

The text published in 1991, however, had not always been edited with the necessary care, and this in turn encouraged mistaken interpretations. One example is the entry for 25 September 1947, where the edition did not clearly distinguish between a quotation from Peter F. Drucker and Carl Schmitt’s own opinion. Inconsistencies and misreadings were soon discovered as well. The Schmitt scholar Piet Tommissen alone produced a twenty-page list of corrections.

Above all, however, the edition remained unsatisfactory because it contained only the first three books and left out the final two. Eberhard von Medem explained this in his preface by arguing that the quality of *Glossarium* declined with Book IV. There is only one limited sense in which this is true: the entries become less dense. Their character does not change. Books IV and V are intellectual journals just as much as the earlier books. They are an inseparable part of *Glossarium* and cannot simply be left out.

The present edition is therefore not merely a corrected second edition of the 1991 publication. It is a complete new transcription of all five books of *Glossarium*, prepared directly from the manuscripts. It also reproduces in full the increasingly numerous newspaper clippings that Schmitt pasted into the final two books and annotated by hand.

Eberhard von Medem’s main aim had been to provide a smoothly readable text. For that reason, he skipped passages he could not decipher, smoothed out confused passages, or replaced them with conjectures that were not identified as such.

The present edition takes a different approach. It does not claim to be a full historical-critical edition, but it does aim to reproduce the text as accurately and completely as possible.

Schmitt was capable of polished prose of an almost literary quality. But even he had to work on his writing. It is obvious that something written quickly “in a notebook” had not received the author’s final approval and therefore could not possess the same aesthetic and stylistic quality as his published books and essays.

We have naturally made no attempt to change this. Occasional roughness, as well as isolated incomplete sentences or sentences whose grammar breaks off midway, have been left as they appear in the manuscript.

Writing in a notebook also means that one makes no special effort to produce beautiful handwriting. This can be seen again and again in the manuscript of *Glossarium*. Schmitt often threw something quickly onto the page and was satisfied as long as he himself could read it.

There is an additional difficulty: Schmitt used several different styles of handwriting. Alongside the German Kurrent script he had learned at school—which he also uses for most of *Glossarium*—there is a flowing and highly legible Latin script of the kind found in his letters. He also occasionally used the much harder-to-decipher Gabelsberger shorthand, though only to a limited extent.

The manuscript is also full of corrections, overwritten words, insertions, and marginal notes whose exact place in the text is not always clear. Passages were sometimes rearranged as well.

Schmitt normally wrote in dark-blue ink, but there are also entries in a lighter blue, as well as passages written in pencil or red pencil. These differences point to different times of composition.

As with his diaries, Carl Schmitt repeatedly returned to the notebooks of *Glossarium*. He deleted text, wrote over it, and added new material. In most cases, it is impossible to date these later additions more precisely. The manuscript therefore contains several chronological layers.

Because of the state of the manuscript, the text cannot always be transcribed with certainty.

Unreadable passages are marked by three dots inside angle brackets. Uncertain readings and editorial conjectures are also marked with angle brackets. Occasional additions by the editors, by contrast, appear inside square brackets.

This method comes at the expense of smooth reading, but that is the price of accuracy.

The shorthand passages that von Medem had transcribed with the help of his expert Heinrich Mauermann have been adopted without being checked again. The shorthand passages omitted from von Medem’s edition—and there are quite a few of them—were transcribed shortly before his death by Hans Gebhardt, wherever he was able to decipher them.

The punctuation of the original reflects the fact that Schmitt was writing rough notes and is often highly individual.

He very frequently separates parts of a sentence, or even complete sentences, with semicolons. Quotation marks are often missing altogether. Sometimes Schmitt puts an opening quotation mark at the beginning but no closing quotation mark at the end. He also switches between German and French quotation marks.

In the present edition, German quotation marks are used throughout. They have only occasionally been supplied where the absence of quotation marks could create confusion—as in the Peter Drucker quotation mentioned above.

Schmitt’s use of upper- and lowercase letters does not always match present-day practice. His peculiarities have normally been preserved. His spelling has also been preserved.

Occasional simple spelling mistakes have nevertheless been corrected without comment. A few archaic forms—such as “Huppe” instead of “Hupe,” “abluxen” instead of “abluchsen,” and “allmählig” instead of “allmählich”—have been modernized.

Abbreviations are expanded in square brackets unless they can be assumed to be generally understood.

The many passages in foreign languages are translated in the commentary appendix, but only when they are in ancient languages, namely Greek and Latin.

Schmitt wrote the names of books of the Bible in several different ways. In this edition they are cited using the abbreviations of the *Theologische Realenzyklopädie*.

Because Carl Schmitt repeatedly returned to *Glossarium*, the entire manuscript is covered with marginal cross-references, and these become increasingly frequent toward the end.

They are reproduced in the printed text as footnotes.

Schmitt normally made these cross-references by date, although he sometimes referred instead to a manuscript page number. Since such manuscript page numbers are of no use to the reader, they have been converted in square brackets either into dates or into printed page references.

The title labels and endpapers of the individual volumes contain several different titles written by Schmitt. These formulations reveal how he understood the work, and they are therefore reproduced in the appendix.

It seems that *Glossarium* only gradually took shape in the author’s mind—in a *status nascendi*, a state of coming into being.

Pages 1 to 9 of the first book show Schmitt’s thoughts gradually taking form through the very act of writing. What begins as little more than notes and extracts from books soon condenses into original thought.

According to a note Schmitt wrote on the endpaper, *Glossarium* proper was only meant to begin on page 10.

On the reverse of folio 66 of Book I—page 386 in the printed text—there is a dated entry that chronologically belongs before the true beginning of the main text. It has therefore been placed within the chronology of pages 1 to 9.

There are also notes on the endpapers of all five volumes. All of these entries are reproduced in an appendix.

In Book III, after folio 75, there is a loose sheet containing a shorthand note. It is extremely difficult to decipher and has therefore not been included here.

Schmitt wrote *Glossarium* in longhand. This is striking because, unlike *Glossarium*, the diaries he kept throughout his life were not written this way.

Von Medem concluded from this that Schmitt must have been thinking about publication.

The editors of the present edition find this unlikely because of the unfinished state of the text described above. Carl Schmitt was far too conscious a stylist to have sent the manuscript to a publisher in this form.

The use of longhand may instead suggest that Schmitt wanted his thoughts to remain accessible to a limited circle of family members and close friends.

Deciding how much commentary to provide was not easy.

On the one hand, the text is extremely compressed, assumes a great deal of prior knowledge, and is sometimes almost impenetrable. It constantly alludes to contemporary history, academic politics, and details of Schmitt’s own life.

Schmitt also liked to use a single line of poetry to summon up an entire mood. Because he was speaking to himself, he did not need to explain further. But an outside reader cannot always understand the meaning so easily.

For this reason, *Glossarium* clearly requires commentary.

On the other hand, the complexity and richness of the text can very quickly make commentary endless.

The editors have therefore chosen to keep their commentary short and restrained. They do not laboriously repeat information that is now easily available to anyone on the internet. In particular, they make no attempt to engage with the now almost unmanageable body of secondary literature on Schmitt.

Carl Schmitt cared about making his books accessible through more than just a table of contents. He was not above preparing detailed subject indexes himself.

He also began work on a subject index for *Glossarium*. These preliminary notes appear on the endpapers of the notebooks and are reproduced in the appendix.

The indexing is incomplete and unsystematic, but it shows that Schmitt understood the importance of his text and wanted to make its contents easier to navigate.

That is not a simple task, given the complexity of *Glossarium* and its frequently aphoristic or heavily abbreviated character.

After some consideration, the editors decided not to provide a subject index.

There is, of course, an index of names.

As a concentrated expression of Schmitt’s thought, *Glossarium* is written in constant relation—sometimes explicit, sometimes unspoken—to both his published and unpublished work.

The commentary appendix provides references intended to encourage deeper reading, although these references are by no means exhaustive.

*Glossarium* cannot replace serious engagement with Carl Schmitt’s wider work. But it can serve as a doorway into that work.

The book was written during a period that threw Schmitt off the established path of a middle-class scholar’s life. He viewed the new situation with resentment, but also with something like Tocqueville’s sharp-sightedness of the defeated.

Henning Ritter described this new situation in a birthday article for Wolfgang Schivelbusch published in the *FAZ* on 21 November 2011. Writing about Schivelbusch’s book *The Culture of Defeat*, Ritter said:

> The book also helps explain why, after the Second World War, the victors no longer left it to the defeated to create their own myths about the postwar period. Instead, the victors themselves organized the culture of defeat. Culture became another battlefield on which victory and defeat were once again at stake. It mattered too much in the process of coming to terms with defeat to be left entirely to the defeated.

This edition could not have been produced without the help of a number of deeply committed people.

This is especially true of Dietrich Nithack, who transcribed the previously unpublished texts directly from the original manuscripts.

Until his death, Hans Gebhardt transcribed those parts of Schmitt’s text written in Gabelsberger shorthand, insofar as this was possible with notes that were usually added later and written down very hastily.

As they have done before, Florian Meinel, Wolfgang Schuller, and Wolfgang H. Spindler provided the editors with valuable clarification and assistance.

The same is true of Harald Bluhm, Peter Heyl, Wolfram Hogrebe, Ernst Hüsmert, Günter Maschke, Matthias Meusch, Andreas Raithel, Angela Reinthal, and Christian Tilitzki.

Corrections to the first edition that Günter Maschke and Piet Tommissen (†) had kindly collected some time ago have been incorporated into the new edition.

Last but not least, thanks are due to the State Archive of North Rhine-Westphalia in Duisburg for making the materials available; to Florian Simon and Heike Frank for overseeing the publishing and printing of the new edition; and to Jürgen Becker, administrator of the Schmitt estate, for permission to use and reproduce all materials important to the edition.

# Book I

28 Aug. 1947–31 Dec. 1947

**28 Aug. 1947**

At night: noble simplicity and quiet grandeur. Yes—quiet!

The quiet of ordinary people living quietly in the land. Pietist and humanist quiet.

But quiet in opposition to what?

“Quiet” becomes a polemical idea aimed against the noise of the Baroque. That is the most concrete thing about this quiet and noble simplicity.

Rousseau as archaeologist: cheerful feelings awaken as Greece is dug out of the earth.

What, then, was this supposed *trahison des clercs*—this “betrayal of the intellectuals”? There certainly was a betrayal.

The intellectuals themselves were shamefully betrayed, worse even than King Peter of Yugoslavia. They were betrayed to money and to the masses.

And when they looked to the state for protection—which was an understandable mistake, and one that showed they still had some historical memory—when they turned to the only refuge that seemed to remain, this was then held against them as proof of their own “betrayal.”

Repulsive frauds. Destroyers of every refuge.

But God transforms the lie even in the liar’s own mouth and gives it the meaning of truth.

*Trahison des clercs* can also mean betrayal **of** the intellectuals. Grammatically, “of the intellectuals” can make them the object of the betrayal rather than its perpetrators.

And that gets to the heart of the matter: spiritual authority is destroyed by intellectuals who have gone crawling for shelter under the ruler of this world.

Speech by Enrico Corradini, Florence, 8 February 1925: presenting fascism as “the revolution of the State against the predominance of private interests.” So this is Sallust fleeing from money into the arms of Caesar.

The virgin takes refuge with the pimp.

Poor intellectuals.

The state Corradini fled to wanted to become a Caesarian empire.

Classicism came with it free of charge.

State = sovereignty = decision = the ending of civil war within the state. And it is only through this ending of civil war that the state itself comes into being.

Does world rule likewise mean the end of civil war? No. It means combining war between states with civil war.

Tacitus, *Histories* I.2: “foreign war and civil wars intertwined.”

Otto Brunner (*Land und Herrschaft*, 1939, p. 170): on the soil of the medieval West, sovereign powers did not exist and could not exist.

During the great struggle over investiture, the Church allied itself with local powers and thereby created “a situation in which kings and princes, caught between the Church and local powers, were unable to attain a sovereign position.”

Between spirit and soil, there can be no sovereignty! Or, more strongly: alongside a *potestas spiritualis*—a spiritual power—there can be no sovereignty.

A desperate unity. A unity born of desperation. That is what this sovereignty based purely on decision amounts to.

Unity only in an emergency and only in the exceptional case.

Brunner says, referring to K. H. Ganahl’s *Studien zur Geschichte des kirchlichen Verfassungsrechts im 10. und 11. Jahrhundert* (1935, p. 7), “that the problem of sovereignty between state and Church cannot, in any event, be raised before the Investiture Contest.”

Neither emperor, prince, nor pope was truly sovereign.

“But as long as sovereign powers did not exist” within the medieval West, “a separation between the idea of law and positive law could not establish itself” (p. 170).

So: disappearance of spiritual power → sovereignty → positive <…> legality.

See Lamennais, above, p. 5.

We are still before 1848!!

In the afternoon: deeply affected by Willy Haas’s May 1932 essay “A New Political Doctrine” in *Die Literarische Welt*. He calls me a nihilist. He says that defining politics through the distinction between friend and enemy is itself a concealed—and indeed the worst—form of neutralization.

An empty eggshell.

Why? Because it abstracts from what he sees as the one concrete cause of hostility that actually matters now: material hostility, meaning class hostility toward the bourgeoisie.

By abstracting from this, he says, my definition neutralizes that conflict and is therefore itself intensely political.

At the same time, he falsely assumes that I understand the enemy as something that can simply “be removed from this world in a war of annihilation.”

How strange.

Because I refuse to identify myself with **his** hostility—the hostility of Marxist civil war—he declares both me and my theory to be the enemy.

A wonderful confirmation.

Everyone agrees with me as long as I agree with **him** about his own concrete distinction between friend and enemy.

Had I said, “The Jew is the enemy,” the Nazis would have agreed with me.

Had I said, “The Nazi is the enemy,” the others would have agreed with me. And so on.

And those are still the relatively honest ones.

The worst are those who deny that hostility exists at all and then make that very denial the basis of their own hostility.

Much more could be said about this: the habilitation thesis written against me by the SS man Lemmel; the concept of “race” seized by village mongrels and then abandoned to them by their enemies; and so on.

28 Aug. 1947, evening <…>[^fn-p01-pdf20-n01]

Now the opening of Tacitus’s *Histories* has taken hold of me.

Is it really nothing more than rhetoric, as Ortega told me? Or is it the fact that the situation itself is the same—an existential participation, a *participatio*, in one and the same original and defining situation of our age?

The *ère actiaque*, as Proudhon calls it—the Actian age, at the origin of our own age?

Every word of this chapter of Tacitus is completely contemporary:

> Great minds fell silent. I begin a work rich in disasters, terrible in battles, torn by seditions, savage even in peace.

Yes: **savage even in peace.**

> Civil and foreign wars were for the most part intertwined.

The combination of foreign war and civil war is not rhetoric. It is the terrible reality itself, recognized and spoken aloud: the inability to distinguish war from peace.

---

**29 Aug. 1947**

The inability to distinguish war from peace is at the same time *fas nefasque mixtum*: right and wrong mixed together.

Law is transformed into mere legality. That means stripping law of its reciprocal character—the idea that the rule applies mutually to both sides. Equal opportunity is one example of this reciprocity.

At the same time, illegality is turned into a tactical maneuver: one of the permitted tricks of war, the *ruse de guerre* of civil war.

I wrote to Hans Barion:

Your essay[^fn-p01-pdf20-n02] marking the hundredth anniversary of Sohm’s death (1941) has been occupying me intensely.

You repel the jurist’s attack with tremendous force and send the reckless aggressor plunging into the abyss of his own problem.

Entirely right.

Could he now perhaps try—following some bad examples—to cling to the victorious theologian, so that he might at least drag part of him down with him?[^fn-p01-pdf20-n03]

Perhaps by taking the chain of opposing concepts that is so fatal to him as a jurist:

Pneuma — tradition
Charisma — office
Decision — institution

and, with the courage of desperation, carrying it further through

Sovereignty — legality

to

Constituent power — constituted power

and then into—or down into—the abyss of metaphysics:

*Natura naturans* — *natura naturata*[^fn-p01-pdf21-n01]

(see p. 142 of my *Diktatur*),

into that which creates organization but cannot itself be organized, the *plenitudo potestatis immediatae in omnes et singulos*—the fullness of immediate power over everyone and each individual?

(Then a question about Otto Brunner, *Land und Herrschaft*, and K. H. Ganahl.)

As far as I can see, even when Luther is justifying his own position, he remains deeply rooted in tradition—indeed, in the medieval tradition of the *ius reformandi*, the right to reform.

The Calvinists, by contrast, recognize the *a Deo excitatus*: the man raised up by God, who proves his authority through signs and wonders.

(Then a reference to a new development in the otherwise completely formulaic field of human rights: the **right to political error**.

The right to religious error—the right to be wrong in matters of religion—became the foundation of modern constitutional law as we have known it until now.)

---

**30 Aug. 1947**

The present legal order “does not recognize enmity” (Otto Brunner, *Land und Herrschaft*, p. 38).

Is that why my definition of the political provokes such horror?

“For the legal historian, the concepts of enmity (feud) and revenge present a peculiar difficulty.”

“He is always convinced that, in the law of feud and revenge, he is dealing either with private phenomena that existed before law or with imperfect beginnings of modern developments, especially in medieval feud law.”

The other reason for this hostility toward hostility itself: H. Heller and Willy Haas. They smuggle in the assumption that enmity necessarily means annihilation.

---

**31 Aug. 1947**

Came across James Shotwell’s Berlin lecture of March 1927—which Ernst Jäckh calls the “formal introduction” to the new understanding of war, with its treatment of the aggressor as a criminal:

“Are We at a Turning Point in World History?”

From a repetitive understanding of the world toward science, democracy, and goals that were once achieved through war. We should add: now achieved in other ways.

The Industrial Revolution is very important here.

Change takes the place of repetition.

In the past, the world was “static” and there were wars. Now it is becoming dynamic, and supposedly there is to be peace.

Strange.

Rage and a bad conscience go looking for someone to blame, for a scapegoat. And there will always be fools and idiots ready to walk straight into the knife and satisfy that need. That too belongs to the dynamism of the new world age.

War is no longer the *ultima ratio*—the final resort. It has lost its reason for existing.

“This new dynamic world, created by the human mind, has no other means of defending itself against this advance of destruction through war, and of saving its most precious inheritance”—what exactly is this most precious inheritance?—“than the very technology on which it both depends and through which it puts itself in danger, since every new discovery forces the enemy to produce something equal to it, or even more terrible.”[^fn-p02-pdf01-n01] That is what the war of 1914–18 revealed to us. It showed us clearly that this was not an accident but something typical, and that it would become more and more so as civilization continued to develop.

But what does that actually mean?

The more terrible the weapons become, the less respect they leave for the enemy. That is what is new: the enemy is disqualified more and more completely.

---

**1 September 1947**

What follows from this? asks J. Shotwell.

His answer: because war has stopped being predictable—as it supposedly was in the static, repetitive age—it no longer belongs to Realpolitik. We must therefore develop a Realpolitik of peace: the League of Nations, international justice, Locarno.[^fn-p02-pdf01-n02]

My view is different. Because war has stopped being predictable, it does not therefore have to stop existing.

War was always a judgment of God and therefore always unpredictable.

The real question is whether enmity has disappeared. Unfortunately, it has not. And if war no longer belongs to the Realpolitik of the old kind, perhaps that simply means that, as the form and substance of war change, the meaning and substance of Realpolitik must change as well.

Perhaps politics can no longer be merely the nineteenth-century “art of what is possible and predictable.”

Perhaps precisely the desire to save our most precious inheritance, precisely the awareness that we are living through an enormous turning point, precisely the dynamic character of the present, precisely our awareness that war has become incalculable—perhaps all of this will produce a new kind of Realpolitik.

A Realpolitik that includes this awareness within itself, and that does not fear matching the other side’s willingness to face danger with an equal willingness of its own, provided it knows that it possesses the right weapons.

---

**2 September 1947**

James Shotwell’s lecture of March 1927 was one of the most fertile and fateful lectures ever given in Germany. It was delivered from the newly founded Carnegie chair at the German School of Politics.

Compare Schelling’s university lecture of November 1841. Who was sitting in the audience?

M. J. Bonn.

Look into this!

(On 26 September 1947 an essay on the subject appeared by M. J. Bonn—the good, clever Moritz!)

The *spiritus malignus*, the *magnus deceptor*—the evil spirit, the great deceiver—whom Descartes speaks of pursues me too.

His great trick is to awaken in us the fear that deception is unavoidable, that all human existence is ultimately exposed to fraud.

The thief who shouts “Stop, thief!” is a fairly harmless figure compared with the deceiver who whispers into our ear that we are so terribly easy to deceive.

Descartes knew this most sinister of all deceivers.

His answer was:

*Sum.*

I am.

Ah yes: *sum, sum, sum*—little bee, buzz around.

Descartes still tried to deal with this woodworm by means of an *ergo*.

Touching.

We can no longer argue our way out of it with an *ergo*. We cannot even escape it by praying as our parents taught us to pray. There is nothing left but the sign of the Cross.

Thank you, Annette.

How magnificent she can be with her Castor-and-Pollux offer to an ambitious man of letters; she, the Penthesilea among the lyrically gifted shop assistants of the Biedermeier age; the fresh green tree standing beside the poison swamp of the German *Vormärz*, decorated with forget-me-nots.

She makes herself so small, calling herself the “little mother” of an imaginary figure—the clever, foolish virgin in whose plain, domestic solidity there was more spirit than in the entire poetry industry of Lenau’s day.

It is too sad.

There is too much in her.

You should have met Heinrich von Kleist.

Perhaps he would have awakened the Amazon in you for one second.

You would have torn him to pieces. But that would still have been a nobler end for him than that bleak suicide at Wannsee.

But here too: away with every “would have” and every “if only.”

Everything that happens is worthy of adoration.

The spaces of Russia are vast and wide. But the spiritual spaces of the country between the Moselle and the Saale, between Friesland and the Breisgau, are deeper and greater still.

I have said it a thousand times: you cannot destroy anything. And Adam Müller said against Fichte: whoever condemns another person absolutely condemns himself to an eternal struggle against him.

But perhaps that is precisely the meaning of an agonistic faith—a faith built around struggle.

Shotwell’s complete lack of understanding of this agonism, which does **not** seek to destroy the opponent. We must distinguish between an agonistic understanding of the enemy and an ethical-moral understanding of the enemy. And when we do, the agonistic understanding comes out unexpectedly well—even morally.

---

**3 September 1947**

To Gerhard Günther:

I would like to rest here from the hunt in which I have been the hunted animal for years.

Three times Leviathan has spat me out again.

I now understand the prophet Jonah, who refused to obey the command of the Lord and go to Nineveh to preach to its people. I do not want to do that either. I do not want to preach repentance now. And I do not want to go to Nineveh. Therefore: I rest, an exile in my own homeland.

On Bernanos: I think he is in extreme danger.[^fn-p02-pdf02-n01]

There is something desperately provocative about the words he spoke at the UNESCO congress in Geneva at the end of 1946.

What was he doing there in the first place?

“The majority of the truly poor did not become people’s commissars. They were hanged by the exploiters of the people, to the applause of the poor. That is what happened to Jesus Christ, and I hope the same thing awaits me.”[^fn-p02-pdf02-n02]

The knightly and peasant revolts of the late Middle Ages, from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century, belonged to a transitional age.

The new organization of the state was already strong enough to weaken and suppress the old forms of order and the protection they had provided—manorial rule and feudal law.

But it was not yet strong enough to establish and secure its own kind of peace.

Otto Brunner, *Land and Lordship*, p. 392. So today: the national-state order is being weakened and loosened before any clear large-area order, much less a world order, has taken its place.

The result is new kinds of enmity that are no longer divided neatly by territory: blurred spaces and pseudo-fronts split from within at their very core.

Suddenly I feel intense curiosity again about the connection between Bruno Bauer and Nietzsche in their shared opposition to D. F. Strauss.

Is it Strauss’s theory of tradition that enrages Bauer and Nietzsche, those two former Protestant theologians?

The concept of the Jew in Hamann, Bruno Bauer, Kierkegaard, and Nietzsche.

A concept becomes virulent once it is stripped of theology.

---

**4 September 1947**

The Protestant origin: charisma against institution.

Charisma is secularized into genius.

From genius comes the absolute leader.

Max Weber played an outstanding part in all of this.

In the history of ideas, the whole development was unavoidable.[^fn-p02-pdf03-n01]

How touching, by comparison, is the cry:

Back to Goethe!

Back to Idealism!

Back to Nathan the Wise!

Yes indeed—back, back!

To these back-to-idealism people I can answer only with the words of Castruccio Castracani:

Now that you are coming out, you have no reason to be ashamed.

You should have been ashamed when you went in.

“Are We at a Turning Point in World History?” That is the question Shotwell used as the title of his Berlin lecture of March 1927.[^fn-p02-pdf03-n02]

The answer is obviously:

Yes!

Otherwise the question itself could not have been asked.

So there is a turning point: from the static to the dynamic, from repetition to change, from dependence on nature to freedom.[^fn-p02-pdf03-n03]

The most important thing, however, is our **awareness** of the turning point. That awareness shows that we are facing a choice: continue further along the path of dynamism, or stop, reflect, and return?

To continue means continuing toward the total rule of the dynamic. We have now reached the point at which this dynamic world must completely destroy the old one.

The free creative power of man must take complete possession of nature.

Complete possession means possession not only of the world outside man but also of man’s own physical and psychological nature. That is the problem of totality. It creates the compulsion toward total planning. It creates this total human power. It removes every remaining natural limit.

The problem is now becoming conscious.

And the despair of the Germans showed itself in the fact that, in the name of the old and the natural, they stumbled headlong into the most shameless dynamism of the new.[^fn-p02-pdf03-n04]

Again and again: this is the problem of totality. And it arises from our awareness that we have reached this turning point.

“Let us make man.”

That is what the dynamic creators of their own world must now say.

Or rather: that is what they must now **do**, even if they would prefer not to speak openly about it in front of these blood-soaked *enfants terribles*.

What a confusion of fronts!

---

**5 September 1947, journey to Dortmund
(6 September to Menden)**

So Annette—or perhaps here it is better to say the Droste—and Heinrich von Kleist: that would have been one of those meetings that German circumstances never permit.

In Dortmund, an especially friendly and intelligent kind of foolish and wise virgin. I am delighted by this friendliness in the middle of this shattered great city.

You probably saw nothing of that, Georges Bernanos, when you were so horrified by the destroyed German cities and apparently thought cities like these must be the end of the world.

Geneva and the audience you have today would seem much more terrifying to me.

Above all, your own situation would frighten me.

Unless you yourself know that you are in the position of Kierkegaard’s clown: the clown who cries “Fire!” because the building really is burning, while the audience applauds because it thinks the cry is an excellent joke. But that is probably the situation of every intellectual, every *clerc*.

Perhaps it is even the definition of the intellectual: the person who knows and speaks instead of remaining silent. Or who writes instead of remaining silent.

Speaking in written form is the worst of all. That black trail of ink that Annette feared so much, with death and life following “softly, creeping” behind it.

(In Neuenrade:

“That passes clearly east and west as a sign.”)

---

**Sunday, 7 September 1947**

Pinder’s death.

Paul Adams knew the passage from *Le Mendiant ingrat* of 22 June 1894:

“I tell you this on behalf of God.”

Fumet leaves it out. So does the new edition of 1928.

Am I right to hide away here in this comfortable form of home?

Reading my notes from 1912–14 leaves me astonished by the infinite immobility of events, by the immobility of what people call time. Or, which amounts to the same thing: the infinite patience of God.

Nothing of what people call development.

Nothing essential in the way of education.

Nothing of speed or haste.

Again and again I am frightened by the hostility that the mere speaking of the word and name “enemy” has unleashed against me.

Did I violate some secret agreement?

Perhaps even one of the hidden mysteries of this age?

A secret of wickedness?

Or did I merely violate one of those harmless lies people need in order to live?

One of those secret agreements that even the simplest age cannot survive without—agreements that are literally necessary for life?

After all, even a gang of criminals cannot function without them.

Did I violate some *raison d’être* or *raison d’état*?

Some secret clause?

Some silent understanding?

What exactly was it?

In today’s Epistle, on the fifteenth Sunday after Pentecost, I hear:

Your enemies are my enemies, and those who strike you I will strike.

And in Claudel, in his introduction to Tardif de Moidrey, I read:

“And *raison d’état*, if you please! Everyone, every single person, has a *raison d’état* of his own.” That applies even to our sensitivity toward particular words and concepts.[^fn-p02-pdf04-n01]

Or was I simply tactless?

Did I violate the rule:

In the house of a hanged man, one does not speak of the rope?

Or: among the proscribed, one does not speak of the list?

Or: in Hell, one must not paint the Devil on the wall?

Had the enemy already been banished into theology?

Does he return in mythology, which arrives with mass society and belongs to it?

So: you are on earth in order to know God. But Marx says: the point is not to know but to change. That means: to master and make useful. So now you are on earth in order to change God, master God, and make God useful to you.[^fn-p02-pdf04-n02]

No one was horrified by that.

But people were horrified by the observation that there is a distinction between friend and enemy, and that something called enmity still exists among human beings. That was a crude grab at the sensitive spot.

The Devil jumped up when someone beat the bushes in that particular place and taught the naive bush-beater a lesson.

Claudel, in his introduction to Abbé Tardif de Moidrey’s commentary on Ruth, 1937:

“The Antichrist, the black Christ, the negative shadow of Christ, began his career together with the other. Every ray that increases the splendor of the one adds another refusal and another outline to the blasphemy of the other … The Christian always has to force a path for himself, crucifix in hand, through the coils and jaws of the two beasts: the beast of the land, which is temporal, and the beast of the sea, which is spiritual.”[^fn-p02-pdf05-n01]

Heart of Jesus, filled with reproach.

---

**8 September 1947**

Annette, the wise-foolish virgin.

Beethoven, then, is the French Revolution. But not only Robespierre. He is also Rousseau.

The *Pastoral Symphony* belongs to it too. Only that makes Beethoven so astonishingly complete. It is the first and only “landscape” in the sense of a secularized paradise. It still believes completely in landscape. This Rousseau-like effect in the *Pastoral* is even more important than Rousseau’s influence on Kant, Fichte, the young Hegel, Hölderlin, and Schiller.

---

**9 September 1947**

Again I am astonished by how closely my thinking is related to Hauriou’s.

Whoever says ceremony or formality is speaking of an action performed in one continuous stretch of time—and, I would add, in one particular place.

A ceremony belongs essentially to the present.

Once it has ended, it is difficult to imagine later additions being attached to it. That is the problem of the irrevocability of an act of state. This is also the unity of place, time, and action, especially in the jurist Corneille.

Play: Act <…>

Or Hauriou: territory helps provide us with the idea of what is public.

Or: law is a general provision.

Or his recognition of “prior obedience.”

Or his remarks on the imperative character of law.

And so on, and so on.

In this man I recognize my elder brother. What happiness there is in meetings and recognitions of this kind.

How can legality survive as a system once nobody can any longer believe in the rationality of the *législateur*, the lawgiver?

Once nobody can even believe in his honest intention to remain impartial? We must recognize the connection between legality, rationality, and political neutrality between parties. It is already there in Bodin, *Republic*, p. 636, and elsewhere.

---

**10 September 1947**

From Cardinal Passionei’s opinion of 1753, written for Benedict XIV on the question of the canonization of Cardinal Robert Bellarmine.

The issue concerns Bellarmine’s autobiography “from faith,” which he wrote in 1613, at the age of seventy-one, at the request of a friend.

May a person write his own life?

May he keep a diary intended to be read by other people?

Answer: a Christian may not do so because of the duty of *humilitas*—humility. He may do it only on the order of a Church superior or confessor, through divine inspiration, or because he is forced to defend himself.

In his *Confessions*, Augustine spoke only of things that counted against him.

Faced with this objection, some defenders of Bellarmine tried to dismiss his autobiography as something insignificant: a *relatiuncula*, a *scriptiuncula*, a *breviculum*, a *notila*— a tiny report, a little piece of writing, a brief note.

Others say: writing one’s own life is morally neutral in itself. One might even do it out of humility.

Passionei answers: it is at the very least an *occasio proxima*, a near occasion, of the most dangerous sin of all: self-love and pride. And because these are sins of the spirit, they are more dangerous than lust.

“Our deeds are our beloved daughters, our all-too-beautiful wives, to whom we are drawn again and again, whose beauty we gaze upon with self-satisfaction, like Lucifer and our father Adam.”

Occupying oneself with one’s own autobiography is therefore just as much an occasion for sin as, for a young man, spending time with a young, beautiful, all-too-lovable woman whom he passionately wishes to be alone with and with whom he wants to speak freely and intimately.[^fn-p02-pdf06-n01]

What a pity I could never show that to Franz Blei. But perhaps he already knew it.

<…>[^fn-p02-pdf06-n02]

---

**13 September 1947**

In Siedlinghausen: barred from fire and water.

Exiled.

**18 September 1947**[^fn-p02-pdf06-n03]

Yesterday Paul Adams discovered the church in Plettenberg.

The magnificent little towers and stones, seen through Knappe’s eyes.

A longing to fetch young Rikus and show it to him.

The Affeln type of gable.

The hand of the Mother of God.

Everything that is due to you comes to you.

What is meant for you really does reach you: every book, every piece of bread, every apple, every human being.

Woe to you if something comes to you that is **not** due to you.

The hand of the Mother of God on the Romanesque tympanum of the church at Affeln: is that hand meant to come to me?

Annette, moderately corrected by Clemens Möllenbrock.

Donoso Cortés, moderately corrected by Father Westemeyer.

There you have the contemporary Catholic revival!

Who are you, you bearers of measure, you carriers of yardsticks? And what is the meaning of what you are doing?

<…>

Reading Otto Veit’s book *The Flight from Freedom*.

Still nothing but criticism of the age.

Still very far from eternity!

Memories of Walther Rathenau and the years 1912–14.

Is this “flight from freedom” a parallel case?

What a strange sameness.

Identity.

Repetition.

The return of the same, even to you yourself, who still remain the same person.

Or is this merely a consequence of my surrendering myself to the past during this stay in Plettenberg?

Leitmotif: the unchangeability of fate and character.[^fn-p02-pdf06-n04]

I am very attracted by the “paradisal little cabinet of inwardness,” Sailer’s phrase emphasized by Karl Eschweiler.

Konrad Weiß, when Karl Caspar accused him of being subordinate:

“I rather like being subordinate.”

The materialist view of the world: the world as an institution for satisfying needs.

---

**19 September 1947**

Conceptual connections: the absolute character of private property
= equality of property, rather than gradations of property
= universal bourgeois equality
= equal freedom. This suddenly became completely clear to me. I wanted to write it down. But in my haste I wrote only:

“enormous insight.” And then I forgot what the insight actually was.

A side effect of realizing how important it seemed.

---

**20 September 1947**

Accompanied <Arnold Schmitz> to Finnentrop and back.

Ivo de Vento, from the school of Josquin des Prés in the sixteenth century, speaks of the *riservata*: musical figures noticed and understood only by those who know what to listen for.

Adrian Petit Coclicus speaks of the same thing.

Kurt Huber wrote his dissertation on this.

Today the whole science of international law and all constitutional law have become *riservata*: reserved knowledge, taboo knowledge.

For example: the total state means total responsibility, as I wrote in my essay on taboo. Or the dialectical relationship between soldier and citizen once war becomes total.

John Quincy Adams, according to Albert Gallatin: a neutral government is one “that recognizes the cause of both parties in a dispute as just—that is, avoids any consideration of the actual subject of the dispute.”

Quoted in Thorsten V. Kalijari, *Europäische Revue*, 1935.

There is an essential connection between the Monroe Doctrine and this concept of neutrality.

Hitler’s stupidity: not merely beginning a discriminatory war against the East, but above all the contradiction in his own position.

In the case of Locarno, in 1936, he had said that an alliance with the Soviet Union would destroy the Locarno Treaty.

Entirely correct.

Any contact with the Soviet Union had an explosive effect.

But if that is so, when in 1941 he attacks the Soviet Union and covers it with war, is that somehow **not** supposed to have an explosive effect on the whole world?

Again: the essential connection between the Monroe Doctrine and this concept of neutrality!

---

**21 September 1947**

Wyndham Lewis called his magazine, which he had published since 1927, *The Enemy*. Yet he did not draw upon himself the kind of hostility that such a title might have been expected to provoke.[^fn-p02-pdf07-n01]

Why? Because in England everything is taken less seriously.

Everything is still padded and cushioned.

Even dissatisfaction with this cushioning is itself cushioned.

Lewis does not merely want to understand. He wants to be conscious and fair, if only to avoid ending up in a muddle.

His difference from the spirit of the age.

The Heraclitean injustice of opposites.

I encountered Wyndham Lewis through an essay by Hans Hennecke in the *Europäische Revue*, March 1938.

Lewis published a book on Hitler in 1931.

A German translation appeared in 1932 with R. Hobbing.

A kindred spirit here?

“I intend, to the best of my ability, to reshape or destroy.”

I direct my attention exclusively to the things that matter most to me, and so on.

Plastic and static, in *Time and Western Man*, 1928.

Vorticism—from *vortex*.

Change?

Ed. Rosenbaum drew my attention to him in 1926. And now Rosenbaum has reappeared too. He has nothing good to say about me.

Full of hatred and resentment. But that makes no difference.

“I do not know that I did well, but I did honestly.”

Grey.

My most personal right of all—a right genuinely earned through my own experiences, sufferings, and discoveries—is my right to *riservata* and *arcana*: to things reserved to myself, to secrets. That matters far more to me than any right to political error.

To be violated in this respect is a far greater injustice than suffering some political failure—in other words, ending up on the losing side during one of the shifts in fortune that occur in civil war.

Mythologization through mass society appears most directly, of course, in a word and concept such as “enemy.”

The German word *Feind* is phonetically much more dangerous than *enemy* or *foe*. It suggests something sharper, something decisively cut.

A kind of decisionism.

Every acted performance in a film is depressing and insulting to me. I am supposed to have something performed for me that is not actually present. It has merely been photographed. I am not dealing with human beings who are there in front of me. The performance is not produced in my presence. It is mechanically reproduced.

Even the worst puppet theatre is more than the best film. There is neither presence nor representation.

Terrifying.

Horrible.

Destructive of soul, eyes, and ears.

Without space.

It even abolishes the spectator, who can no longer meaningfully applaud.

The cave-dwellers of the cinema: an expression of their already subterranean form of existence.

Space = presence. This is the thought that has made it impossible for me, for the past ten years, to enter a cinema and watch a feature film.

In this way I remove myself from the reality of my own age. I lose my time and gain my space.

<…>

My present.

I lose my time and gain my space.

---

**22 September 1947**

The “ground” of our being is our body in all its complicated functioning. Just as the “ground” of the sound of a violin is the friction and vibration of sheep gut or catgut, horsehair bow, and a box made of spruce, maple, and ebony. Or the ground is an irritation, like a wound.

Pan sinks away.

I am.

A single tone holds me.

Or else:

Pan appears, and one dissonance turns me into nothing.

Only one thing I inherited: my own body. While living, I consume it.

---

**23 September 1947**

Keywords for you:

Unreal
(Frau K. Weiss)

Desert Fox
(Podszus)

Mannered
(Joh. P.[opitz])

Antique
(Rud. Sm.[end])

I hear: ambivalence, antinomy, aporia, and I already know what all of them mean, because at the same time I hear: dead end, tritone.

I hear: criticism, critical, and I already know and hear: crisis, crisis.

I hear: primordial slime, and I see the whole nineteenth century from 1848 to 1948.

There is a universe and there is a pluriverse. But there is no duo-ambiverse.

The number two is infamous.

Whoever says ambivalence, antinomy, or aporia has already said nuclear fission. And that means civil war. And that means friend and enemy.

I have always spoken and written only as a jurist. As a result, I have really spoken only to jurists and for jurists.

My misfortune was that the jurists of my age had turned into positivist technicians for handling statutes. They were profoundly ignorant and uncultivated.

At best they were followers of Goethe and neutralized humanitarians. So the non-jurists who were listening in could leap upon every word and every formulation and tear me apart as a “Desert Fox.”

---

**24 September 1947**

Conceptual realism as the necessary basis of jurisprudence.

Letter to Otto Veit.

(In truth, then: flight from freedom into technology.

Compare 21 April 1948.)

---

**25 September 1947**

Peter F. Drucker, *The End of Economic Man* (1939):

“To the extent that the problem of self-assertion and self-justification becomes more and more urgent, totalitarianism must invent new personifications of new demons. In comparison with the Jews, even the communists are of doubtful value as demonic enemies.”[^fn-p02-pdf09-n01]

Because Jews always remain Jews.

A communist, by contrast, can improve himself and change. This has nothing to do with Nordic race and so on. It is precisely the assimilated Jew who is the real enemy. There is no point proving the story of the Elders of Zion false. There is a compulsion to find a total enemy.

But there must be only **one** total enemy, not two: not East and West at once, not Russians and Anglo-Saxons at once, not communists and capitalists at once.

<…>

---

**26 September 1947**

Back then, in the years 1933–36, I compromised myself and the dignity of my ideas less than Plato compromised himself and his ideas through his journeys to Sicily.

Bernanos, in *France Against the Robots* (1947), writes about machine civilization: it “exploits the selfless work of the scholar and today is less inclined than ever to entrust him with even the smallest share in its authority to teach.”

The problem of *pouvoir spirituel*: spiritual authority.

The situation: where you have no power, desire nothing. Therefore: the isolated individual.

Retreat.

The wise man as the *kechōrismenos*—the one set apart. But Heraclitus does not say:

*outopos*—nowhere.

---

**27 September 1947**

Memory of Fritz Eisler. At Christmas 1913 I wrote to him from Cologne. He understood: the time is ripe for dictatorship.

The identity of our space even while time changes. This space has remained the same since 1907. There are no essential changes or transformations.

All of that is only time and the illusion that comes with time.

Everything essential remains unchangeable and unchanged and reappears at regular intervals.

Development.

Progress.

Process.

All of them merely illusions of time. Only the costume worn by time changes.

Is it the living garment of divinity? Or the dry rustling leaves of dead gods?

Time and sea.

Space and land.

Space and land lie there complete, like the score of a symphony that is performed at one time and then not performed again for years. That is how I grasp you: eternal presence.

On Gerhard Nebel, *Plato and the Polis*—which stands far above Werner Jaeger’s *Paideia*:

1. **State.**

He calls the polis a state. But the state is an even more unique, concrete, historically limited form.

Indeed, it is more so precisely because its form has been sharpened by historical and dialectical development. It belongs to the period from the sixteenth to the twentieth century of the Christian age and is tied to those four centuries. It therefore makes no sense to speak of a medieval “state.”

The state emerged from the Renaissance, Humanism, the Reformation, and the Counter-Reformation. It is the neutralization of religious civil war. It is therefore a very specific achievement of Western rationalism.

To call the polis a state is like going in the other direction and calling belief in Zeus and the other gods a “state religion.”

The state is essentially the product of religious civil war.

More precisely, it comes from the overcoming of that civil war through the neutralization and secularization of the confessional battle lines. That means de-theologization.[^fn-p02-pdf10-n01]

See pp. 13, 21, 31, 36, 39, 54.

The state creates the opposition between inward and outward. It creates the separation between internal and external.

All of this is essential to the state and completely alien to the polis.

Let us not be careless with words.

Truth is in the Word of God.

De-theologization means: turning things into law, into metaphysics, into philosophy. But not yet turning them into positivism and technology. It is still the realm of objective reason, and so on.

Not even Rome was a polis.

See p. 22.

*Civitas* + *res publica* is something fundamentally different!

The Roman <genius> stayed with the individual case and avoided law in the sense of a <rule of grace>.[^fn-p02-pdf10-n02]

2. **Nomos – law: constitution.**

On p. 16.

Very fine, p. 17: the soul being walled into the structure of the polis.

Heraclitus: the *nomos* is a space.

The four constitutional oaths sworn by German civil servants, however, are nothing compared with the twelve such oaths sworn by French civil servants after 1830.

And then there is the French answer supposedly given by a French dignitary when someone reproached him with having sworn a dozen of them:

“Oaths are there to be sworn.”

Page 74: the Greek genius did not seek the individual case but the law. But this was no Enabling Act.

Life-time does not produce the anxiety that living-space produces.

Why? Because death is already contained within life-time as its boundary.

*Survivre*: to survive.

Mme Guyon says the same. I see nothing but the will to survive. So this, then, is the Overman: the man who wants to outlive.

Nothing else remains.

Whom does he outlive?

The competitors in the struggle against the threat to life?

Those threatened along with him?

Or those doing the threatening?

Naturally, if possible, all of them.

But perhaps only his fellow-threatened.

What does he survive?

The threat to life.

They want nothing more than this: to survive.

All of it confirms the picture Hobbes drew once and for all in order to find the starting point from which political unity could be constructed. But it also confirms the most vicious biologism.

The path of spirit is the detour.

Hegel.

Distance.

<Separation.>

Mediation.

The result of every human work.

My path from Berlin through Nuremberg to Plettenberg.

---

**28 September 1947**

Freedom from want. So that means: freedom from lack.

Freedom from Christ.

The fixed and unchangeable character of species: the fixed character of the social order and of social ranks.

Unlimited possibilities of development: the dissolution of social ranks and universal massification.

Darwinism as the scientific myth of the nineteenth century. That is why Hitler’s people had to be Darwinists despite all their myths of nobility and their programs for elites.

The human sciences must have priority over the natural sciences. Only then does a *pouvoir spirituel*, a spiritual authority, become possible. And only then can unleashed technology be domesticated.

Otto Veit seems to be missing only two problems:

1. The logical consistency of the ruler of the world in planning and technology, myth and mass society.

Compare what I said above about Shotwell.

In particular: the logic of planning a reduction of the masses through birth control— “the birth rate will decrease until the standard becomes maintainable.”

2. The logic of political mythology:

the enemy manufactured by the ruler of the world as a mass myth.

The self-correction of industrialization.

Freedom for what?

For the creation of paradise!

Naturally, only for the survivors! Therefore: the struggle for survival becomes more intense the closer paradise comes.

Forward, to the final battle!

---

**29 September 1947**

I discovered in Donoso Cortés, in a letter of 1851 to the Queen Mother Maria Cristina, the sentence:

“Today only saints can save nations.” That is Kierkegaard’s sentence about martyrs. He too rises above the juridical plane.

The *Heraldo* analogous to Kierkegaard’s <…>. Or, as Kierkegaard calls himself, the “enemy of the public.” And his despair as well.[^fn-p02-pdf11-n01]

“I await the Flood and laugh at fools.”

“Distance is necessary for perspective.”

(<Courage> too is seen by us more clearly in perspective.)

“As far as law is concerned, I believe that human law does not exist and that there is no law except divine law.”

All right belongs to God.

To man belongs only duty.

Letter to the editor of the *Heraldo*, Paris, 15 April 1852.

Terribly sad that decent men such as Westemeyer and Möllenbrock can pass by the work and the great creations of Catholic Christians so blindly, acting as censors. They would never have dared to do this with Kierkegaard.

Why do they dare it with Catholic authors?

The old force still pours unchanged from Donoso. He is one of my guardian angels.

His enemies, God says, are my enemies.

Astonishing, in his letter to the editor of *El Orden*, Paris, 10 June 1851:

“The I is satanic by nature and unsociable by character. In Hell there is no pronoun except ‘I.’”[^fn-p02-pdf11-n02] That would make a beautiful illustration for Stirner’s *The Ego and Its Own*. I already knew this unconsciously in 1908. But between 1905 and 1907 it was confused by the philosophy of the “I” inherited from the German educational tradition and by Kluxen’s boasting. That is also why Stirner impressed me back then: as the swaggerer of the I, the boor of the I, the consistently nihilistic I.

A figure that could probably exist with such journeyman-like consistency only in the vacuum of German Idealism, forever positing and dissolving itself;

only on the soil of the failed Germanization of the East;

and only between 1840 and 1848.

Lortzing’s opera *The Poacher* belongs there too.

At bottom it is always ironic.

Ironic and witty in the same way that everything merely restorative is ironic and witty—for example Rossini’s operas.

Lortzing, the friend of Glaßbrenner.

Berlin wit.

A streak of sentimentality.

The whole Restoration dissolving itself from within.

Biedermeier as a mask of feeling placed over nihilism.

Lortzing’s *The Poacher* is just as clear a symptom and even a document of Berlin and Prussia as Offenbach’s *La Belle Hélène* and *Orpheus* were of Paris and France.[^fn-p02-pdf12-n01]

---

**30 September 1947**

The elite of the drivers.

The chauffeurs.

The motorists.

*Fahrer*, not *Führer*: drivers, not leaders.

Ernst Jünger’s Worker: eyes shut and step on the gas.

Today the man in the street is the chauffeur.

The others walk on the pavements, where pavements still exist, as a concession granted by traffic police.

The man in the street is the master of the street. That is modern democracy.

---

**1 October 1947**

Again and again, Donoso. He says that he neither polemicizes nor argues.

“The word is a seed. I throw it into the wind and leave it to God to decide whether it falls on barren rock or fertile soil.”

Or:

“Freedom is absent from the earth.”

Wonderful on the Middle Ages:

“To be king was neither to reign nor to govern. It meant simply and purely to receive homage.”

In England.

The Crown: the symbol and emblem of the nation.

Astonishing: the last reforms of 1831 brought England a continental form of parliamentarism.

“At the very moment when England was convinced that it had conquered us through its institutions.”

Again and again: the hard and unchangeable fate that has existed since 1789.[^fn-p02-pdf12-n02]

The Constitution of the United States is a symbol from the age before 1789.

Strange.

The terrible, paralyzing feeling that every human effort is useless and meaningless, while all the feverish activity itself forms part of that meaninglessness.

People would beat this man to death like a dangerous dog if they understood what he thinks about them—and what he even says and writes down about them.

What draws me to this desperate man? What holds me to him?

To Kierkegaard?

To Pascal?

To poor Bruno Bauer, surrounded by the rubble of academic fraud?

I found great pleasure in an interesting task: comparing the picture of France between 1848 and 1851 drawn by Donoso with the picture drawn by Karl Marx.

---

**2 October 1947**

Very struck by H. Blüher’s *Erhebung*, especially the remarks on the king. But there is something deliberate in the tone.

A conscious, polemically Protestant effort to distance himself.

Even a kind of swagger.

Very different from Donoso’s desperate and involuntary theological intensifications.

But Donoso too still knows what a crown means, even though he does not clearly distinguish dynastic legitimacy.

Also this formulation, spoken by a Bavarian after the first judgment of the new Bavarian Constitutional Court in the Haußleiter matter: they had “taken the legal path of juridical instinctlessness.”

Nothing is as touching as Machiavellianism turned into a doctrine.

Surely the very thing that people condemn as “Machiavellianism” ought, above all, to avoid producing doctrines of this kind.

Every person thinks himself infallible and behaves as though he were. But to **proclaim a doctrine of infallibility** raises the matter to a completely different level.

One would think.

“Everything must be dared.”

That is Platonic.

“Noble is the danger.”

Seneca’s:

“he always obeys, having commanded once.”

The lawgiver bound by his own law. He may take comfort from the fact that his law is often more intelligent than he is.

Carl Schmitt: the one compelled.

The man of blind prior commands.

---

**3 October 1947**

My sympathy for two outstanding canon lawyers, Teodoro Andrés Marcos and Hans Barion, reveals the whole unhappy incompleteness of my position between theologians and lawyers of secular law. There are no better lawyers than us. But we are crushed between theology and technology. Those two canon lawyers are jurists of theology. I am a theologian of jurisprudence.

The result is failure in an age of massive secularity, cast-iron concepts, and the most delicate and cautious forms of indirect power.

Sohm’s historically conditioned errors: customary law serves the strong; statutory law protects the weak.

A touching Rousseau-like faith in the lawgiver, the *législateur*.

“He commands once and then always obeys.”

Today everyone knows: the strong person makes the law into his weapon against any possible attempt by the weak to become strong.

(And freer still are the sources!)

Today: faith in law = the lack of instinct found in living creatures doomed to extinction.

Hitler’s method of oaths to legality turns the formula around:

“He obeys once and then always commands.”

The *législateur* and dictatorship.

Law is dictation.

First a dictate of reason. Then of will. Then of desire.

Every law is a dictate.

Like Hindemith, who makes melodies and harmonies from the material of tonal possibilities, I make my positions and concepts from the material of the primal institutions of law.

The only difference is this: I first have to shape my own material.

As jurists, we have not even reached the level of mensural notation, much less the level of musical scores.

Perhaps constitutional law is the **material** of jurisprudence, not statute law.

Object and material.[^fn-p02-pdf13-n01]

How is it that all these excited detractors—Radbruch, Schwinge, and the others—cannot see that their outrage against me is intellectually identical with Hitler’s rage against “degenerate art”?

Brother Straubinger was simply too ignorant to notice me. That was precisely why I could and was permitted to involve myself with him.

So the German state constitutions of 1946/47 are based on an “exchange of intellectual values” with the United States.

All that is missing now is a cultural agreement in the style of the German-Slovak exchange.

And what, then, is my *Constitutional Theory* of 1928 based on?

Comfort in Annette’s suffering.

A Klemens Möllenbrock, of course, establishes: lack of virginity, lack of *ordo*, ideological emergency exits, and so on.

“Redeeming human liberation was never granted to her.”

What is that supposed to mean?

Redeeming, human liberation?

The disciplinarian concludes:

Droste never reached, on any point, a worldview “superior to her age.”

Wisely, he puts “superior to her age” in quotation marks.

A worldview—certainly not. He himself is not quite so “superior to his age” either.

“Droste belonged neither to the pious people who can no longer see the earth, nor was she bindingly”—*sic*—“bound to earthly existence.”

Listen to the Headmaster.

How sad all of this is.

All I can say to you is:

“only the pilgrim will bless her,”

you stern Klemens.

But all of us will hide from you when you appear with your *baculus*, your staff.[^fn-p02-pdf14-n01]

I am in the position of Ginés de Sepúlveda.

The others are cleverer.

Go where people respond well to you.

Listen to the response.

Do that instead of following the inner compulsion of your own thought.

I was one compelled by thought rather than one who listened for applause.

Sepúlveda’s *Democrates alter*, written in 1547, was not printed until 1892.

For that long, the reviewers employed by those supposedly gentle and tolerant humanitarians managed to keep him silent.

---

**4 October 1947**

So:

I am I.

I alone.

He would have to add: and only at this moment.

Only *hic et nunc*.

Here and now.

Without any guarantee, because a guarantee would bind me.

Always free to change my position.

Yes. That is what he is: the free man who always remains uncommitted.

A cheerfully crowing I, not one that gnashes its teeth. It does not regard itself as hateful in the least.

At most, it would feel flattered if someone called it “satanic.”

What a devil of a fellow!

Irrefutable, you know.

Demonic. What people used to call genius.

Both concepts equally stupid.

Are you really going to envy him his irrefutability? Or his certainty? Or his inability to develop?

What will become of my great theme:

“Francisco de Vitoria and the De-theologization of International Law”?

Could my encounter with Don Teodoro Andrés have been meaningless and fruitless?

Be still.

Remain even now: without willing it, simply faithful.

The great view opening onto a Marian *empresa*: the greatest historical undertaking since the Middle Ages.

Of my three names, I will probably have to surrender the third [correctly: first], Konrad Weiß, to those who possess a better personal claim to him;

the second, Bruno Bauer, to those with a better material knowledge of him;

and the third, Vitoria, to those more securely situated in the tradition.

And so I stand here: naked and bare as at birth, seeing and feeling that Being itself is all I possess.

---

**Sunday, 5 October 1947, Plettenberg**

Look up what Klemens M.[öllenbrock] says about Annette’s poem on the Trinity!

Does he quote the line from the twenty-first Sunday <before> Pentecost:

“My hand was still permitted to touch the Cross”?

I have no light. That means: I do not belong to the world of German Idealism.

Only a voice.

Delight in Cardinal Melchior de Polignac’s *Anti-Lucretius*, printed in 1754.

In the preface there is already the couplet that supplied the feathers with which Franklin was later adorned, and which glorifies Epicurus:

“Assailing the thunderous temples of heaven,
he snatched the thunderbolt from Jove and the arrows from Phoebus.”

In Books II and III there are delightful hexameters about atoms and infinity.

Especially beautiful are these lines on eternal recurrence, pp. 95–96:

“Nor does it help to imagine countless worlds elsewhere,
where an unlimited abundance of every kind of thing
bursts forth without measure, while our own world receives so little …

Atoms must have a measure, a limit, and a bridle.”

I want to send that last line to Heisenberg or Pascual Jordan.

---

**6 October 1947**

I walk around this landscape of the Lenne valley.

If landscape is an *état d’âme*, a state of the soul, then I am apparently walking around inside myself.

Inside the memories of my youth, and so on. This is obviously even more dangerous than having conversations with oneself. It is an *occasio proxima*, a near occasion, for every sin of subjectivism, egotism, and armoring the self. It is a self-created paradise in which I play both the part of God the Creator and the part of Adam.

The cultivated person walks through a landscape carrying quotations from poets and philosophers, memories of classical or Romantic paintings, Impressionist or Expressionist paintings.

In short: he walks through the landscape as though he were walking through a library and an art gallery. He enjoys his education. That means: he enjoys his own enlarged self.

Surely belief in law is really belief in the lawgiver.

In Michelet’s *Pologne et Russie* of 1852 this belief is almost touching.

Humanity no longer has a father as the source of authority.

Law has taken the father’s place.

Patriarchally.

That is why the crisis of legality is more than just another temporary difficulty.

According to Michelet, the geographical boundary of this new faith is: the Vistula!

Deeply moved by Kütemeyer’s afterword to Kierkegaard’s *The Concept of Irony*. He writes in the same annihilatingly polemical tone as Theodor Haecker.

It frightens me.

And in Haecker’s own style he destroys poor Theodor Haecker because Haecker quoted one of Kierkegaard’s pseudonyms as though it were Kierkegaard himself.

Sacrilege.

Forgery.

The truly rabid ones fighting among themselves.

“He will not escape his fate.”

Poor Haecker has already been overtaken by his.

Today his *Satire and Polemic* of 1926/27 has to be carefully kept quiet by his admirers.

Haecker’s false reputation has been grafted onto this wild shoot.

But what about Kütemeyer himself?

Wilhelm, the destroyer of the destroyer? And his own transformation?

The completely solitary man as holder of License No. 32.

Bravo.

He will not escape his fate.

He will **not**!

Judge not, that you be not judged.

Then another beautiful expression:

“from printer’s ink scattered by the wind.” Now it comes back to confront me. Now it is thrown into my eyes.

Invitation from G. Nebel.

Delighted.

But again and again: hide your life and spread your spirit.

Annette writes to Sprickmann, Cardauns, *Letters*, p. 9:

Your dear image “always remains a pure, quiet ground on which I can paint whatever I wish.”

Klemens M.[öllenbrock], p. 70, quotes this as an example of how the object is transformed into an *occasio*, an occasion. But Annette says **ground**. How profound that word is in her. And how un-Romantic.

As with Konrad Weiß.

---

**7 October 1947**

Deeply frightened by the real irony contained in the fact that a thick book about the concept of irony is lying in my room.

Irony is so actively destructive that merely naming it determines the whole atmosphere.[^fn-p02-pdf16-n01]

Perhaps the same is true of every concept and every word. That is conceptual realism.

Deeply frightened.

Deeply shaken.

To be the victim of the irony of world history, the irony of fate—that is unbearable.

Unbearable even as a hypothetical possibility.

Even as a danger or a risk.

God is easy to deceive. But God cannot deceive.

God cannot become ironic either.

The Hegelian Spirit can.

In fact, that is almost what it always is.

Were you deception, you blessed silver-blue day? Or, worse still: were you irony?

Because when the strong practice irony upon the weak, irony becomes the most terrible form of cruelty.

Devilishness.

A haunting from Hell.

Madness.

There is something almost animal-like in the matter-of-fact way Hegel knows himself to be identical with the subject of the “irony of history.” He shows no fear when speaking of such things.

So does Hegel too belong to that little nation of people who never sense the Devil?

Descartes’ deepest motive, the final thing driving him, was fear of the *spiritus malignus*: fear of the abyss contained in the possibility of ironic deception.

I have a sin to confess.

At the end of August 1946, in the despair of the camp, early one morning as the first rays of sunlight fell across my bunk, I spoke aloud to the sun and said:

You deceiver.

That was terrible.

Like the statement Kierkegaard’s father once made about God.

Since then my external circumstances have improved, and the worst mistreatment has stopped.

Is all of this, then, deception?

A desperate entanglement in the labyrinth of negations.

The deadly rebound of this ugly stone once one has thrown it.

What remains once a person has allowed himself to enter the realm of irony?

I stand there like a ghost and scream without a throat. And yet I myself made practical use of the most intense irony.

The ironic superiority of the person who knows over Papageno or Caliban.

The Greek over the barbarian.

Good-naturedly.

With exaggerated kindness.

Expecting far too much hidden goodness from them.[^fn-p02-pdf16-n02]

In doing this I committed an injustice for which Kierkegaard too felt guilty:

I placed Caliban in a test that was bound to drive him deeper into wickedness as soon as he sensed my irony.

My irony inflamed his hatred. And he attributed that irony to the cause he believed I represented:

Catholicism and Christianity.

Stirner’s irrefutability lies in the fact that a single empirical I knows how to use the weapon of irony consistently.

In an age built around the philosophy of the I, this I stands beyond every attack.

*Ego cogito, ergo ego sum.* I think, therefore I am.

*Sum, sum, sum*—little bee, buzz around.

The infinite ambiguity of the word “I” gives it an infinite number of ironic hiding places and possibilities for attack.

I am I.

I alone. And therefore **I** define, interpret, and illustrate Myself and tolerate no intervention from forces foreign to the I.

At one moment I am the intelligible I.

At another I am the empirical I. Who is going to tell me I cannot? I, the lout, affirm myself as the lout I am. But ironically.

The most shameless insult ever inflicted upon God and man, an insult that would justify every curse of the synagogue, lies in the *sive* of the formula:

*Deus sive Natura.*

God, or Nature.

Our Stirner does not do that. He does not say: I, or God. Or perhaps he does. But he does it loutishly, not deceitfully.

---

**8 October 1947**

Disgusting aftertaste from Däubler’s *Africana*.

As though one had wandered into a cheap cabaret led by a five-penny d’Annunzio. So he really does belong to the horrifying milieu in which I was trapped between 1912 and 1919. And I too was apparently good enough to be worked into the mixture.

Kluxen recognized him for what he was and immediately noticed the similarity between Däubler’s own existence and that of his African heroine. I was too naive.

Too much “from the country.”

Strange how Däubler was replaced by Haecker and Konrad Weiß. But all three of them—Däubler, Haecker, Weiß—were professional journalists. So this is what the figures of today’s *pouvoir spirituel*, spiritual authority, actually look like in concrete reality.

The sociology of intellectuals in the age of capitalism.

Second disillusionment of yesterday: the photograph of G. Bernanos in *Le Figaro*, July 1939. So he too has firmly established himself as a professional man of letters.

A very fine gentleman as well.

Extremely serious.

Authentic Oberammergau in the Hollywood of the Coop. Int. Int.

The devastating feeling of having been deceived.

No longer even capable of using irony as a form of self-defense.

Defeated?

Oh no.

Destroyed and trampled underfoot.

The defeated man in someone else’s just war.

How horrifying are Maritain’s whorish enticements in *Humanisme intégral* (1936):

“The theologians and moralists explain to us under what conditions the physical means of war are just. It is not their task to open new doors to violence.”

But, Monsieur Maritain, that is their **effect**!

“Once the doors have been opened, however, they justify whatever can be justified.”

Yes indeed. That is exactly what it says on p. 262.

Apparently it is not their task to **close** the doors to violence either. They justify whatever can be justified.

The doctrine of the just war is exceptionally well suited to this. It already did the same thing regarding long-range crossbows and projectiles at the Second Lateran Council in 1139.

And today it does the same thing regarding the atomic bomb and the other new means of annihilation.

The just war means: the enemy is stripped of his rights, while the just side authorizes itself to do what is necessary.

The result is the transformation of war between states—that is, war governed by international law—into a war that is colonial war and civil war at the same time. This is logical and irrefutable.

War becomes world civil war. It stops being war between states.

(I am suffocating beneath the fraud of the ideology of world civil war.

Does no human ear hear my voice?)

Poor dispenser of justice that you are.

---

**9 October 1947**

The poor Germans today are really the orphans of Leviathan.

All I can still do is pray:

Lord, deliver me.

Break my chains.

Lead me back to my father,

to my homeland,

to my house,

to my inheritance.

Let what belongs to me be returned to me,

so that You may be glorified in Your justice.

Whoever ruined his longing for some good of this world …

We Germans are being pushed *beyond the line*.

Into a perfect beyond.

Driven out of the world.

Into the condition of the peaceless and outlawed.

*Peripsēma*: the refuse.

The disinherited of Leviathan. Those whom Leviathan has spat out. We, who possess the great possibility of advancing from the relative beyond into which we are being pushed toward the absolute beyond: the overcoming of the world itself.

---

**10 October 1947**

“Stricter than art” are “the measures and proportions of concrete law.”

This belongs with the Hölderlin quotation in *The Three Types of Juristic Thought*, p. 17.

So: be careful.
