(Dix called my memorandum from the summer of 1945 “a seminar exercise in international law.”)

---

**25 April 1948**

The point at which the entire logic of objective power relations became choked together with the completely subjective opinions of an individual who happened to possess power.

Stalin: world revolution in Germany.

Hitler: attack on allied Russia.

---

**26 April 1948**

On the question of whether the word “state” should be used as a universal concept that applies across every historical age, Heinrich Weinstock wrote to me that it was right to resist “turning history into mush.”

“On the other hand, you will probably not succeed in abolishing the word ‘state’ as the now customary name for a ‘political association,’ whatever its structure may be.”[^fn-p06-pdf15-n01]

That phrase—“you will probably not succeed”—hit me very hard.

I found it arrogant and irritating. It gives the impression that W. feels entitled to dismiss the whole point of the dispute from some lofty position. He fails to see that we are not dependent on the word “state” in order to have the general term we need.

I never said that general concepts which remove things from their historical setting are impossible or always illegitimate. That would simply be another false generalization.

I say only that such generalizations, though possible, legitimate, and necessary, belong to particular historical periods, and that a word is capable of becoming a valid universal term only within a specific age. For the word “state,” that age is over.

What was the secret—the *arcanum*—of the word “state”?

Its connection with *ratio*.

With *ratio status*: reason of state.

All the qualities of the impartial third party—or, in Hegelian language, of objective reason—that were historically connected with the state during this period disappeared once the totality of the state could become an instrument of the totality of a party. And once that happened, the word also lost its logical capacity to serve as a genuine universal concept.

---

**27 April 1948**

Infinitely important, Gregory the Great, quoted by G. Krauss:

“It must be understood that Satan’s will is always unjust, but his power is never unjust, because his will comes from himself, while his power comes from the Lord.”[^fn-p06-pdf15-n02]

So even Satan’s power, as power, comes from God and is not evil.

How did Burckhardt arrive at the opposite thesis?

The “will to power” would then be the good will!

Yes—provided it is divine power and the will submits itself to it.

There is only one evil will: the will to powerlessness. That is: the refusal to carry out what must be carried out.

Execution seen from that side.

An ethics of execution.

Home is the house.

The grave is part of the homeland.

What Peterson says about clothing applies equally to landscape: that fabric of memories, psychological coverings, institutional investitures, emotional pathways, and reserves that have accumulated there.

The fact that Kempski dares to quote Bruno Bauer—and through Barnikol at that—is merely a sign of the half-informed person who thinks he knows too quickly.

Nothing will change in Bruno Bauer’s isolation.

Since 1840, poor Bruno has been surrounded by an ever-thickening layer of mud made up of badly written essays and journalism, so that the essential core of his work cannot simply be recognized in passing.[^fn-p06-pdf15-n03] So far, everyone who thought he was in a position to comment on him has become stuck in the mud.

Bruno is a well-protected partisan.

First seizure of power: under Constantine, with the esoteric substance still well preserved.

Difficult after the second seizure of power, beginning with Gregory VII.

Still: scholasticism.

Today an entirely different problem: retreat from the remaining traces of *potestas*, actual governing power, into pure *auctoritas*, authority.

Hard and difficult to find the way back into the crypt.[^fn-p06-pdf16-n01]

Günther Krauss’s *Captiva Captivitas* is full of beautiful formulations:

“Our guilt would have become fatal to us only if we had won”—if we had built the atomic bomb and dropped it.

The sufferings of captivity are, after all, the surest protection against Pepysian self-indulgence.

Jünger never spent a single day in captivity.[^fn-p06-pdf16-n02]

---

**28 April 1948**

The fate of my little essay *The Concept of the Political* is already becoming part of the concept itself. That is the highest praise one can give the essay.

A sure sign of existential authenticity.[^fn-p06-pdf16-n03]

The essay identifies the criterion of the political in the distinction between friend and enemy. And look: the essay itself produces friendship and enmity. It proves that it has the power to arrange whatever encounters it into friends and enemies. It is not studied very much.

Often it is not even read.

Instead it is used, with the greatest intensity, as a criterion.

All of these are good signs.

“Throw me into the sea, if this storm arose because of me!”

The fate of Jonah.

In this respect too. And at this point.

Came across Hegel’s remark:

“Humanity needed gunpowder”—at that time, for the transition from feudalism to absolute monarchy—“and so, before long, gunpowder appeared.”

I put this at the end of a chapter from *The Nomos of the Earth*, on modern war of annihilation, and asked:

What did humanity need today when the modern means of annihilation appeared?

---

**30 April 1948**

Found in E. Jünger’s *The Adventurous Heart* the motto:

“The German’s occupation at this time is to drag material in from every corner of the world in order to feed the fire he has lit beneath his concepts.

So it is no wonder that everything capable of burning is now in flames.”

Compare my remark to Smend of 6 January 1948.

The poet who truly corresponds to this is not Rilke but Theodor Däubler.

To E. Rothacker:

The exclamation mark after *sive* in the brazen two-part construction

*Deus sive Natura!*

God or Nature! That exclamation mark helped me recognize whole libraries of neo-scholastic phrases about natural law, together with all their intellectual pieces written for two hands.

I am very susceptible to this kind of influence, and equally grateful for it. Then the conversation with Friedrich Meinecke about the treasure houses hidden in the astrological remarks of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century authors, above all my brother in fate Jean Bodin. But the minds of Meinecke’s period were too afraid for their reputation as proper scholars.

In the end they remained positivists, even—and especially—when they presented themselves as great scholars of the humanities.

Recently one finds remarkable astrological intuitions and productive uses of them in Gerhard Nebel’s reflections on the elements.

My little book *Land and Sea* was meant to be a step beyond the merely mythological and into the mythic itself.[^fn-p06-pdf17-n01] That is why, for example, the passage about the two hunters on p. 23 is an important corrective to the superficiality of many versions of the choice that otherwise threatens to cut us apart:

West or East.

The question of who, in the long run, will become the authentic successor of the German soldier of the East has not yet been answered.

---

**1 May 1948**

The third confirmation of my thesis about the “Disraelitism” of rabid Germanness—Hitler as a Disraelite.[^fn-p06-pdf17-n02]

First confirmation: race = key, etc.

Second:

Christianity = Judaism for the people.

Third:

“Our age is infinitely romantic.”

Disraeli, letter to Mrs Willyams of Torquay, 9 December 1862, quoted in Froude’s biography:

“How full of adventure life is!

It is monotonous only to monotonous people.

There may no longer be fiery dragons, magic rings, or fairy wands interfering with its course and shaping our careers. But relations between human beings are far more complicated and numerous than they were in the age of Jove.

And in the play of the passions, and in the inventions of creative spirits—which now have a correspondingly greater field in which to act—there are forms of social sorcery more powerful than all the necromancy of Merlin and Friar Bacon.”[^fn-p06-pdf17-n03]

That is Hitler’s:

“My life seems to me like a novel.”[^fn-p06-pdf17-n04]

Meaning: subjectivism, immoralities, and reversals of fortune.

(First confirmation: race = key, etc.

Second: Christianity = Judaism for the people.)

To Frau von S.[chnitzler]:

You know how deeply the “impatience of justice” torments me, and how immeasurable the responsibility that must grow from it.[^fn-p06-pdf17-n05]

I can no longer make things easy for myself.

Every day I am frightened by the weight of the knowledge expressed in an overwhelming sentence by Saint-Martin:

“To be certain that you yourself have been reborn, you must cause everything around you to be reborn.”

Back then, in the summer of 1945, I raised my helpless and feeble voice and was immediately silenced.[^fn-p06-pdf17-n06]

At that time, through my account of the criminalization of the enemy in international law and my distinction between enemy and criminal, I saved the honour of European legal scholarship.

Not only all of Germany but all of Europe had been struck senseless. Yet even in America no one could be found who spoke a word of calm or dignity.

In that great country, no voice could be heard except the demand for revenge.

No lawyer.

No diplomat.

No public thinker.

No one found the words of a victor who knew himself to be above the defeated.

Everywhere there was only the noise of *ira* and *iracundia*—anger and rage.

At other great historical moments, classical sayings and memories so often rise to the surface. This time there was no reflection and no sense of superiority.

No one had the composure needed to remember the ideas in the speech by the young Caesar recorded by Sallust. Those great and proud words of a great and proud man who later proved, as victor in wars between nations and in civil wars, that he knew how to remain free both from anger and revenge and from false pity.

At that time Caesar spoke in the Senate about what should be done with the captured criminals and Catilinarian conspirators. He said:

Precisely when facing monstrous crimes—*nefaria facinora*—one should think more about preserving one’s own dignity than about asking what the law allows one to do to captured criminals:

*magis quid se dignum foret, quam quid in illos iure fieri posset.*

Still less should one simply cast aside the law that had applied until then, the *lex Porcia*.[^fn-p06-pdf18-n01]

One must be careful not to let their crimes matter more to you than your own dignity:

*ne plus apud vos valeat illorum scelus quam vostra dignitas.*

Otherwise you begin to care more about satisfying your own anger than about your reputation and honour:

*ne magis irae vostrae quam famae consulatis.*

Punishment too must preserve dignity.

One does well to remain within punishments already provided for by law.

A great holder of power must not behave like a petty man in a rage.

What looks like righteous zeal and anger in small, vengeful people appears in a great man as arrogance and cruelty.

Should one invent a new kind of punishment—*genus poenae novum decernere*?

Especially in times of civil war, every act of revenge—even when people’s immediate sense of justice applauds it at first—grows into a terrible practice.

All of this is stated very clearly in that classical speech.

I ask everyone to read it in Sallust, *The Conspiracy of Catiline*, chapter 51. But in Germany in the summer of 1945, one could not even have alluded to it without becoming a victim of the prevailing hunger for revenge. That too belongs to the honour of my memorandum of August 1945.

Is it surprising that I am tormented by the impatience of justice when I remember it?

From Don Capisco’s Pocket Oracle for Mass-Psychology Situations:[^fn-p06-pdf18-n02]

1. If you find yourself inside a loudly shouting chorus, you must shout the words along with them as loudly as you can.

   Anything else will mean a certain and ugly death.

Your ears and brain will be smashed from the outside unless you defend yourself from within by shouting too. So I am recommending only a purely physical defence against this highly modern method of destruction by sound waves.[^fn-p06-pdf18-n03]

2. Do not let people sitting safely outside encourage you to resist from inside.

   Never forget the connection between protection and obedience.

3. Go into the shelter when the signal tells you to.

   Raise your hands when the order is given.

4. Never forget the connection between protection and obedience.

   But also never forget that the connection between protection and obedience is no longer valid today.

The shelter may turn out to be the gas chamber. So learn in time to recognize all the relevant signals. That is the situation of legality today.

5. Right is right only in the right place.

   Right is right only at the right time.[^fn-p06-pdf19-n01]

   Whoever is right a few years too early is simply wrong.

   Whoever throws light on something that is supposed to remain hidden is a traitor.

Whoever analyses the revolution is a reactionary. But whoever analyses the revolutionaries is a counterrevolutionary swine.

   Clear enough, my good Don Capisco.

6. Few people deserve to be contradicted.

   Good.

   Even fewer are worth openly resisting.

   Rarest of all are those before whom one can afford to give up every form of cover.

7. Definition of the elite:

   the elite are those whose sociology no one dares to write.

Further rule:

29 June 1948.

---

**4 May 1948**

New joy in my work so far on *The Nomos of the Earth*.

We in Germany have thought more, and more deeply, than people in other countries. For a moment I become conscious again of my own contribution to that thought.

What is all of this?[^fn-p06-pdf19-n02]

Defenceless, rich fruit of the years
still dawning somewhere in the future.[^fn-p06-pdf19-n03]

Understand the ruler who reaches for you.

Do not answer his grasping with counter-grasps on the same level.

Instead use his movements to test your own power of concepts. He will reach for your concepts too.

Let him. He will cut his paws on them.

---

**5 May 1948**

Sent Ernst Jünger, for his “collection of last words,” the note containing Chopin’s last words:

“Since this earth will suffocate me, I beg you to have my body opened so that I am not buried alive.”

Fear of being buried alive has often been encouraged and exploited as propaganda for cremation and crematoria.[^fn-p06-pdf19-n04]

I would like to know which kinds of people and which kinds of situations this fear is typical of.

Ask your wife about Chopin sometime.

Musicians, after all, do not belong to your world. Then drew his attention, in connection with his plan for an “inversion of utopia,” to Samuel Butler’s *Erewhon*.

---

**6 May 1948**

What remains specifically distinctive about a “crime against humanity” once one subtracts the old and familiar crimes: murder, robbery, rape, and so on?

Crimes “that reveal a blatant will to annihilate.” So something additional must exist on the subjective side: something specifically anti-human.

What exactly is added?

Not a new *reatus*—not a new kind of criminal act.

Only a new *animus*: a special state of mind. These are crimes of disposition, approached from the negative side. They had to appear with dialectical necessity once crimes based on a “good” disposition had been discovered in the name of humanity.

In other words: they are acts that arise from a hostile attitude toward humanity and reveal such an attitude. That means: acts committed by someone who has been declared an enemy of humanity.

Political in the most extreme and intense meaning of the word.

“Crime against humanity” is simply the broadest possible blanket clause for destroying the enemy.

The enslavement of peasants who owed service but had until then remained free began with the transition from measured and fixed duties to unlimited duties.

Likewise, the enslavement of a population subject to the state but previously free begins with the transition from precisely defined statutory offences to so-called blanket clauses. This too belongs to the modern problem of legality.

Legality in the sense of fixed offences defined in advance, and legality in the sense of broad, undefined grants of power, are two different concepts.

Once what is unlimited enters the picture—and is therefore potentially total—the matter becomes “political” in the modern sense. That is the essence of the indictment and of criminalized offences in political trials.

The only interesting question concerns the situation itself:

Are we still capable of measuring at all?

Can we still find standards that are neither the old standards, which have become false, nor arbitrary new ones, but standards appropriate to the actual matter and the actual situation?

Eureka.

I have found him.

The enemy.

It is not good for man to be without an enemy.

Woe to the man who has no enemy, for he will be my enemy on Judgment Day.

So there he is again. Filled with so much hatred that he cannot tolerate even a formulation coined by me without attempting to exterminate it.

(Ipsen’s report on the meeting of German law professors in Hamburg in mid-April.)

Machiavelli says (*Discourses* II, 26):

Neither threats nor insults deprive the enemy of strength. That is what matters: **depriving him of strength.** That is also the standard by which one should receive such insults.

Do they take strength away from me?

Only to the extent that I spend time on them and think about them.

---

**7 May 1948**

Theodor Haecker said in 1917 that the old medieval cathedrals must cry out for their own destruction when the aesthetic literary class covers them in the slobbering cultural and educational slime of this kind.

If that is true, then our old German cities were rightly destroyed. But does the same not apply to every one of us who feels spat upon by that cultural slime?

Should I not also cry out for this cultural brothel finally to be destroyed?

We are taken at our word. This is the age of existentialism.

Spirit finds executors and people willing to carry things through who are themselves without spirit and who perform the work of the knacker’s yard and the levelling ground.

Yet as accelerators against their own will, they end up accelerating things entirely different from those they themselves wanted to accelerate.

---

**8 May 1948**

To a legal scholar:[^fn-p07-pdf01-n01] I have reread the good old Hall, *International Law*, in Higgins’s edition (8th ed., Oxford, 1924). He is old, and probably old-fashioned too, but that is exactly what makes him so instructive and so superior to positivists of the Strupp, Lauterpacht, etc. variety. His criticism of the doctrine that an occupying power exercises the sovereignty of the occupied country deserves very close attention: this would “enable to brand acts of resistance on the part of an invaded population with a stigma of criminality which is as useless as it is unjust.” Hall even has a separate chapter entitled “Postliminium.” The whole thing, in this 1924 edition, is a good example of how English jurists never experienced the break with the pre-positivist tradition that had such catastrophic consequences in Germany.[^fn-p07-pdf01-n02] I already noticed this years ago when reading Westlake.

Then there is the question of how to distinguish the theatre of war from occupied territory, especially the meaning of *autorité établie*—“established authority”; the difference between the executive authority of the military commander in the two cases; and the question whether, in occupied territory, this executive authority of the military commander is not itself shaped, in its organization and internal structure, by the constitutional structure of the occupying state. Here too the Hague Regulations remain at the standard of 1907, including in the relationship between military and civilian authority.

(I am deeply grateful to you simply for the possibility of talking about these things with you and telling you what is on my mind.) I am often tormented by what I call the “impatience of justice,” and it is an immense comfort to know that you understand the intention and intellectual impulse behind my way of practising legal scholarship. It matters not in the least whether, in the end, you agree or disagree with my conclusions.[^fn-p07-pdf01-n03] Your visit to Plettenberg continues to bear fruit even now, and nothing could give me greater pleasure than the further certainty that there is complete reciprocity between us in this respect. Then 21 April 1948 and 1 May 1948: Formosus, *Titulus*, Sallust.

Belgium, which you have come to know, has become a peculiar centre from which the destruction of the classical law of war first began.[^fn-p07-pdf01-n04] Neutrality was originally devised to guarantee security, and <…> the atomic bomb stripped that security away. You will read something in the *Nomos* about the genuine and great scholar Ernest Nys. But also read note 39 in my *The Concept of the Discriminating War*; and remember Cardinal Mercier’s Christmas pastoral letter of 1914: the legitimate authority is and remains the government of the occupied state, not the occupying power. In itself that is correct. Here, however, it was meant in a discriminatory sense and had a discriminatory effect, with the result that even the remarkable, classically developed institution of *occupatio bellica*—military occupation—was destroyed by it.

---

**10 May 1948**

I came across the sentence *L’initié tue l’initiateur*—the initiate kills the initiator—and thought of W. Fraenger’s Grand Master of the Free Brotherhood, who was overcome by his pupil Hieronymus Bosch.[^fn-p07-pdf02-n01]

There is a mysterious cruelty in this world of initiation and mystery.[^fn-p07-pdf02-n02] The *état d’esprit*, the state of mind, is even crueller than Hobbes’s *état de nature*, the state of nature.

Here the son kills the father, the young kills the old; Zeus kills Cronus, Cronus kills Uranus. This eternal and biologically obvious process is reflected in the mysteries. They reveal, precisely by concealing it, the core of things.

Against this, Christianity, as a religion of the Father, is the true religion of peace: remaining in the Father’s house; the return of the prodigal son; the Ascension of Christ; Christ himself is the prodigal son.[^fn-p07-pdf02-n03] But there is no suggestion that the prodigal son brought some of the companions from his dissolute life back home with him. So how is the noble prodigal son supposed to take one of us back to the Father?

Let us therefore return to nature! But that means nothing other than this: let us kill our fathers, our teachers, our initiators, our creators, our benefactors. And at the same time: let us make sure that we ourselves never become fathers, teachers, initiators, creators, or benefactors!

The programme of Bakunin’s anarchism combined with Western individualism.

A prediction for a consistently Americanized world.

The true German—that is, the productive German—is still more likely to be a Bakuninist than an Americanist.

Do not let yourselves be deceived about that.

---

**15 May 1948**

*Homo homini homo*: man is man to man. That means nothing more than standing still, marking time at the zero point of a purely polar concept, which immediately splits in opposite directions: left and right, down and up; *homo homini lupus* or *deus*—man is either a wolf or a god to man.[^fn-p07-pdf02-n04]

The typical neutralization at this dead centre consists in refusing to let the split happen, or at least postponing it. One would rather stand still: on the knife-edge, right on the boundary, balanced to the finest possible degree in the transcendental space between the transcendent and the empirical; committed to nothing, keeping every option open, remaining in the undisturbed purity of the concept. But this is an untouched purity, which means an unrealized purity. It belongs to German idealism, from pure reason all the way to pure unreason.

How, then, did the fall into hell, into utter impurity, happen?

We lived through it and came to understand it.

What has happened in Germany since 1918?

Out of the darkness of social, moral, and intellectual nothingness, out of the pure lumpenproletariat, out of the refuge of homeless non-culture, rose the unknown soldier of the First World War: until then a completely empty individual, who now filled himself with the words and passions of educated Germany at that time.[^fn-p07-pdf02-n05]

H. S. Chamberlain introduced and initiated him at Wahnfried. With that, he was admitted into the temple of culture. And he took it seriously—with the seriousness of an animal.

What did he take seriously?

The passions and formulas that were offered to him.

Concepts such as deed, will, power, race, genius, Führer, charisma. And conversely, these passions and formulas, which until then had been thought in a fairly pure and abstract way, were surprised and delighted that someone was finally taking them seriously.

Now there was a man who took them seriously, who made them serious: nothing but a realizer,[^fn-p07-pdf03-n01] someone to whom one could leave the rest, nothing but an executor and enforcer.

Through sheer “carrying-through,” the I comes into being—Fichte.

The pure executor of ideas that had until then remained so pure.

The pure henchman.

The pure perpetrator.

The pure function of doing.

The work without faith.[^fn-p07-pdf03-n02]

This individual read enormously, in order to fuel himself.

From Mirko Jelusich’s historical novels he learned how the great men of world history talk—“these brainless fools,” Julius Caesar is fond of saying in Jelusich—and how they destroy peoples.

So here is the intellectual-historical formula for those twelve years: the great historical opera of the pure execution—that is, nothing but execution—of the pure German cult of genius.

A man condemned by history to act: Schiller’s great theme, and the great theme of his concept of tragedy.

Three ugly jabs, poisonous and yellowish, delivered in that spiteful voice:

1. The mention of Freisler. Curiously, Carl Brinkmann and Helmut Rumpf do the same thing. *Ecco*: where is the common source here?

2. A sentence such as: “The hatred directed at me is found only among people who do not know me, whereas the hatred directed at you exists precisely among people who do know you.”

3. The matter of “Stahl” must have harmed you greatly.

Yes indeed, you money-minded idealist. It harmed me greatly. Curious, once again, how well informed you are.

So:

First: recognize the situation!

Gottfried Benn is magnificent in *The Ptolemaic Man*: One must be honest whatever the danger. But, by the way, what dangers do these continents really have to offer? Bourgeois dangers. Death is too far outside the human world to be degraded into a mere “danger.”

“I turn a disc and am myself turned; I am a Ptolemaic man.”

I do not groan like Jeremiah, nor like Paul. I do what appears before me. I am not “thrown,” and I do not drape myself in wife, child, and summer cottage either.

First: recognize the situation!

Existentially understood, that is the death blow to utopia.

The existentialists: the new Captains of Köpenick.

---

**16 May 1948**

For the isolated individual struggling to maintain himself, and especially for the great “untimely” individuals—those who are precisely suited to the wrong time—the objective powers automatically become relative.

One must therefore always ask what each of these objective forces—the state, the Church—means at that particular moment in relation to the isolated person.

When Bruno Bauer speaks of the Catholic Church, for example, he constantly means different things depending on its relationship to himself.

Around 1870 he values the Catholic Church not only as a counterweight to the coming ruler of the world. It has also become something different for him from what it was in 1843, when he still regarded it as Judaism in its purest form.

The same applies to the Prussian state, to Judaism, and so on.

What else is an isolated individual supposed to do? He jumps from one sheet of ice to another.

For Barbey d’Aurevilly, the great teacher of Léon Bloy, the Catholic Church was—not only, but also—the high balcony from which he could spit down onto the heads of the rabble of his age. And then there is Nietzsche, with his use and exploitation of every value, his thousand escapes and hiding places. That is existentialism in its pure form.

The moment it is taught from university chairs, of course, it becomes comic.

Then comes a cramped, convulsive moment of mutual revenge: the empty individual takes revenge on the objective powers and uses them merely as instruments of power for his own empty ego; and the objective powers take revenge for this abuse on an individual who has become crazed by his own ego.

---

**17 May 1948**

An idea takes possession of an individual and, by doing so, always appears in the world as a foreign guest.[^fn-p07-pdf04-n01]

The foreign guest was Adolf. He was foreign almost to the point of caricature.

Foreign precisely because of the antiseptic, empty purity of his ideas about the Führer, charisma, genius, and race. He was an executor with no prior commitments or assumptions.

The mass of educated people was uneducated.

The few genuinely educated people were still standing with Goethe and Carus. They had not yet experienced the crisis of 1848.

Bruno Bauer and Max Stirner were regarded as comic oddballs.

Adolf, by contrast, who intellectually was less than Max, was regarded even by educated men such as Popitz as a genius.

<…>[^fn-p07-pdf04-n02]

And so he entered into appearance.

“Existentialism” is the appropriate word: it therefore also delivers the death blow to this cult of genius inherited from eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Germany.[^fn-p07-pdf04-n03]

This key concept in intellectual history—the genius as executor—also clarifies my personal relationships with Franz Kluxen, who initiated me into the thoroughly genius-centred intellectual world of nineteenth-century Germany, into Richard Wagner and Otto Weininger, and with Hugo Ball, who suffered under the German cult of genius without ever overcoming it.

Ball fled from his age into humility, after having first fallen deeply into that age.

Existentialism kills the novel?

Not a chance!

Sartre keeps happily writing novels.

Existentialism kills the cult of genius?

Yes!

Heidegger interprets Hölderlin.

The decisive step around 1900 was the transition from the Goethean cult of genius to the Hölderlinian one. That is where Heidegger remained.

What a betrayal of Kierkegaard, of Bruno Bauer, and of the Christianity that was discovered—and rediscovered—in about 1840.

---

**18 May 1948**

“Youth without Goethe” (Max Kommerell): for us, from about 1910 onward, that meant in concrete terms youth with Hölderlin.

It meant the transition from an optimistic, peace-seeking, neutralizing cult of genius to a pessimistic, activist, tragic cult of genius. But it remained within the cult of genius and, in fact, deepened it to infinite depths.

Norbert von Hellingrath is more important than Stefan George and Rilke.

---

**23 May 1948**

Not only the idea, but power too, appears only as a foreign guest.

When analysed as a historical fact, power is always also powerlessness, compulsion, prison. The earthly ruler who seems all-powerful becomes completely cut off from everyone else and therefore completely powerless.[^fn-p07-pdf05-n01] This is the dialectic of absolutism and sovereignty.

In the end, the absolute sovereign sits in the icy loneliness of his omnipotence, blocked off by antechambers and chiefs of staff. That is power as it appears in the world.

How can this be explained?

Probably only by saying that idea, being, and power are one and the same.

The source of all the errors and dehumanizations lies in the fact that this unity was misunderstood in empirical, positivist terms. This also gives me the connection with the note of 27 April 1948.

Eureka.

Being appears only as non-being!

The moment it becomes visible, it steps outside itself. This is Rudolf Sohm’s problem, and the problem of the visibility—the public visibility—of the Church.

Helmut Rumpf’s reply to my letter of 20 April 1948,[^fn-p07-pdf05-n02] which arrived recently, is a document of the will to intellectual deafness. He mistakes deafness for decisionism. He does not even respond to my reference to Rudolf Sohm, although that reference concerns his very existence as a scholarly jurist.

Instead he solemnly tells me about the impression made on him by an atrocity film.

So: decisionism built on the shifting sand of impressionistic agitation.[^fn-p07-pdf05-n03] He does not even mention Rudolf Sohm.[^fn-p07-pdf05-n04]

Even when I write him an entire letter specifically to encourage him to read Sohm’s *Church Law*, it does not occur to him to do so.

So what does he want from me?

Let us leave him to his further impressions. There will certainly be no shortage of atrocities and atrocity documents.

Today he interests me only as an occasion to think about the different ways in which people are made deaf.

Becoming part of the mass means losing one’s intellectual hearing and one’s creative language.

In exchange, the deaf person develops feelers and antennae for receiving orders and, when necessary, passing them on. That need not be terrible. In an individual case it can even be a blessing, perhaps even a salvation, just as it saved the sailors of Odysseus when their ears were stopped with wax. But I am an Odysseus tied to the mast.

Encounter with Joachim Schoeps: first through Cramer von Laue, and now through a sentence in Hans Blüher’s *Debate About Israel* of 1933 (p. 50), which leapt at me as my first Sunday-morning greeting:

“And this—that Jewish chosenness was the model for the medieval Reich—is also the reason why a believing Judaism has an imperial, not a royal, disposition!”

No, Joachim Schoeps, that is not the reason!

The reason lies in John 19:15. And the Christian Reich of the medieval emperors derived its legitimacy from being a *κατέχων*, a restraining power, according to 2 Thessalonians 2:6–7.

The tragedy of Jewish assimilation from around 1900 onward: as a whole, they could not make the great transition from Goethe to Hölderlin, but remained within the old culture and then used that old culture to criticize the new one, with an irritatingly unsuspecting sense of superiority. They did not understand the transition from concept to form, or what was meant by it in the German spirit. Or they understood too much, as Gundolf did.

A few did make the transition—that is, they were crushed beneath its wheels, as Rosenzweig and J. Schoeps were.

We Germans, meanwhile, are paying instalments toward “reparation”[^fn-p07-pdf06-n01]—the German has no time now; he has to <read Kafka>.

On Karl Schulte: he does not know what he is doing when, from the murky twilight of a licensed public sphere, he shoots into the darkness of my silence, which is completely hidden from him.

I am not one of those moths that consider it good fortune to flutter around in the miserable light of such a licensed public sphere.

---

**24 May 1948**

To Gerhard Hess in Heidelberg:

For several months I have been reading, with growing pleasure and even amazement, Cardinal Melchior de Polignac’s *Anti-Lucretius*, in a Paris edition of 1754.

As for the amazement, that concerns physical problems of the atom, empty space, matter, and nothingness.[^fn-p07-pdf06-n02]

On those questions I will have my impressions corrected and checked by Pascual Jordan.

As for the pleasure, I need not worry about that. The book contains delightful hexameters and formulations later taken over and made famous by the Encyclopaedists—for example, *Eripuit Fulmen Jovi*.

But as a casualty of the decline of the West who still feels responsible for intellectual history, I am also—and above all—interested in the position of this author in the period between the first and third Cartesian generations.

All I know is that he had conversations with Bayle around 1697, and I would very much like to know more.

I am writing to you because your Gassendi appears in the work: *Gassendo amatus surculus erroris* ….[^fn-p07-pdf06-n03]

Perhaps the cardinals of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries really did know somewhat more than the socially successful chaplains of the nineteenth and twentieth.

A decline into the great bureaucracy of celibacy, into vicars-general administering the machinery of scholastic routine. It is all a problem of elites.

The Jews as a secondary Christian elite; as more or less faithful placeholders whenever the Christian elites decline into mere legality.

For when it comes to the logic, tactics, and practice of an emptied-out legality, the Jews are in any case more skilled than any Christian people, which can never entirely stop believing in love and charisma against the law.

(How could Hess, that profiteer from penitence, know this?)[^fn-p07-pdf06-n04]

---

**26 May 1948**

Read the following sentences aloud to anyone today, in 1948:

“He spoke a great deal about race. He possessed a powerful and elaborate machine for spreading principles that he himself did not possess.[^fn-p07-pdf07-n01]

“What he called his ideals were the dregs of a Darwinism that had not only begun to stink but had already become poisonous.

“That the weak must go under, and that anyone he failed to understand must therefore be one of the weak—this was the philosophy he loudly professed throughout his life.

“All his opinions about religion were the stalest ideas of his age.

“He was a modest and honest recipient of the overworked popular science of his time.

“He spread no ideas that some office clerk could not equally well have spread for him.

“But precisely because he had no ideas to spread, he caused human slaughter, violated justice, and ruined whole states in order to spread—this idea.”[^fn-p07-pdf07-n02]

Today, in 1948, everyone would immediately assume this was about poor Adolf Hitler and would consider it an accurate description of him. But it appeared in a journal edited by Franz Blei in 1913, *Der Lose Vogel*, published by K. Wolff in Leipzig, p. 246. And it refers to Cecil Rhodes.

---

**27 May 1948**

Son of this consecration, you should tremble!
Listen and suffer!
(Th. Däubler, *By the Sea*).

The water demon dies and Pan no longer smiles
(*Christmas Triptych*).

---

**29 May 1948**

Some beat from a deeper, hidden rhythm in Gerhard Nebel’s lecture last night in Werdohl has not stopped pounding inside me since then. It began during the lecture at the passage and the word “earth-burrower.”[^fn-p07-pdf07-n03]

Now it is flowing into the utterly overwhelming rhythm of Theodor Däubler’s “Ethiopian Dance of Death.”

I am certain that great things will become clear if Gerhard Nebel reads this *Dance of Death* aloud to us one day.

(Mythology of the dwarf.)

---

**30 May 1948**

Happiness: I walked out of the sermon.

My child, without seeing me do it, did exactly the same and went home as well, because it had become far too tasteless for him.

*Patri succedens*—following the father.

Genius, whom you do not abandon!

Poor Konrad Weiß and his poem of 1933.

Here the desperate Hohenstaufen from Schwäbisch Hall breaks loose; the trampled South German peasant of 1525; the Westphalian Anabaptist broken on the wheel in 1535 lashes out once more; the betrayed citizen of 1813; the humiliated democrat of 1848; the defeated victor of the battles of the First World War; the mercenary cheated of his pay by world history.

The poor, tormented foot soldiers of all those who possess power and all those who claim to possess right—they all break loose and strike out once more in madness before finally recognizing the identity of Christianity and Judaism and sinking away as victims.[^fn-p07-pdf08-n01]

We were all still deeply moved by a sentence from Ernst Jünger’s *Radiations* that Gerhard Nebel quoted the evening before last in Werdohl.

When Jünger’s son Ernst died, Jünger said:

“The good boy! He always wanted to equal his father; now he has done better.”

The simplest, deepest, and most beautiful words a father could speak in such a situation.[^fn-p07-pdf08-n02]

How sad that reading many passages from these *Radiations* will have to be a great disappointment to Gueydan and cause him deep pain.

What confusion in the so-called battle lines![^fn-p07-pdf08-n03]

---

**31 May 1948**

“Heaven and earth will pass away”—is that not the purest nihilism?

“But my words will not pass away”—is that not the purest existentialism?

Again and again I return to a theory of the Italian jurist Gabba.

Under a *occupatio bellica*, a military occupation, the population of the occupied territory—as distinct both from its former state and from the occupying power—is a separate third entity. It cannot simply be treated as an object, at least not when it is the civilized population of a civilized country.

Gabba was really right: the population of occupied territory ought to be understood as a legal subject in its own right. For its connection with its previous government—the government of the occupied state—is precarious.[^fn-p07-pdf08-n04]

After a *debellatio*, the complete defeat and destruction of the occupied state as a political power, no such relationship is possible at all.

According to the <classical> doctrine, the population of occupied territory is famously required to serve two masters: the absent old master with loyalty and fidelity, and the new master who is physically present with legal obedience.[^fn-p07-pdf08-n05]

The Belgians played such an important role in this classical international-law theory of occupation.

In 1914–18, because of their particular situation, they strongly emphasized attachment to the absent government as a general principle and a general right.

But the entire construction of this double relationship becomes completely meaningless once the state power of the occupied territory has been destroyed or is entirely in the hands of the occupying power. Then there is no longer any possibility of loyalty or fidelity, unless the occupying power is regarded as succeeding to the old government’s right to loyalty—which Hall rejects.

What remains is pure legality: obedience to the measures of the occupation authorities. But then it ought to be self-evident that the population cannot simply disappear into a void in international law if the territory itself is not annexed.

---

**1 June 1948**

The enemy is not something that is simply expelled or excreted.

The relationship between friend and enemy is not the relationship between food and excrement. It is much closer to mixture and mating: the wedding night of opposites, a Heraclitean orgy. That is true even in civil war, so long as the war between citizens remains a war between brothers.

Civil war is the great war of mixture.

Marxist class struggle is no longer a civil war.

There is something horrifying in this kind of hostility: the banquet of Leviathan and, finally, Köppelsbleek, the flayer’s pit.

The defeated man is thrown onto the dung heap—or, in modern terms, into the rubbish bin. He is handed over to the knacker.

---

**2 June 1948**

He wanted to force his way into the class that ruled the world and gain access to its secret. He did not want to tear that secret away from them. He merely wanted to share in it. He wanted to be admitted to the exclusive club, finally to become a truly great gentleman, a lord.[^fn-p07-pdf09-n01] But that secret really did lie in the idea of race.

---

**3 June 1948**

Power is not something evil. It is something utterly alien—just as alien to the person who possesses power as it is to the person subjected to it. That is why struggles for power become so intense between relatives, between brothers, between father and son.[^fn-p07-pdf09-n02]

I think of Otto the Great’s struggle with his brothers, who had to be killed, or of the wars of extermination between the Red Rose and the White Rose, and similar cases.[^fn-p07-pdf09-n03]

Power remains completely “other” even in relation to the individual clothed in power.

Naturally, it remains equally alien to the person subjected to it.

(Here it touches the definition of God: power does, after all, come from God.) And here lies the great problem: all power comes either from God or from the people.

From the people—in the sense of an identity between power and powerlessness, in the sense that the command is made legitimate by obedience.

---

**4 June 1948**

Do I have the right to speak about power? I think one can say that I do. I have experienced every kind of power on my own body. I have sat in the belly of the fish. I have observed power from close by and from far away. I have always looked for good places from which to observe it, and I have found them: on the left ear or the right ear of Leviathan, inside his jaws, and on his tail. And finally: I myself have never sought power and have never possessed power. Nor am I sitting somewhere safely out of range. It is not in my nature to call upon poor, tormented people to resist while I myself remain in the most comfortable shelter.

And when, twenty years ago, I often used the word “existential,” I used it existentially, not yet existentialistically. It was still closer to Søren Kierkegaard’s room than it is in the hands of those who exploit him today; closer to Barbey and Villiers than to the present-day *profiteurs de Léon Bloy*, the profiteers of Léon Bloy.

Do we still remember those critical schoolmasters who portrayed Cicero and Seneca to us as cowards, weaklings, opportunists, and mere rhetoricians?

A well-fed professor, comfortably established and wrapped securely in the wool of pre-war prosperity, found Cicero and Seneca insufficiently heroic.

Seneca perhaps received a little mercy. But they tore Cicero apart, with the great Theodor Mommsen leading the charge.

*Exul in patria mea*—an exile in my own country.

Compared with these Californian radio heroes, one could easily be tempted to start boasting.

I could say in the style of Walt Whitman:

Whoever speaks of law wants to deceive.

Whoever speaks of power wants to reveal.

The powerful man does not speak of power. He does not think about power.

---

**5 June 1948**

The word is a sign from beyond. It is a phonetic hieroglyph. It is an echo that shares in primordial worlds. This is what Konrad Weiß means by the creatureliness of the word: the word as distinct from the neutralizing thing called language, as Theodor Haecker speaks of it.

That is it.

That is my hopeless position within a German Catholicism devoted to neutralization, in which the objective has become nothing more than a “bourgeois concept of preservation.”

Theodor Haecker’s polemic against my concept of the political also came out of this neutralism.

How alone I stand there, with poor Konrad Weiß.

Haecker, the outsider, triumphed.

Even the weakling Maritain, and his hate-filled Raïssa.

“Now you stand naked, naked as at birth, in desolate spaces.”

---

**6 June 1948**

What did humanity need when these weapons of annihilation arrived?

Then: *ratio*, reason—the dictatorship of reason.

Today: a *pouvoir spirituel*, a spiritual power.

Then: the leap into absolutism.

Today: the leap into an absolutism infinitely more absolute. That would be the leap into the realm of freedom—naturally only for those who are free.

(4 September 1947, Shotwell.)

The leap into the fantastic and utopian, into Huxley’s *Brave New World—or* onto the Way of the Cross of God made man.

The answer has already been given.

Everything has already been accomplished, and all that you do is answer.

What humanity needs is a martyr, not a Napoleon.

The martyr is at once a subhuman—from the viewpoint of the ruling type—and a superhuman, seen in truth.

The deficiency that is not a zero point.

The tremendous effect of Napoleon.

Power: the true motive behind the will to power can only be the right to renounce power.

We seek to take possession of the world so that we can throw it away.

Every other motive is meaningless or comic. Or do you really want to take possession of the world so that you can enjoy it?

Well then, cheers, you poor Sybarite. You poor pleasure-seeker.

The world will certainly serve you.

*Avoir pour savoir*—to have in order to know.

---

**8 June 1948**

Gueydan is magnificent:

*Le maquis est une création posthume.*

The Resistance is a posthumous creation.

Or:

*Les attaques de la presse sont un brevet d’honnêteté pour ses victimes.*

Attacks by the press are a certificate of honesty for their victims.

The press sentences people to death and disgrace, and the state courts carry out the sentence.

---

**9 June 1948**

We have long since been living in the fulfilled here-and-now.

The eighteenth century, Rousseau, Goethe: all of it was a marvellous mythology of real existence in this world. But then unpleasant types crowd around the beautifully laid table, and it is all over.

Now the better beyond begins again.

That is all.

Today’s practitioners of myth, such as Friedrich Georg Jünger, live on the leftovers and on dreams that come far too cheaply.

The poor devils who tried once more to take the fulfilled here-and-now seriously were quite rightly hanged and burned by the more experienced practitioners of this world.

That is all.

Nietzsche was already among the latecomers.

The will to power is the will to a fulfilled existence in this world.

Arnold Gehlen is right when he says:

Every human type can fulfil its own ethos only when it rules. Everything else becomes moral degeneration.

The will to power is the will to *potestas directa*—direct power. But what is the will to *potestas indirecta*, indirect power, mere influence?

Is the will to indirect power somehow morally superior to the will to direct power?

---

**10 June 1948**

To Hanns Winckelmann, together with the reply about the state secretaries:

On legality and legitimacy.

Legality becomes something independent, something new.

Its foundation in “value-rationality”—in reason based on values—ceases to be interesting.

The law becomes the plan, and the plan becomes law.

Indeed, the plan becomes the constitution. And something more becomes clear: it is not the planners who rule. It is the rulers who plan.

Reason does not merely slide from the “value-rational” into the “purpose-rational,” from reasoning about values into reasoning about practical means and ends.

The very meaning of *ratio* changes completely as soon as it is transferred from value to purpose.

Do not forget: for an entire generation, not only technicians and industrialists but major philosophers as well demonstrated and celebrated the idea that the great advance consisted in functionalization—in moving from concepts of substance to concepts of function.[^fn-p07-pdf11-n01]

Remember Ernst Cassirer’s *Substance and Function* of 1910!

The primitive thinks in substances.

The civilized person thinks in functions!

And then, on top of that, “reason”!

Eduard Heimann recently gave a lecture in Berlin, in May, organized by *The Socialist Century* at the Wilmersdorf district office, with the following thesis: Because reason presupposes only one truth and one justice, the leadership at the summit of a rational society must become infallible.

*Sic.*

His exact words were:

“Dictatorship follows from reason.”

He could have read that as early as 1921 in my book *Dictatorship*.

But woe to the diagnosticians!

The rage directed at Ernst Jünger’s *The Worker*, and perhaps even more at my *Concept of the Political*, is the rage of a spa director at the doctor who diagnoses a case of plague in the resort.

I have made enemies of all the spa directors.

A society at once philanthropic and malicious.

I spoil the pleasure of a thousand harmless people.

A few factory owners developed worse heart trouble when they heard rumours of the plague case.

The diabetes of several bankers became alarming.

The season was in full flower, with delightful, long-awaited meetings in the most cultivated Marianne von Willemer style, and now it has all been ruthlessly trampled underfoot. So answer for yourself, you miserable criminal against human happiness!

A new criminal offence:

Anyone who destroys the human feeling of happiness in a heartless way attacks the foundations of the social order and shall be outlawed as an enemy of humanity.[^fn-p07-pdf12-n01]

---

**11 June 1948**

Tried in vain to decipher Däubler’s two “brother” sonnets, addressed to R. Pannwitz and me.

A magnificent flight and a miserable fall, directly beside one another.

Especially bad in the “Iranian Rhapsody.”[^fn-p07-pdf12-n02]

And yet:

Däubler is an ocean containing seaweed, plankton, octopuses, shoals of herring, fish spawn—but also magnificent dolphins.

Beside him, the early Rilke is a neatly polished goldfish bowl.

The Rilke of the *Duino Elegies* is a park pond.[^fn-p07-pdf12-n03]

Kelsen’s reasoning is designed to prove that Germany is a nothing in international law—truly nothing but nothing—and that only the Allies could create *ex nihilo*, out of nothing, an entirely different Germany with no connection whatsoever to the previous one.

The sight of this eager manufacturer of legal instruments of annihilation reminds me of the little helpers in the hell scenes of Hieronymus Bosch. But we have already experienced and survived destroyers, exterminators, erasers, and crushers of an entirely different scale. So let us leave him to himself.

In the seventeenth century, Spinoza took great pleasure in watching spiders and flies annihilate one another. It was his only recreation from thought.

You, as a great entomologist, might also be inclined today to enjoy this little spectacle. For me it produces a deep melancholy, and I prefer to look away.[^fn-p07-pdf12-n04]

Horror at laws.

Above all, horror at the autonomous logic of legality itself.

P. Humbert Clérissac, *The Mystery of the Church*.

Jacques Maritain’s preface is sprinkled with self-satisfied hints: Clérissac was a guest in Maritain’s home; Maritain served his Mass for a year, and so on.

Denis de Rougemont’s *The Devil’s Share* is very beautiful, delightful even.[^fn-p07-pdf12-n05]

Too beautiful and too delightful for its subject.

Perhaps this way of speaking about the subject is itself the ultimate form of cunning, taken to a level that cannot be surpassed.

The test is simple:

Does he really risk coming into conflict with the devil as the devil appears concretely today?

Or does he remain with the triumphant exposure of yesterday’s devil and, when it comes to today, content himself with saying that some ancient devil is common to everyone and that everything is somehow the devil’s doing?

That is exactly it.

He remains posthumous.

His *maquis est une création posthume*—his Resistance is a posthumous creation—as Gueydan puts it so nicely in his *Thoughts of a Dean*.

---

**12 June 1948**

Oppressive evening.

[astrological signs for Jupiter]

---

**13 June 1948**

Now they all shout, with the malicious Niekisch leading them, that Nietzsche fathered Hitler.

Above all, Nietzsche’s Übermensch. But surely this Übermensch is the obvious consequence of believing in man as the maker of his own fate, a being who can raise himself beyond himself.

What, after all, is Shotwell saying that is any different?

(See 1 September 1947.)

Can an activist atheist want anything other than the Übermensch?

In 1923 Leon Trotsky wrote essays and gave lectures on literature and revolution in which he said:

“It lies in the direction of development that man will drive out everything dull, elemental, and unconscious; replace religion with science; and drive the unconscious out of politics through democracy, parliamentarianism, ‘and finally through the transparently clear dictatorship of the soviets.’”

*Sic.*

“But the blind elemental force hangs most heavily over the economic sphere; that too will be driven out by socialist organization.

“But surely we did not do all this only to crawl on our bellies before the dull laws of heredity and capitulate before blind sexual selection.

“Man will rationalize this too and banish the dull fear of death.

“Man will make everything transparently clear and ‘create a higher social-biological type or, if one prefers, a superman.

“‘The average human being will rise to the level of Aristotle, Goethe, and Marx; above this mountain ridge, new peaks will rise.’”

That is how Trotsky ends his 1923 essay on revolutionary art and socialist art.

How sad this optimism is!

How much more fulfilled existence in this world there is in Wagner’s pessimism:

“Hail to you, radiant earth!”

Nietzsche, then, was not merely a precursor of Hitlerism. He was also a precursor of Bolshevism.[^fn-p07-pdf13-n01]

---

**14 June 1948**

Humanism: memories of youth, of our Latin-school days.

In Europe, the alliance between the Church and humanism can be explained through shared memories of youth and childhood from the pre-war world before 1914.

Now they all have a common enemy.

Christianity, which in Kierkegaard knew how to wipe the slate so completely clean and could appear so “inhuman,” now profits politically, in Karl Barth, from memories of the sermons delivered by the well-fed and securely established witnesses to truth of the nineteenth century.

Completely blind chance and the most exact, detailed planning are conceptual opposites, like emptiness and fullness.

The moment we begin to think, we find ourselves caught between such opposites. But people then group themselves into friends and enemies by using these patterns of thought.

---

**15 June 1948**

Many people sense that the part of Europe represented by Germany is dying through a terrible *dysthanasia*—a prolonged and agonizing death.

Few understand that the euthanasia of France and England belongs to the same process.

*La France se meurt, ne troublez pas son agonie*—France is dying; do not disturb its agony—Renan said sixty years ago.

Toynbee is fundamentally saying the same thing about England.

Today the Germans long for euthanasia and envy their Western neighbours the relative absence of pain in their dying. For the type of person devoted entirely to this world, dysthanasia is the great crime against humanity.

Anyone who grants a people euthanasia, by contrast, becomes a benefactor of humanity.

Hitler’s euthanasias were fraudulent, and were therefore crimes.

But his final political aim was to attach himself to the British Empire, to enter that distinguished firm, finally to become a great gentleman—in other words, to participate in the British agony and the British euthanasia.[^fn-p07-pdf14-n01]

To Hans Beyer, who wants to work on grace and law with reference to Nuremberg and thinks that the situation might be healed through “grace”:

The subject of grace and law is a great one.

I cannot properly connect it with Nuremberg so long as Nuremberg’s legal problems remain so monstrous. For the moment, Nuremberg belongs instead to the subject “grace and politics.”

And that is certainly a structural transformation of grace, something different from the kind of grace that can be related to law.

Then legality and the concept of the political; see 28 April 1948.

---

**16 June 1948**

But I am no Ptolemaic man.

I turn no disc and am not myself turned.

I am no unmoved mover.

To Herbert Nette, together with Konrad Weiß’s *The Creature of the Word*:

I am still occupied by your sentence that we use language as a vehicle in the same way that Black people drive cars or listen to the radio.

One could vary a sentence of Karl Marx in response:

The emancipation of Black people took place in such a way that white people became Black.

Again, great strength from Konrad Weiß, *The Creature of the Word*: the Tower of Babel of neutralizing linguistic unity.

“Even the confusion of languages is better today than this Babylonian unity.”[^fn-p07-pdf14-n02]

The *κατέχων*, the restrainer, can be recognized by the fact that he does not seek this world unity but instead lays down the imperial crown.

Making the imperial crown hereditary is naive. But the crown becomes hereditary through its connection with the practical power of a ruling house. And <can> a ruling house not itself be a *κατέχων*?

Then Konrad Weiß says of Theodor Haecker’s statements about language—which is, after all, something different from the word and has a stronger tendency toward neutralization:

“Haecker’s thought belongs to the Catholic literary movement, though it did not arise from that movement, because Haecker entered it as an outsider.

“He therefore did not pass through the earlier conflict within that movement between ‘classicist’ neutralization and ‘poetic’ realization.

“But now he too is struggling toward a specifically Catholic sharpening.

“The movement itself has in many cases—just as one can say of other intellectual and artistic decisions made by the older generation—turned, through its failure to bear fruit in creaturely and historical knowledge, from the word toward language, from the particular toward the universal, and from a neutralized form of life toward political confession.

“And now Haecker too is struggling for a genuine Catholic sharpening.”

That is the secret key phrase of my entire intellectual and public existence: the struggle for a genuinely Catholic sharpening of the issue.

Against the neutralizers.

Against the aesthetic lotus-eaters.

Against abortionists, cremationists, and pacifists.

Here, on this road toward Catholic sharpening, Theodor Haecker could no longer follow me.

Here they all fell away from me.

Even Hugo Ball.

Only Konrad Weiß remained, and faithful friends such as Paul Adams.[^fn-p07-pdf15-n01]

---

**17 June 1948**

On Güllich:

First impression: language let completely loose; an extremely full-mouthed and wildly mixed vocabulary.

Is this the rhetorical ease of the Palatinate? Or is it an effect of Hitler and the Hitler Youth, which learned how to manipulate words?

Second impression: the need to find saviours and prophets and immediately greet them as such with loud enthusiasm. So he quickly turns Marshall, Toynbee, and Walter Lippmann into saviours.

Third impression: the young General Staff officer.

Exact, pointed.

Danger of ingratiating oneself.

Danger of losing one’s dignity before people who simply do not want to be loved by us.

To Dr Wilhelm Schmitz, who sent me K. Schulte’s pamphlet and drew my attention to G. Radbruch’s favourable review of it in the *SDJZ*, April 1948:

Even poisonous mosquitoes such as Schulte have their meaning, or at least their function.

In Radbruch many things come together, not least an anti-Roman impulse that continues, unconsciously, to rumble around in the buried cellars of his emotional life.

A Holsteiner who has become a late Social Democrat—which means helpless—must find the unconstrained freedom of a man of Catholic stock opaque, meaning inaccessible to him, and therefore mythologize it into something Machiavellian and monstrous.

I find that touching.

His fellow Holsteiner Ferdinand Tönnies, a Social Democrat of the old school, is of an entirely different calibre.

---

**18 June 1948**

(To E. R. Huber:)

The direction in which my thoughts are moving after the first reading of *Idea and Reality of the Free German Movement* can best be indicated by the phrase *pouvoir spirituel*—spiritual power.

I know how irritating this expression must be to you. But I am not thinking of the long-established institutional forms that such a spiritual power has taken.

The whole of so-called nineteenth-century socialism was, in its original impulse, an attempt finally to create a spiritual power once again.

The first great document of socialism is not the *Communist Manifesto* of 1847, but Saint-Simon’s *New Christianity* of 1825, which explicitly proclaims the necessity and the goal of a new *pouvoir spirituel*.

The posthumously published second volume of Rudolf Sohm’s *Church Law* is a treasure house for every problem of constitutional and administrative law.

(Then more in the spirit of 1 May 1948: I saved the honour.)

---

**19 June 1948**

Hobbes is the first modern thinker in whom hatred of ideologues becomes visible.

But wonderfully, this includes hatred of the ideologues of the right of resistance as well: the resistance ideologues who tyrannized us then just as they do today, who call upon others to commit sabotage while remaining safely out of range themselves, and who afterwards declare us criminals because we could not bring ourselves to become saboteurs.

In the case of Christianity, Hobbes takes them at their word: the only person obliged to die for his Christian faith is the person who preaches it. That is not so very far from Kierkegaard.

Kierkegaard would certainly have agreed with him enthusiastically.

A preacher of repentance such as Jaspers, who has not even been beaten up, does not deserve our interest.

---

**20 June 1948**

*Je faisais ce que faisait la magistrature*—I did what the magistracy did.

Robert Brasillach’s great answer.

The great problem of the right not to resist—the right of non-resistance.

Non-resistance automatically becomes collaboration.

The trial of Robert Brasillach became a *procès d’opinion*, a trial of opinion.

Jacques Isorni, *Avocat à la Cour*, published *The Trial of Robert Brasillach* with Flammarion in Paris in 1947.

On p. 167 comes the answer, to which the government prosecutor M. Reboul can reply only:

*Il n’y a pas d’ordre légal*—there is no legal order. And the authorities themselves committed sabotage as well.

To defend the old doctrine of non-resistance, which had been valid for four hundred years, now becomes a *crime intellectuel*—an intellectual crime.

The criminalization of aggressive war must go on reproducing itself and giving birth to ever new forms of criminalization.

The *Diabolus ethicus*, the ethical devil, stirred up the *furor accusandi et persequendi*—the frenzy of accusation and persecution.

There is a fine three-way dialogue between Robert Brasillach, the prosecutor M. Reboul, and the defence lawyer Jacques Isorni.

In the end, prosecutor and condemned man shake hands. But Brasillach is shot all the same.

Is the only thing that matters, then, the fact that the jury sentenced Brasillach to death and that the sentence was carried out?

No.

What matters is that this discussion was published.

With us, people were—and still are—silenced.

I would gladly have died if my argument about the criminalization of aggressive war, written in August 1945, could have been published at the time or during the trials.

The intellectual struggle between the French republican and the fascist is impressive.

The defeated fascist is helpless, intellectually still embryonic. He finds no protection. But he still receives a public trial.

I think the passage describing the Republic as a whore was probably what emotionally tipped the jury toward a death sentence.

In substance, M. Reboul says:

*Le crime intellectuel: la trahison des clercs*—the intellectual crime: the betrayal of the intellectuals.

“You were tearing apart a memory of yourselves, the memory we all share, the memory possessed by all of us intellectuals: the memory of the twenty-year-old student who, if he hungers for knowledge, can satisfy himself in France because every door to knowledge stands open to him and no tyranny closes any of them.”

(p. 166)

It would be instructive to transfer these arguments and viewpoints to Germany.

Could anyone dare to say the equivalent to me?

Today!

The holders of licences issued in 1945 as heroes of free speech!

Radbruch as a member of the Resistance!

The greatness of present-day Germany: it talks about former colleagues who were silenced.

---

**21 June 1948**

An ugly stab when Gerhard Nebel wrote to me that he and Gebhard had tried in vain to discover the meaning of Konrad Weiß’s *Cumaean Sibyl*:

“I cannot help it. The man is a fraud. Give me my Friedrich Georg instead.”

*Sic.*

Weiß remains the great test.

The terrible loneliness of this recognition.

Iskar comes with friendly eyes.
Enticingly he swings his rope.
Follow me; I know the hole
through which Thomas Hobbes once crawled.

---

**22 June 1948**

Ernst Jünger often speaks—in *Gardens and Roads* and in *Radiations*, for example on 9 December 1943—of the ordering power of my thought and of my ability to define things.

Many people have noticed this power and spoken about it. But they saw me only in public, presenting and representing my field and profession. They did not see my hard, ruined private life, which I sacrificed to that task of creating order.

The old <Privy Councillor and jurist> am Zehnhoff did see it. He once said to me:

“In my long life as a jurist, I have never known a man who possessed more order in his thoughts and concepts than you.

“But neither have I known anyone who had more disorder and confusion in his private life.”

But these are only the superficial, antithetical aspects.

If one went a little further back, one would probably come upon a desert from which, in the whole of world literature up to now, only Annette’s *Spiritual Year* has allowed a human cry to reach the ears of mankind.

The first requirement for the ability to produce good definitions is a rare ability: the ability to exclude what cannot be bounded. That is the beginning, and it is extraordinarily difficult both in practice and dialectically.

Every important definition begins there.

Very few people can cross this threshold.

To distinguish what has been enclosed, and what can be enclosed, from what is unenclosed and cannot be enclosed: that is the first of all distinctions.

Just as, for the Stoic, every virtue begins by distinguishing the sphere that lies within our power from the sphere that lies outside it.

---

**23 June 1948**

The human body and soul are like a musical instrument on which invisible players, in some mysterious performance, produce music that is often pleasurable and often extremely painful to us, the instruments themselves. But our pain or pleasure has nothing to do with the melody.

Fine. Then we can divide human beings into those who are violins and other string instruments, those who are woodwinds or brass, and those who are percussion.

The growing preference for jazz is merely a symptom of the fact that the mass of humanity feels itself to be a percussion instrument in the hands of terrible rulers.

Poor in deeds and rich in thought.

The dialectical reverse test also works: poor in thought and rich in deeds.

In that case, I still prefer Genoveva, rich in suffering.[^fn-p07-pdf17-n01]

---

**24 June 1948**

Does every power theory of law reduce power to causality?

Certainly. But to divine power as *causa prima*, the first cause.

Only power consecrates law.[^fn-p07-pdf17-n02]

Only power invests law.

Only power clothes law!

Naked law is more terrible than naked power.

“Law as such” against “power as such”: this is the great reversal performed by the nineteenth century on behalf of the defeated—that is, on behalf of Satan against God.

Byronism and Proudhonism.

Burckhardt.

Causality is power.

Hobbes knew that.

The whole world must be thought according to one single image.

The law of causality is merely a law of power formulated for mechanistic experiments.

Incidentally:

(The hatred Kaete E.[isler] feels toward me and continues to stir up can no longer know any boundary. It is the hatred of the Jewish woman for the German, for the Roman Catholic, for the peasant boy, for the *περίψημα*, the outcast. But alongside all these objective motives comes the most private one of all, which must complete the hysteria: the struggle over the soul of the husband.

The woman’s hatred of her husband’s friend.)

Power:

Lucan’s atheism.

*Sunt nobis nulla profecto Numina*—there are, in truth, no gods for us—against the gods.

*sed victa Catoni.*

The *Sanctus Cato*, the holy Cato.

The *surdae aures Coelicolum*—the deaf ears of the heavenly beings.

*Mortalia nulli Sunt curata Deo*—no god cares for mortal affairs.

*habemus vindictam, quantam terris dare numina fas est*—we have our revenge, as great a revenge as the gods are permitted to grant on earth!!

(VII, 455–56)

*Mentimur regnare Jovem!*—we lie when we say that Jupiter rules!

(VII, 447)

“A criminal deed in the clothing of law, where with victorious fists a mighty people tore through its own entrails.”

This is how the young Hölderlin translates it (Hellingrath, vol. VI, p. 120):

*jusque datum sceleri canimus, populumque potentem
in sua victrici conversum viscera dextra.* This translation dresses the passage in Baroque costume!

Beside it, even a rhetorician such as Lucan seems very matter-of-fact.

The *dextra*, the right hand or right arm, becomes a fist.

To “give” *jus*, law, becomes clothing.

*Potens*, powerful, becomes “mighty.”

*Scelus* becomes “criminal deed.”

*Jus* and *fas* are not distinguished!

The difference between these billowing Baroque robes and the rhetorical gesture of antiquity: the ancient gesture does not disappear into infinity. It remains within a frame. It grinds its teeth, but it does not call out for an echo from infinity.

---

**25 June 1948**

But I will cultivate within myself the seed of freedom.
My only companions remain a flock of jackdaws.
I love their coming and their ever-deeper blueing into distance.
Isn’t that so, beggars of the air? We shall remain forever strong and poor.

(II. 495)

Isn’t that so, beggars of the air!

---

**26 June 1948**

Hopeless, the case of the bourgeois family’s only sons: complete monads, full of maggots, protected on every side, padded in cotton wool.

The peasant has only one child.

The bourgeois has only this one son.

*Fils de famille*.

A hopeless case.

Am I supposed to waste my time on that?[^fn-p07-pdf18-n01]

Re-encounter with Theodor Däubler.

Only now is our conversation of 1912 unfolding in all its fullness and becoming fully present.

*Jamjam hiscit flammeus!*

Now the fiery one is opening his mouth!

---

**27 June 1948**

Read Nicolaus Sombart’s *Capriccio*. It reminds me of the young Walter Fuchs.

Not much comes of it.

A sad thought: this young man, whom I love, has gone over to the abortionists. He possessed a magnificent seed of genuine scholarly intuition—the existence of the person against the apparatus—and he aborted it in literature.

Out of impatience, laziness, hunger for pleasure, vanity, and the need to display his boyish mysteries of relations with girls.

Behind the question, so often posed in an abstract and general way, of whether only states or also individuals are subjects of international law, there lies a far more concrete, deeper, and more disturbing question:

Should the individual himself be able to decide independently on war and peace?

Does he possess his own *jus ad bellum*, his own right to go to war? That means the right, and even the duty, to resist.

Yes: a return to private war. And now there he stands, with his honourable subjectivity, helpless between the objective powers, which tear him to pieces.

---

**28 June 1948**

To Gerhard Günther:

Magic and space belong together.

Not magic and time.

I, here in Plettenberg, in the mountains beside the Lenne, lose my time and gain my space.

Time falls away from me.

Space approaches me and holds me in its embrace. It encloses and protects me.

Could you not come here sometime and question me as a “primitive,” and make me an object of your research into magical thinking?

Space is paradise.

Time is hell.

Boundary is magic. There is no empty space. But there is empty time.

Law is order, which means location.

See Corollary 1 to *The Nomos of the Earth*.

The two hunters on p. 23 of *Land and Sea* are mythical, and not merely mythology. For all the talk about myth that has gone on for years, I know only one man who truly realizes myth as a poet:

Theodor Däubler.

In him, the dissolution and self-dissolution of the great philosophy of German idealism releases theogonic transformations.

Thirty-two years ago I published a small book on Däubler’s *Northern Lights*, which I had pulped in 1925.

Today he confronts me again with immense power. And the little book contains completely different things from what I thought it contained at the time.

Däubler, incidentally, was the first to make use of the magic in the word “space,” long before the Expressionists and before Rilke.

But, however, and in spite of everything:

I know the dear Germans already, etc.[^fn-p07-pdf19-n01]

---

**29 June 1948**

Further rules of Don Capisco:

Beware of every loudspeaker.[^fn-p07-pdf19-n02]

Beware of every microphone that carries your voice into the wrong public sphere.

Every amplifier of sound is a falsifier of meaning.

World public opinion is the deception of the world.

What belongs to the world belongs to the devil. That is as true again today as it was in the year 63, in the time of Nero, Seneca, and the Apostle Paul.

Today the beautiful Christian forms of creaturely life developed by the Middle Ages have once again been completely abolished and assimilated away. But beware also of the false echo produced in the winding vaults of the catacombs.

Last night I almost succumbed again to the impatience of justice when I reread Francisco de Vitoria: the seven *tituli idonei et non idonei*, the valid and invalid titles,[^fn-p07-pdf19-n03] and once again recognized the horrifying abuse made of his doctrine of just war.

Especially the five *Dubia circa justitiam belli*, doubts concerning the justice of war, and the nine *Dubiosa quantum liceat in bello justo*, doubts concerning how much is permitted in a just war.[^fn-p07-pdf19-n04]

Anyone who speaks of just war without showing that all these *dubia* and *dubiosa* have become part of his practical, moral, and historical consciousness no longer has any authority on his side.

The ideological fraud involved in exploiting and using all these doubts becomes all the clearer.

The trick is one that Francisco de Vitoria himself already employs:

*omnia cedunt in favorem et jus justum bellum gerentium.*

Everything gives way in favour of those who wage a just war and of the rights they claim through it.

With the help of this principle, even the otherwise so cautious Vitoria allows captured war booty not to be counted against claims for reparations and requisitions:

*si licite sunt capta, puto quod non sunt obnoxia restitutioni.*

If they were lawfully captured, I think they are not subject to restitution. So says the great theologian in *De jure belli*, second doubt concerning how much is permitted in a just war.

*Tantum licet in bello justo!!*

So much is permitted in a just war!!

Perhaps this sentence can help me identify my own *peccatum*, my own sin, and thereby answer the question that has tormented me for years:

Why does everything I say provoke such inexplicable hostility?

What terrible thing have I done?

*J’ai montré la porte secrète de ce sanctuaire écarté où se jugent les perplexités de la justice et tous les problèmes, pour lesquels Thémis n’a pas de balance: car si on les montre, l’avide intérêt et tous les sophismes des passions forcent bientôt la porte et violent la conscience dans son dernier asile.*[^fn-p07-pdf20-n01]

I showed the secret door of that secluded sanctuary where the perplexities of justice are judged, together with all those problems for which Themis has no scales.
