Some will also understand why I so often quote the sentence:

**I do not compare the victims. I compare only the judges.**

And the few who are initiated will understand where the development is heading—a development that does not yet fully take the form of justice being killed by political overburdening, but which already reveals precisely that tendency.

Out of *homo homini homo*—man is man to man—out of the complete humanization of law, there arises: *judex homini lupus.* The judge is a wolf to man.

10. Gelimer’s laughter does not stop.

But that does not have to prevent us from seeing our reality. On the contrary: it can and should shake the scenery and stage sets of deception. In that way, it becomes a form of appeal appropriate to the situation:

*J’en appelle de ta justice à ta réalité.*

I appeal from your justice to your reality.

**End of Gelimer’s laughter.**

# Appendix to Books I–V

Asylum and Location.

1. **Location**

All roads lead to Rome.

The problem of *Roma aeterna*, Eternal Rome.

An indissoluble connection—in law, even if not always in fact—between the universal episcopate and the Roman episcopate:

Charles Journet, *L’Église du Verbe incarné*, I, *La hiérarchie apostolique*, Paris 1941, p. 522.

The Pope always remains Bishop of Rome, even if he moves his residence somewhere else.

*Siège de Rome / résidence.*

Péronne:

“Wherever he resides, the true successor of Saint Peter must necessarily remain Bishop of Rome.”

*Praelectiones theologicae*, Paris 1856, vol. IV, p. 257.

Ch. Journet agrees.

**Dissoluble:**

Jean de Saint-Thomas:

“It is a matter of divine faith that the papacy and the See of Rome were united in the past and remain united today; nevertheless, this union is temporary.”

It is not irrevocable.

The bond can be changed under Church law; it is not indissoluble under divine law.

The “Roman Church” would therefore be such a <soul?> only in name.

**Indissoluble:**

in law and in fact.

It is impossible for Rome ever to exist without clergy or faithful people.

Thus Bellarmine, *De Romano Pontifice*, Book IV, ch. 4.

Even the very soil of Rome cannot disappear:

Billot, *De Ecclesia Christi*, p. 596.

*Roma aeterna*.

A Swiss scholar, R. M. Schultes, states this explicitly in *De Ecclesia Catholica*, Paris 1925, p. 455.

Thesis:

There are just wars, but only in the sense of wars conducted according to proper form.

There are no just wars except formally regular wars.

“In 1858 the whole plain of northern Europe, as well as the Danube in the south, bore evident marks of being still the prehistoric highway between Asia and the Ocean. 1901!

“and Russia was the most indigestible morsel he ever met; but the sum of it, viewed from Cologne, seamed reasonable.[^fn-p20-pdf16-n03] From Hammerfest to Cherbourg on one shore of the Ocean, from Halifax to Norfolk on the other, one great empire was ruled by one great emperor – Coal.[^fn-p20-pdf16-n04] Political and human jealousies might tear it apart or divide it, but the power and the empire were one. **13 August 1947**

The verses by Lenau from the *Travel Pages*—“The Log Cabin,” 1833 [recte: 1839]—and sentences in the log cabin in the <Agir>.

Look at the burning logs:

These trunks are burning here upon the hearth
To keep me warm for one brief hour,
Though soon enough I too must grow cold,
And I myself will sink into ash.

Perhaps there is no loneliness at all?
Am I myself only a burning log?

And while I warm myself beside the oak,
Perhaps an unseen guest is warming himself
In secret at my consuming flame of life,
Stirring and fanning the fever of my thoughts?

His constant wavering between belief in God, <panegyric> moods, despair, nihilism, engagements, and ridiculous adventures.

All of it amounts to so little.

And finally, madness.

And yet this is the greatest poet of the period before 1848.

How secure and courageous Annette seems by comparison.

She was challenged just as deeply, and she was every bit as lovely, but infinitely stronger.

How firmly she keeps both her reason and her moral bearing!

**26 August 1947**

Law is eternal.

Only form is eternal.

*Ê* and *Ewe*, marriage and property—the same thing: form.

Form means deliberately looking away from the interest, mood, and plan of the moment.

A leap into eternity.

Holding back and holding down immediate interest.

The *katechon*, the restrainer, is present here too.

Only in this way does form become possible.

A reach from what cannot be understood into what cannot be grasped.

That is the legal concept.

Legal form is therefore an angling, a folding together of the eternal and the temporal: within temporal material, an eternal moment.

It appears as an institution rooted in a place: the enclosed Thing-site where the assembly meets; the judge’s seat; the defendant’s bench; the crown of the land of Hungary, Bohemia, Castile and León, England.

Location is this angling: the folding of the eternal into something temporal.

Law depends entirely on this form.

(Consequence: the angle in which x temporal and <…> x earthly and unearthly concepts meet.)

That is why the jurist has a theological origin.

And that is why he displaces the theologian when the theologian is no longer capable of creating such institutions and instead crawls into a *potestas indirecta*, an indirect power.

That is also why legal science comes to an end when the jurist becomes a technician.

At that point he is no longer even capable of forming a concept.

Punishment then becomes: security; hygiene; pest control; the extermination of bedbugs.

And its great form, the criminal trial, accordingly becomes a technical measure carried out by police officers, doctors, propagandists, and the chemists of wars of annihilation.

---

**26 August 1947**

The distinction often made between jurisprudence and legal science—for example by Karl Renner—rests entirely on the assumption of a positivist, natural-scientific idea of what “science” means.

Once that assumption is made, legal science becomes a wretched technical science.

Theology and legal science, however, are sciences of a particular kind.

An internal tension is essential to both of them.

Only this tension sets thought in motion.

In that respect they resemble the opposing tensions from which genuine natural sciences begin and toward which they move: positive and negative; full and empty; particles and waves; and so on.

In theology this tension can take forms such as:

Infinite — finite.

*Natura naturans* — *natura naturata*.

Constituent power — constituted power.

Compare *Dictatorship*, p. 142.

Substitution — decision.

Charisma — office.

Pneuma — tradition.

Compare the marvelous essay by Hans Barion on Rudolf Sohm, *Deutsche Rechtswissenschaft*, January 1942.

But is the infinite not precisely the absence of form?

Does the formless not break through at this point?

This is where jurisprudence touches theology and finds in theology the support without which jurisprudence sinks.

Correct.

Theology does not find that support in another science.

It finds it directly in “revelation.”

Legal science therefore presupposes a constituted theology—not merely a “religion.”

It is a science modeled on theological science.

Jurisprudence in general is possible when it can lean on a constituted religion.

Law and religion.

Legal science and theology.

Pity = selfhood and its apparent opposite.

One only ever feels pity for oneself.

What is pity?

Identification with another person.

So the other person becomes identified with me—but even more importantly, my own self becomes identified with the other.

Therefore all pity is self-pity.

And I am ashamed of the accusation made against Germans that they feel sorry for themselves.

When things are going this badly for someone, and pity is supposed to be the first humanitarian virtue, is the wretched German really forbidden to feel pity for himself?

The shameless Phariseeism of these smug little guardians of humanitarian virtue!

Rousseau stands at the beginning of all such lies.

But at least he himself was still a poor tormented devil, a helpless bohemian.

Now, by contrast, along come the fat, overfed gluttons and declare our starving corpses morally disgusting.

*[Folio 8r]*

I do not barricade myself inside a conclusion.

I do not bury myself in an achievement.

That means I do not die and I do not look backward.

I continue to serve, and therefore I continue to live.

I do not stop at any thought.

I do not remain with any conclusion.

I keep going and keep pushing onward.

That is why only a few people can follow me.

Most run out of breath.

They stop at some particular point in my process of thought and try to pin me down there.

In other words, they declare me dead because they themselves are dead.

They want to fix me in place and make me rigid, just as they themselves are fixed and rigid.

Anyone who wants to hold me to my <yesterday’s> thought will find that I am already in the beyond.

I am no longer there.

I have disappeared into what cannot be grasped.

And this is why they become furious when they discover that physically I am still alive, however modestly and secretly, somewhere in some miserable refuge.

Their hatred only grows stronger.

Their desire to persecute me bursts into flame at the thought that I am still alive not only intellectually, but physically as well.

These people belong to the past.

For that reason they are dead.

But they do not know death.

I have known it for a long time.

It is constantly reborn from the spirit and from thought: life as the great festival of <metaphysics>, in whose constant transformation physical death is only one moment among many.

I have already died many times.

And I am still alive.

As for what there is to fear in physical death, and what there is **not** to fear, I have considerable experience.

I have tested it.

I fear physical death less than I fear the filthy meanness of those shades who tried to drag me down onto the level of their own corpses: those poor fat caterpillars trying to glue a butterfly in flight with their slime.

(Form = distance;

= perspective;

and precisely that is supposed to disappear early!)

**26 August [1947], evening**

Again and again:

“the prey of the mighty moment,” which tears me upward and downward.

The tutor of Friedrich Wilhelm IV used the expression “the prey of the mighty moment” in front of his pupil.

But we are all prey to it.

Annette above all.

Her letters affected me profoundly.

How charmingly she speaks, in her language and her surroundings: a girl; a bright and intelligent, wisely foolish virgin; one could imagine nothing more beautiful.

Then she falls in love twice.

First with Heinrich Straube.

Then with Levin Schücking.

Each time with a bourgeois literary man who probably won her heart only because he offered her the literary understanding she could not find among people of her own estate, class, and caste.

These infatuations were intense.

But they never reached the core of her being.

She remained a virgin.

Amazon-like.

An intelligent girl, intelligent even in a practical domestic sense.

Nothing decadent about her.

Levin Schücking’s <fraternally bound> “little mother.”

In an age that was coming apart, she remained unstupid, indestructible right down to the heart.

And yet she was obedient, as every good woman was expected to be, obedient to her time.

She went along with its currents.

She dutifully participated in the literary business of her age.

At times she <bobbin-laced> verses together in a Schillerian <manner>, in the <pseudo-agitation> of this <…> and of this dissolved Lenau.

The doubts of *The Spiritual Year* are the recoil back into herself after those foolish infatuations with literary men.

The imperfect nun.

The faithless Druidess.

Her accusations against herself become so terrible because she carries a great standard within herself.

At the beginning of the age of *l’art pour l’art*, she certainly participates in the literary world—but no more than is proper for a well-brought-up, respectable, obedient girl.

At the deepest level she knows the nihilism of her age.

And it shatters her.

That is the meaning of *The Spiritual Year*.

Her aversion to the schoolmaster Julius Schering.

That is why the greatest <…> of the young girl;

the first half of the poems of *The Spiritual Year*, the Holy Week poems;

the second part of *The Spiritual Year* already laments consciously, already becomes a hand-wringing cry over what is being lost;

while the first part is still a lament.

She could not look upon the Virgin Mary.

Mary was too “bright” for her.

She could think of Mary’s purity only with terror.

Oh, poor Annette.

*[Folio 9r]*

**27 August 1947**

The infatuations were literary mutations of love.

She was not a saint.

But her sadness came from knowing that she was not a saint.

*La tristesse de ne pas être des saintes.*

The sadness of not being saints.

That sadness lies closer to holiness than any other human condition, including <…>.

Anyone who does not know this has no choice but to become a schoolmaster, whether he gives *The Spiritual Year* a good grade, as Kreiten did, or a bad one, as Julius Schering did.

A saint with a laurel wreath: the poetry business of the time, publishers’ theatrics, pseudo-fame.

The most successful and famous poet of the time was Lenau.

Yes, he fishes pearls and jewels,
And they cost nothing but his soul.

The genuine pearls are tears of repentance.

*The Spiritual Year*, fourth Sunday after Pentecost, p. 121.

The core of her work is the poems of *The Spiritual Year*.

What is this foolish historiography with its endless “if only” and “what if”?

If this or that had not happened, everything would have turned out differently.

The horrifying madness of these unreal fantasies.

All this “if only” and “what if” is a symptom.

These historians are merely the exhaust pipe for an activism that was prevented, obstructed, or defeated.

Prometheus raging on paper.

The worst example is Mommsen’s portrayal of Julius Caesar.

Here <…>, not Caesar, but an example in vers<…> secures all his <activist> wish-dreams:

the symbol of nerve and spirit,

*mens sana in corpore sano*—a healthy mind in a healthy body—<…>.

The other possibility is the contemplative one: the Christian Epimetheus.

He does not want to think the already-thought all over again.

You cannot walk through the same river twice.

You cannot think the same thought twice.

The second time, it will be either more correct or more false.

Anyone who does not know that cannot really think at all.

Above all, he cannot reflect.

To reflect means to think differently.

But then the thought is no longer “genuine.”

This dreadful obsession with authenticity among historians, art historians, and legal historians!

Everything withers miserably under their sterility.

They want to think everything again: how everything was; how it happened; how it came about that it happened.

Everything all over again, and this time more correctly.

That is not merely a ridiculous claim.

It is an impertinent one.

To claim that one has found an “authentic” <bright> image of the Middle Ages on the basis of extremist art-historical categories <?>—what inwardly falsified authenticity!

The authenticity and purity of these zealots.

What does this whole myth of the Worker actually mean?

The technologization of soldiers.

The <…> of the Saint-Simonian, Comtean, Spencerian antithesis: the opposition between the military and industry.

Democratized industry?

The activated Promethean.

The bride earns herself more with one kiss for God <?> than all the half-breeds <?> do through labor unto death.

But according to Ernst Jünger’s *The Worker*, even a kiss is “work”!!!

[On the right:]

The whole mythology of the Worker comes from this.

So at its core all this Promethean noise surrounds a nothing: everything is supposed to become <…>, and tomorrow my graves <?>, when we create the world.

Yes indeed, Professor.

We’ll take care of that.

Then the great Gustav Klemm:

Here matters become clearer.

Either protection among active and passive races, <…>.

Everything else follows automatically once the framework of the inherited Christian churches falls away and the restraints people still feel come to an end.

Night of 16–17 October 1931:

O my poor soul.

It lies exposed to everything, helpless like a country road over which we hardworking people walk; where thieving Gypsies and <desert robbers> stand; where beautiful pilgrimage processions pass, and then again, gladly and <beautifully> <…>.

I immediately see the furthest <consequence> in the <observation/remark>, <…> are the final thing; this is not symbolism but <…>; sound understanding.

Say that this wish, this spirit of a human being, that <stupid> <Potzner>, is already a murder.

This other suicide of the spirit (a drinker, out of rage, pours schnapps into himself) (like a woman <…> entirely to <…>).

This is not symbolism but <lack of consequence>.

Sexual excitement and <…>; not really sexual at all, <knocking> fantasy; not something that can be judged by its value, but the filthy fermentation of suicidal masturbation, new nourishment for the frenzy of his <fantasy-images>.

The declaration of someone as *hors-la-loi*—outside the law—is always the <…error>; either it succeeds or it <is/becomes> meaningless, in which case a new regime has been created without <gain>, or an old one has been abandoned. (Nap. 12 June 99) <…>.

A diseased vine on Hegel’s tree.

# Commentary

**28 August 1947**

**Noble simplicity** — J. J. Winckelmann’s highly influential definition of classical art.

**trahison des clercs** — Julien Benda, *La trahison des clercs*, Paris 1927; German: *Der Verrat der Intellektuellen*, Munich 1978.

**King Peter** — Schmitt is presumably referring to Peter II Karađorđević (1923–1970), King of Yugoslavia from 1934. In November 1945 the Communists forced him to give up the throne.

**God transforms the lie** — Allusion to Romans 1:22 ff.

**Enrico Corradini** — Italian nationalist writer and journalist (1865–1931); became a minister in 1928.

**Sallust contra pecuniam** — In his *Bellum Iugurthinum* (*The Jugurthine War*), Sallust describes how King Jugurtha was able to bribe the Roman nobility with money.

**bellum externum …** — *Quattuor principes ferro interempti: trina bella civilia, plura externa ac plerumque permixta.*

“Four emperors were killed by the sword. There were three civil wars, more foreign wars, and most of them were mixed together.”

Tacitus, *Histories* I.2. Tacitus is speaking here about the bloody Year of the Four Emperors, AD 69, which was disastrous for Rome.

**Otto Brunner** — Otto Brunner, *Land und Herrschaft*, 1973. The first quotation (lines 5–7) is on p. 145; the second (“that the problem of sovereignty …”) is on p. 144, n. 1; and the third (“As long as …”) is also on p. 144. Schmitt’s quotation, however, includes the second word *aber* (“but”), which is missing here.

**Ganahl** — Karl-Hans Ganahl (1905–1942), Austrian legal historian.

**Willy Haas** — Willy Haas, “Eine neue politische Lehre,” in *Die literarische Welt* (Berlin), vol. 8, no. 12, 20 May 1932, pp. 1–2.

**The habilitation thesis by the SS man Lemmel** — Herbert Lemmel, *Die Volksgemeinschaft, ihre Erfassung im werdenden Recht*, Stuttgart/Berlin 1941. Berlin habilitation in law and political science, dated 14 July 1939. Submitted under the title *Die Erfassung der Gemeinschaft im lebensgesetzlichen Recht*. Reinhard Höhn was the first examiner and Carl Schmitt the second.

See Carl Schmitt, report on the habilitation thesis of Dr. jur. Herbert Lemmel, RW 265 no. 19074; Christian Tilitzki, “Carl Schmitt – Staatsrechtler in Berlin. Einblicke in seinen Wirkungskreis anhand der Fakultätsakten 1934–1944,” in *Etappe* 7, 1991, pp. 62–117, especially pp. 65–66 and 72–74.

In his habilitation thesis, Lemmel criticized Schmitt’s concepts because they had no connection with “race” or with the “blood-structure of the people.”

The SS officer Lemmel (1911–1990), after returning from Soviet captivity, became a commercial judge in Frankfurt am Main in 1950, and later a businessman and factory owner in Bad Homburg.

Schmitt’s papers contain seven letters and two postcards from Lemmel dating from 1948 to 1978 (RW 0265 nos. 8724–8732), in which Lemmel unsuccessfully tried to establish a closer relationship with Schmitt.

**28 August 1947**

**as Ortega told me** — Schmitt spoke with the Spanish philosopher José Ortega y Gasset (1885–1955) in Lisbon on 20 May 1944. See Christian Tilitzki, “Die Vortragsreisen Carl Schmitts während des Zweiten Weltkriegs,” in *Schmittiana* VI, 1998, p. 249.

**Tacitus** — Quotations from Tacitus, *Histories*:

I.1: *magna [illa] ingenia cessere* — “Those great minds have disappeared.”

I.2: *opus adgredior optimum casibus, atrox proeliis, discors seditionibus, ipsa etiam pace saevum* — “I approach a work rich in reversals of fortune, savage in battle, divided by sedition, terrible even in peace.”

**29 August 1947**

**nefasque mixtum** — *Conquerar, an moneam mixtum fas omne nefasque?*

“Should I lament, or should I warn that good and evil have become completely mixed together?”

Ovid, *Ars amatoria*, Book I, 739–740.

**Barion essay** — Hans Barion, “Der Rechtsbegriff Rudolph Sohms. Zur 100. Wiederkehr von Sohms Geburtstag,” in *Deutsche Rechtswissenschaft* 7, 1942, pp. 47–51; reprinted in H. Barion, *Kirche und Kirchenrecht. Gesammelte Aufsätze*, ed. Werner Böckenförde, Paderborn 1984, pp. 115–119.

**plenitudo potestatis …** — “Immediate absolute power over everyone and over each individual.” This was the formula used from the High Middle Ages onward for the pope’s claim to power. Compare *Dictatorship*, pp. 42–43.

**a Deo excitatus** — In Protestant historical writing, Luther was said to have begun his Reformation *a Deo excitatus*: “called forth by God.”

**31 August 1947**

**Berlin lecture** — James T. Shotwell (1864–1965), American historian and politician, and a leading promoter of the Kellogg Pact.

The lecture was “Stehen wir an einem Wendepunkt der Weltgeschichte?” (“Are We at a Turning Point in World History?”), given on 1 March 1927 at the German Academy of Politics in Berlin as part of the newly established Carnegie chair. In it, Shotwell called for the renunciation of war.

Published in Henri Lichtenberger / James Shotwell / Max Scheler, *Ausgleich als Schicksal und Aufgabe*, Berlin 1929, pp. 15–28.

**Jäckh** — Ernst Jaeckh (1875–1959), journalist, founder and lecturer at the German Academy of Politics; emigrated in 1933.

**2 September 1947**

**M. J. Bonn** — Moritz Julius Bonn (1873–1965), political economist. In 1919, as director of the Munich School of Commerce, he secured a lectureship there for Carl Schmitt; in 1928 he brought Schmitt to the Berlin School of Commerce.

In his memoirs Bonn wrote very negatively about Schmitt. See M. J. Bonn, *So macht man Geschichte. Bilanz eines Lebens*, Munich 1953, pp. 330–332, with a note in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 25938.

**Spiritus malignus, magnus deceptor** — “The evil spirit, the great deceiver.” In Cartesian philosophy, our ability to know is threatened if we mistake what is false for what is true.

**Castor-Pollux offer** — Refers to the poem “An Levin Schücking” by Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, final stanza:

Pollux and Castor—alternating glow and pallor,
The light of one taken only from the other,
And yet the sign of the most faithful loyalty.
So give me your hand, my Dioscurus!
And may the lovely myth renew itself,
Where the twin flame burned above the helmet.

**Tout ce qui arrive est adorable** — “Everything that happens is worthy of adoration.”

Léon Bloy used the sentence repeatedly, for example in letters to Julien Leclercq dated 31 July 1894 and to Heinrich de Groux dated 8 June 1895, published in L. Bloy, *Le mendiant ingrat*.

The sentence confirmed Schmitt’s view of history, which had been shaped by Konrad Weiß. Schmitt also liked to quote it as a way of expressing his dislike of unreal “if only” statements about things that had already happened.

**3 September 1947**

**Gerhard Günther** — (1889–1976), conservative journalist, brother of Albrecht Erich Günther.

**The Leviathan has spat me out three times** — Namely in 1936, when Schmitt survived an attack by the SS; in 1946, when he was released from the American camp at Berlin-Lichterfelde; and in 1947, when he was released from detention as a witness at Nuremberg.

**Quiesco, exsul in patria mea …** — “I remain quiet, an exile in my own country.”

The phrase *ex[s]ul in patria mea* appears often in these years. See the entries for 4 June 1948, 16 September 1949, and 25 November 1949; *BW Forsthoff*, p. 52; *BW Mohler*, p. 67; *FoP*, p. 590.

Its importance to Schmitt’s understanding of himself is clear from the fact that he placed it at the head of Book III of the *Glossarium*. See the appendix.

**Bernanos** — Georges Bernanos (1888–1948), French Catholic writer. He was discussed as a possible French ambassador to Rome, but was never appointed. On the speech, see the entry for 13 March 1949.

**4 September 1947**

**Castruccio Castracani** — (1281–1328), Italian mercenary commander.

Machiavelli writes of him:

As he was walking through a street, he saw a young man coming out of a prostitute’s house. The young man blushed deeply when he realized Castruccio had seen him.

Castruccio said:

“Do not be ashamed when you come out. Be ashamed when you go in.”

Niccolò Machiavelli, *Das Leben des Castruccio Castracani von Lucca*, German-Italian edition, Cologne/Vienna 1969, p. 81.

**“Let us make man”** — Genesis 1:26.

**5 September 1947**

**“creeping softly”** — From Annette von Droste-Hülshoff’s *Geistliches Jahr*. In the poem “Am zehnten Sonntag nach Pfingsten”:

And let me only look upon
A feather, trembling secretly,
Remembering that behind its black trace
Death and life creep softly.

**7 September 1947**

**Pinder** — Wilhelm Pinder (1878–1947), art historian; professor at Friedrich Wilhelm University in Berlin from 1935 to 1945.

**Fumet** — As part of the twenty-volume collected edition of L. Bloy, Stanislas Fumet edited Léon Bloy, *Le mendiant ingrat*, Paris 1948.

When Schmitt writes “likewise the new edition 1928,” he apparently means this edition.

**Claudel** — Paul Claudel, *Introduction au “Livre de Ruth.” Texte intégral de l’ouvrage de l’Abbé de Moidrey*, Paris 1938, pp. 109–110.

**Cor Jesu, saturatum opprobriis** — “Heart of Jesus, filled with reproaches,” from the Catholic Litany of the Sacred Heart.

**9 September 1947**

**Hauriou** — Maurice Hauriou (1856–1929), French jurist.

**already in Bodin** — Jean Bodin, *Les six livres de la république. Rev. corrigée & augm. de nouveau*, Paris 1580 (RW 265 no. 22687).

**10 September 1947**

**Bellarmin** — Roberto Bellarmino (1542–1621), Jesuit controversial theologian and important cardinal. He developed the doctrine of the Church’s *potestas indirecta*, its indirect power.

His *Autobiografia*, written in 1613, was not published until 1751 in Ferrara.

**relatiuncula, scriptiuncula, breviculum, notila** — Dismissive Latin terms for a “work” or piece of writing: roughly, “little report,” “little writing,” “little brief,” “little note.”

**13 September 1947**

**aquae [correctly: aqua] et igni interdictus** — “Someone denied water and fire,” meaning denied hospitality. A Roman formula of outlawry.

There is no evidence at all that Schmitt was unwelcome in Dr Schranz’s house in Siedlinghausen in 1947. It is possible, however, that some of the other guests treated him with reserve.

**18 September 1947**

**Visit from Paul Adams** — Paul Adams (1894–1961), editor of the cultural supplement of the Centre Party newspaper *Germania*. From 1934 he worked in radio in Munich and belonged to the Siedlinghausen circle. Schmitt regarded him as one of his closest friends. See p. 125.

**Knappe** — Karl Knappe (1884–1978), sculptor and stained-glass artist in Munich, and a friend of Konrad Weiß.

**Rikus** — Josef Rikus (1923–1989), sculptor. In January 1946 he moved to Siedlinghausen to work with the sculptor Eugen Senge-Platten (1890–1972). From 1947 he continued his training under Karl Knappe.

**Möllenbrock** — Klemens Möllenbrock, *Die religiöse Lyrik der Droste und die Theologie der Zeit. Versuch einer theologischen Gesamtinterpretation und theologiegeschichtlichen Einordnung des “Geistlichen Jahres”*, Berlin 1935; doctoral dissertation in philosophy, Münster 1934.

**Westemeyer** — Dietmar Westemeyer, *Donoso Cortés. Staatsmann und Theologe. Eine Untersuchung seines Einsatzes der Theologie in die Politik*, Münster 1940; Spanish translation published in 1957.

Joseph Westemeyer (1908–1997) took the religious name Dietmar when he entered the Franciscan order.

The published book was based on his 1940 Catholic-theology dissertation at Münster.

**Veit** — Otto Veit, *Die Flucht vor der Freiheit. Versuch zur geschichtsphilosophischen Erhellung der Kulturkrise*, Frankfurt am Main 1947.

**Memories of Walther Rathenau** — On Schmitt’s relationship with Rathenau, see his account in *Schattenrisse*, as well as *Tb 1912–15*, pp. 333–335, and *Tb 1921–24*, pp. 103–107, 116–119.

**Goethe, “We live …”** — Probably Schmitt’s paraphrase of Goethe’s maxim:

“We all live from the past, and we perish from the past.”

Goethe, *Maximen und Reflexionen*, 167.

**paradisiacal little chambers** — A phrase used by the Catholic pastoral theologian Johann Michael Sailer (1751–1832), which Schmitt may have known through Eschweiler.

See Karl Eschweiler, *Die katholische Theologie im Zeitalter des deutschen Idealismus. Die Bonner theologischen Qualifikationsschriften von 1921/22. Aus dem Nachlaß hrsg. und mit einer Einl. vers. von Thomas Marschler*, Münster 2010, p. 163.

**20 September 1947**

**Coclicus** — Adrien Petit Coclico (1499/1500–after September 1562), composer and music theorist.

**Huber’s dissertation** — Kurt Huber (1893–1943), musicologist and member of the White Rose resistance group.

Kurt Huber, *Ivo de Vento (ca. 1540–1575)*, Lindenberg im Allgäu 1918; doctoral dissertation in philosophy, Munich 1918.

**in my essay on the taboo** — Not identified.

**Kalijarvi** — Thorsten V. Kalijarvi, “Die Neutralität Amerikas,” in *Europäische Revue* 11, 1935, p. 721.

Kalijarvi (1897–1980) was professor of political science at the University of New Hampshire in the United States.

**21 September 1947**

**Lewis** — Wyndham Lewis, *The Enemy. A Review of Art and Literature*, London 1927 ff.; idem, *Hitler und sein Werk in englischer Beleuchtung*, Berlin 1932; idem, *Time and Western Man*, London 1927.

In the second edition of *Die geistesgeschichtliche Lage des heutigen Parlamentarismus*, Schmitt had already referred in 1926 to Wyndham Lewis, *The Art of Being Ruled*, London 1926: GL, p. 11, n. 1.

The text here is in shorthand. It probably reads:

“did not arouse the hostility that I aroused.”

**Essay by Hennecke** — Hans Hennecke, “Wyndham Lewis. Vision und Satire,” in *Europäische Revue* 14, 1938, pp. 205–214.

**Rosenbaum** — Eduard Rosenbaum (1887–1979), Schmitt’s fellow student and friend from Strasbourg. See *Tb 1912–15*, pp. 404–405.

On 25 November 1950 he wrote against Schmitt in the *Rheinischer Merkur* under the title “Carl Schmitt vor den Toren.”

It is unclear whether he had already expressed criticism of Schmitt in 1947.

**“I do not know that I did well, but I did honestly” (Grey)** — The British Foreign Secretary Edward Grey (1862–1933) wrote this sentence to his wife in 1906.

See Viscount Grey of Fallodon, *Twenty Five Years*, vol. 1, Toronto 1923, p. 79.

**Film** — Schmitt’s attitude toward film here was completely different from his attitude in the 1920s and 1930s. Compare his diaries.

**22 September 1947**

**“All I inherited was my own body …”** — Richard Wagner, *Götterdämmerung*, Act I, Scene 2.

**23 September 1947**

**Podszus** — Friedrich Podszus (1899–1971), literary scholar and editor, and co-editor of the two-volume Benjamin edition of 1955.

See Helmut Peitsch, “Wolf von Niebelschütz, Walter Benjamin und ihre Leser im ‘Dritten Reich’. Zur Erinnerung an Friedrich Podszus,” in *LiLi. Zeitschrift für Literaturwissenschaft und Linguistik* 16, 1986, pp. 170–178.

**Binaris numerus infamis** — “Two is an evil number.” Meister Eckhart.

See Wouter Goris, *Einheit als Prinzip und Ziel. Versuch über die Einheitsmetaphysik des Opus tripartitum Meister Eckharts*, Leiden/New York/Cologne 1997, pp. 106 ff.

**25 September 1947**

**Drucker, “For Jews always remain Jews …”** — Peter F. Drucker (1909–2005), Austrian economist. He emigrated to England in 1933 and became a US citizen in 1943. He later became an influential writer and teacher on management.

Peter F. Drucker, *The End of Economic Man: The Origins of Totalitarianism*, first edition, London 1943; German: *Ursprung des Totalitarismus. Das Ende des Homo Oeconomicus*, Vienna 2010.

In the third edition, New Brunswick/London 1995, reprinted 2009, the first sentence quoted by Schmitt appears on p. 213:

“To the extent that the problem of self-assertion and self-justification becomes more and more urgent, totalitarianism must invent new personifications of new demons.”

The second sentence appears on p. 209:

“In comparison with the Jews, even the Communists are of doubtful value as demonic enemies.”

Shortly afterward Schmitt continues:

“For Jews always remain Jews. A Communist, by contrast, can improve and change. This has nothing to do with Nordic race and so on. It is precisely the assimilated Jew who is the true enemy. There is no point at all in proving the *Protocols of the Elders of Zion* false.”

These five sentences summarize the following four passages from Drucker:

“For the individual Communist can always recant; but, once a Jew, always a Jew.” (p. 209)

“Nazi anti-Semitism is therefore due neither to the irreconcilable conflict between the Nordic and the Semitic principle as the Nazis assert, nor to the inherent anti-Semitism of the German People, as is so often said in the outside world.” (p. 209)

“The Nazis do not persecute the Jews because they remained a foreign body within Germany, but actually because they had become almost completely assimilated and had ceased to be Jews.” (pp. 209–210)

“The famous Protocols of Zion can be proved a hundred times a clumsy forgery; they must be genuine, as the Jewish conspiracy against Germany must be real.” (p. 210)

**26 September 1947**

**Bernanos** — Georges Bernanos, *La France contre les Robots*, 40th ed., Paris 1947; German: *Wider die Roboter*, Cologne 1949.

**ubi nihil vales ibi nihil velis** — “Where you have no power, desire nothing.”

A phrase frequently quoted by the Flemish theologian and philosopher Arnold Geulincx (1624–1669).

Schmitt often used it as a formula of detachment, for example in relation to organized Catholicism. See *Gespräch*, p. 57.

**κεχωρισμένος** — Correctly: *κεχωρισμένως*, “separately,” “set apart.”

**οὔτοπος** — “No-place.” Compare “utopia.”

**27 September 1947**

**Fritz Eisler** — (1887–1914), Schmitt’s friend from his student years. Schmitt dedicated his 1916 book on Däubler and his 1928 *Constitutional Theory* to Eisler.

See Reinhard Mehring, *Die Hamburger Verlegerfamilie Eisler und Carl Schmitt* (*Plettenberger Miniaturen*, 2), Plettenberg 2009.

**“the living garment of the Godhead”** — Goethe, *Faust*, Part I, “Study.”

**Nebel** — Gerhard Nebel (1903–1974), writer, whose difficult and contradictory relationship with Schmitt went back to 1933.

Nebel’s *Platon und die Polis* appeared in 1947. In a letter to Nebel dated 10 October 1947, Schmitt praised the study enthusiastically.

See Ernst Jünger / Gerhard Nebel, *Briefe 1938–1974*, ed. U. Fröschle and M. Neumann, Stuttgart 2003, p. 608.

**Jaeger** — Werner Jaeger, *Paideia. Die Formung des griechischen Menschen*, first ed., Berlin/Leipzig 1934.

**πάντα [γάρ] τολμητέον** — “For one must dare everything.”

Plato, *Theaetetus* 196d.

The complete sentence reads:

“But what if we were to dare to be completely shameless?”

**καλός [γάρ ὁ] κίνδυνος** — “For the risk is beautiful.”

Plato, *Phaedo* 114d.

In context:

“… this, I think, is fitting and is worth risking: that one should believe things are so. For it is a beautiful risk, and one must as it were enchant oneself with such things. That is why I have been spinning out the story for so long. For this reason, a man should be of good courage concerning his soul …”

The immortality of the soul, although repeatedly “proved” in the *Phaedo*, nevertheless remains a myth—but a beautiful risk.

See Eveline Krummen, “‘Schön ist das Wagnis’. Rituelle Handlung und mythische Erzählung in Platons Phaidon,” in A. Bierl / R. Lämmle / K. Wesselmann (eds.), *Literatur und Religion. Wege zu einer mythisch-rituellen Poetik bei den Griechen*, vol. 2, Berlin/New York 2007, pp. 91–139.

**ne simus faciles …** — “Let us not be careless with words. Truth lies in the Word of God.”

See also C. Schmitt, *Die Tyrannei der Werte*, 3rd corrected ed., Berlin 2011, p. 52.

It reverses the Latin proverb *In verbis simus faciles*—“Let us be easygoing in words.”

Bismarck ended his *Gedanken und Erinnerungen* with that phrase, which Schmitt thought showed “a very high degree of head-forester mentality.”

See *BW EJ*, p. 175 and the commentary there, p. 605; see also below on p. 69.

**Mme Guyon** — Jeanne Marie Guyon du Chesnoy (1648–1717), mystic whose many writings strongly influenced, among other things, German Pietism.

Schmitt probably knew her through his study of Pietism. See Johann Arnold Kanne, *Aus meinem Leben. Aufzeichnungen des deutschen Pietisten Johann Kanne*, ed. Carl Schmitt-Dorotić, Berlin 1919; reprint Vienna 1994.

Schmitt quotes Guyon in his *Political Romanticism*: PR, p. 38, n. 1.

**“The path of spirit is the detour”** — “Nature reaches its goal by the shortest route. That is true; but the path of spirit is mediation, the detour.”

G. W. F. Hegel, *Vorlesungen über die Geschichte der Philosophie*, in *Werke*, ed. Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 18, Frankfurt am Main 1979, p. 55.

**29 September 1947**

**Donoso, “Seuls aujourd’hui …”** — Schmitt quotes from the following edition: Juan Donoso Cortés, *Oeuvres*, vol. 2, Paris 1858, p. 165 (RW 265 no. 23878).

**Kierkegaard’s sentence about the martyrs** —

“For tyrants—in the form of emperors, kings, popes, Jesuits, generals, diplomats—have until now been able, at the decisive moment, to govern and direct the world. But from the time the Fourth Estate is established—once this fact has had enough time to become established in such a way that people truly understand it—it will become clear that only martyrs can govern the world at the decisive moment.”

S. Kierkegaard, *Das Buch über Adler*, Düsseldorf/Cologne 1962, p. 207.

Schmitt refers to this passage in C. Schmitt, *Donoso Cortés in gesamteuropäischer Interpretation*, Cologne 1950, p. 107.

**Pascal’s “Moi haïssable”** — “The hateful self.”

Blaise Pascal, *Pensées* (Brunschvicg), fragment 455.

**30 September 1947**

**“Eyes shut and gas”** — A saying of Heinrich Oberheid that became a stock phrase in the Siedlinghausen circle. See *Schmittiana* III, 1991, p. 72.

**2 October 1947**

**Blüher, *Erhebung*** — Hans Blüher, *Die Erhebung Israels gegen die deutschen Güter*, Hamburg 1931.

**in the Haußleiter matter** — August Haußleiter (1905–1989).

This refers to the judgment of 22 September 1947, file no. Vf. 23-IIIa-47, concerning an election dispute over the invalidation of the election of a member of the Bavarian state parliament.

See also *Der Spiegel*, no. 41, 11 October 1947.

**πάντα τολμητέον** — See above, note to p. 15.

**ἀναγκαζόμενος** — *οὐδεὶς ἑκὼν δίκαιος ἀλλ᾽ ἀναγκαζόμενος*: “No one is just willingly, but only under compulsion.”

Plato, *Republic* 360c.

The person compelled by fate was a widespread idea in Greek philosophy. Schmitt repeatedly recognized himself in it. See below, p. 19 and p. 260.

**blind command in advance** — A phrase coined by Konrad Weiß that was important to Schmitt. Compare 7 April 1951, 24 June 1951, 15 October 1951, and 12 September 1954.

For Schmitt, history was a mystery contained within God’s plan of salvation. Human action could therefore only ever carry out a “blind”—that is, humanly unknowable—command given in advance.

This also explains the importance to him of Léon Bloy’s sentence discussed above in the note to p. 7.

**3 October 1947**

**Marcos** — Teodoro Andrés Marcos (1880–1952), professor of canon law at the University of Salamanca and specialist in Vitoria.

**semel paret …** — *Ille ipse omnium conditor et rector scripsit quidem fata, sed sequitur; semper paret, semel iussit.*

“That very founder and ruler of all things did indeed write fate, but he also follows it: he always obeys, though he gave the command once.”

Seneca, *De providentia* 5.8.

**“and freer still are springs”** — “The ocean is free. And freer still are springs.”

Theodor Däubler, *Das Nordlicht* (Geneva edition), vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, *Lieder im Seelenschein*, p. 544.

**dictamen …** — “First the command of reason, then of the will, then of desire.”

**Like Hindemith** — Schmitt owned and knew Hindemith’s *Unterweisung im Tonsatz*.

On 24 November 1947 he wrote to Wilhelm Fraenger:

“I am reading Hindemith’s wonderful theory of composition—published by Schott in Mainz in 1940—and I cannot stop thinking about what you say on p. 80 of your Bosch book. Could you not somehow bring it to Hindemith’s attention? It would have to thrill him.”

Wilhelm Fraenger, correspondence with Hans Arp, Carl Schmitt and Franz Roh, in *Sinn und Form* 57, 2005, p. 323.

The reference is to Fraenger’s interpretation of the right-hand inner panel of *The Garden of Earthly Delights*, which he calls the “Musical Hell,” in W. Fraenger, *Das Tausendjährige Reich*, Coburg 1947.

**Radbruch and Schwinge** — The jurists Gustav Radbruch (1878–1949), whom Schmitt had already criticized in his doctoral dissertation but with whom he was still on friendly terms in 1930—see *Tb 1930–34*, p. 166—and Erich Schwinge (1903–1994), who in 1930 called Schmitt a “Sphinx among modern constitutional lawyers,” both took a critical view of Schmitt after 1945.

See also below, notes to pp. 103 and 125.

**Brother Straubinger** — A figure from a nineteenth-century student drinking song who represents a rogue or tramp. Carl Schmitt uses the name for Hitler.

**in the manner of the German-Slovak exchange** — After the annexation of the Sudetenland and the resulting weakening of the Czechoslovak Republic, Slovakia declared itself autonomous within Czechoslovakia in October 1938.

Hitler wanted an independent Slovak state and brought this about in March 1939 by placing massive pressure on Slovak prime minister Jozef Tiso.

See also below, note to p. 292.

**“only the pilgrim will bless it”** — Final line of Annette von Droste-Hülshoff’s poem “Mein Beruf.”

**baculus** — Staff, stick.

**Ginés de Sepúlveda** — Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda (1490–1573), Spanish theologian and historian to Charles V and Philip II.

Against Bartolomé de Las Casas, he argued that the Indigenous peoples of the Americas were savages and barbarians and therefore, on the basis of Aristotle, lacked legal rights, so that their lands could be treated as open to free seizure.

See G. de Sepúlveda, *Democrates alter, sive Dialogus de justis belli causis adversus Indios*, ed. Menéndez Pelayo, *Boletín de la Real Academia de la Historia*, XXI, Madrid 1892.

**ἀναγκαζόμενος** — See above, note to p. 18.

**4 October 1947**

**hic et nunc** — “Here and now.” One of Schmitt’s personal mottos.

**Vitoria, Francisco de** — c. 1483–1546, Spanish theologian, Dominican friar, and scholar of international law. Founder of the School of Salamanca and a critic of Spanish practices of conquest in Latin America.

See C. Schmitt, “Francisco de Vitoria und die Geschichte seines Ruhmes,” in *Die neue Ordnung* 3, 1949, pp. 289–313.

**my meeting with Don Theodore Andres** — See above, p. 18, “Marcos.”

Schmitt met him during his lecture tour in Spain in June 1943. See Christian Tilitzki, “Die Vortragsreisen Carl Schmitts während des Zweiten Weltkriegs,” in *Schmittiana* VI, 1998, p. 235.

**unintended and merely faithful** — Paraphrase of Konrad Weiß. See C. Schmitt, “Was habe ich getan?” in *Schmittiana* V, 1996, p. 19.

**naked as at birth** — Quotation from Theodor Däubler’s poem “Perseus,” in T. Däubler, *Dichtungen und Schriften*, ed. Friedhelm Kemp, Munich 1956, p. 250:

“Now you stand naked, naked as at birth, in desolate expanses.”

**being is all I possess** — Allusion to the poem “Manchmal, wenn man sich vergißt” by Konrad Weiß, dedicated to Carl Schmitt.

In Weiß, p. 655.

**5 October 1947**

**Coeli tonitralia templa lacessens …** — “Challenging the temples and thunder of heaven, he tore the lightning bolt from Zeus and the arrows from Phoebus.”

A modified version of this quotation appeared on Houdon’s bust of Benjamin Franklin, inventor of the lightning rod.

On the *Anti-Lucretius*, see Rainer Specht, “Über Polignacs Antilucretius,” in *Epirrhosis. Festgabe für Carl Schmitt*, ed. H. Barion / E.-W. Böckenförde / W. Weber, 2nd ed., Berlin 2002, pp. 697–707.

Schmitt gave his copy of Polignac to Specht and referred to this essay in the dedication.

**Nec iuvat innumeros alibi confingere mundos …** — “There is no use inventing countless other worlds in which masses of every conceivable thing whirl about, while giving almost nothing to our own realm … The atoms must be given a measure, a boundary, and a restraint.”

**6 October 1947**

**occasio proxima** — “A proximate occasion,” a term from Catholic moral theology.

**Michelet’s book** — Jules Michelet, *Pologne et Russie. Légende de Kosciusko*, Paris 1852.

Schmitt is referring to the following passage on pp. 131–132:

“We must therefore, provisionally and simply, regard Russia as a whole as a force—a barbaric force, a world without law, a world hostile to Law, making no progress in that direction but on the contrary moving backward and returning to ancient barbarism; a world that accepts modern civilization only in order to dissolve the Western world and kill Law itself.

The world of Law has its frontier where it had it in the Middle Ages: on the Vistula and the Danube.”

**Kütemeyer’s afterword** — Søren Kierkegaard, *Der Begriff der Ironie mit ständiger Rücksicht auf Sokrates*, translated by Wilhelm Kütemeyer, Munich 1929.

**Ne judicate, ne iudicemini …** — Vulgate, Matthew 7:1:

“Judge not, that you be not judged.”

**cache ta vie et répands ton esprit** — “Hide your life and spread your spirit.”

From Victor Hugo’s poem “À un poète.”

**Annette writes to Sprickmann** — Schmitt quotes from A. von Droste-Hülshoff, *Die Briefe der Dichterin Annette von Droste-Hülshoff*, ed. and annotated by Hermann Cardauns, Münster 1909.

**7 October 1947**

**“Were you meant to have been a deception, you blessed silver-blue day?”** — Correctly:

“Were you meant to have been in vain,
You blessed silver-blue day?”

Weiß, p. 722.

See also *BW Mohler*, p. 104; *BW EJ*, p. 146.

**Deus sive Natura** — “God, or rather Nature.”

Schmitt repeatedly felt provoked by this equation in Spinoza. His reaction to it can already be found in his 1919 lectures on Hobbes.

See *Schmittiana* VII, 2001, p. 18.

**8 October 1947**

**Africana** — Theodor Däubler, *L’Africana*, novel, Berlin-Grunewald 1928.

**Kluxen** — Franz Kluxen (1887–1968), businessman, art collector, fellow student and friend of Schmitt from Strasbourg.

Schmitt says below, p. 114, that Kluxen “initiated me into the cult of genius that shaped the spiritual world of nineteenth-century Germany …”

See *Tb 1912–15*, pp. 403–404.

**9 October 1947**

**“Whoever ruined his longing for the sake of some worldly good”** — From the poem “Am ersten Sonntag im Advent” by Annette von Droste-Hülshoff.

**περίψημα** — *Peripsema*: “scum,” “refuse.”

Here the reference is to the Greek New Testament, 1 Corinthians 4:13. In Luther’s translation:

“We have become like the scum of humanity, everyone’s refuse, to this very day.”

**10 October 1947**

in the “Three Types” (p. 17) — C. Schmitt, *On the Three Types of Juristic Thought*, 3rd ed., Berlin 2006, pp. 14–15.

*mysterium iniquitatis* — The “mystery of evil” held back by the *Katéchon* (2 Thessalonians 2:6–7). See below, note to p. 47.

To deceive someone into the truth — This refers to the following passage in Kierkegaard:

“Do not let the word ‘deception’ deceive you. A person can be deceived about what is true; but, to recall old Socrates, a person can also be deceived into the truth. In fact, this is really the only way to bring someone who is trapped in an illusion into the truth: by deceiving him.”

Søren Kierkegaard, *Gesammelte Werke*, section 33: *Die Schriften über sich selbst*, Düsseldorf/Cologne 1964, p. 48.

May a person allow himself to be killed for the truth? — See below, note to p. 208.

Bernanos in Geneva — In September 1946 Georges Bernanos gave an impassioned speech in Geneva in which he said: “European civilization is collapsing, and nothing will replace it.”

*Ecce ancilla* — *Dixit autem Maria ecce ancilla Domini*: “And Mary said: Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord.” Vulgate, Luke 1:38.

**11 October 1947**

*μάκρος ἄνθρωπος* — “Great man.” The expression goes back to Plato, who uses it in the opening chapter of his work on the state.

**12 October 1947**

*amor mortis Scaeva* — Scaeva fought with fierce determination in the Roman civil war against Pompey’s overwhelmingly superior forces. He claimed for himself a “love of death.” See *Pharsalia* VI, 245–246.

*Jus se defendendi contra hostem deponere nemo potest* — “No one can give up the right to defend himself against an enemy.” Thomas Hobbes, *Leviathan*, chapter 14.

**13 October 1947**

*obéissance préalable* — “Prior obedience,” a concept Schmitt took from Maurice Hauriou. See M. Hauriou, *Principes de droit public. A l’usage des étudiants en licence et en doctorat ès-sciences politiques*, 2nd ed., Paris 1916, p. 804. Schmitt’s copy, with notes and an introduction, is preserved among his papers, RW 265 no. 27583.

Schmitt seems to have first quoted the expression in 1935: C. Schmitt, *Was bedeutet der Streit um den Rechtsstaat?* in SGN, p. 126. The idea itself, however, had already appeared in *LuL* as one of the three “premiums attached to legal possession of power.”

Hohe Molmert — A hill near Plettenberg which Schmitt often climbed.

“Toward the Godhead one composes letters that have remained unspoken from the beginning …” — From Theodor Däubler, *Attische Sonette* (“Der Zug”).

“the piano playing beneath me” — Schmitt’s younger sister Anna Schmitt was a piano teacher and taught lessons in the house they shared at Brockhauser Weg 10.

**14 October 1947**

Bentham’s “Expectation” — Jeremy Bentham, *Principles of the Civil Code*, 1838.

**22 October 1947**

*Coups d’état intellectuels* — Paul Valéry, *Oeuvres*, vol. 1, Paris 1957, p. 815.

*Carpe diem; veniet hora* — “Enjoy the day; the hour [of death] will come.”

**23 October 1947**

Parmenides, Nebel — Gerhard Nebel, “Das Sein des Parmenides,” in *Der Bund*, 1947, pp. 87–119.

Prayer of Duns Scotus — See *Tb 1930–34*, p. 375.

**29 October 1947**

*Histoire des Treize* — Stories from Balzac’s *La Comédie humaine* cycle. German title: *Geschichte der Dreizehn*, published in numerous editions.

Goethe’s idea of the “smallest company” — From Goethe’s poem “Vermächtnis”:

And if at last you have succeeded,
And if your whole being has come to feel
That only what bears fruit is true,
You test the universal course of things;
It will proceed according to its way—
Join yourself to the smallest company.

Hitler: “My life is a novel” — A remark by Hitler recorded by Hans Frank. See *Gespräch*, p. 189, note 45.

**30 October 1947**

Eduard Rosenbaum claimed … — No source has been identified.

“The path that led us — Lassalle” — A quotation from the “German Workers’ Marseillaise,” the song of the General German Workers’ Association. It ends with the lines:

“Now we follow the daring path
That Lassalle led us along.”

**3 November 1947**

*Tantulus homo, tantus peccator* — “Such a little man, such a great sinner.” See Friedrich Reck-Malleczewen, *Bockelson. Geschichte eines Massenwahns*, Berlin 1937. Schmitt owned a marked-up copy of this first edition, which was banned immediately after publication.

*abyssus vocat abyssum* — Vulgate, Psalm 42:8. Luther: “One depth calls to another.”

**5 November 1947**

“The ocean is free, and freer still are springs” — See above, note to p. 18.

**7 November 1947**

“What Bruno Bauer calls Judaization” — Bruno Bauer speaks of the “Judaization of peoples.” See B. Bauer, *Das Judenthum in der Fremde*, Berlin 1863, p. 48.

*Sic exspectatur iudicium* — “Thus the judgment is awaited.” Apparently modeled on Cicero’s *Argumentum orationis pro M. Tullio*: “*hoc iudicium sic exspectatur*.”

Nette — Herbert Nette (1902–1994), journalist, editor, and writer. Nette, who also knew Ernst Jünger, met Carl Schmitt in the autumn of 1947 through Heinrich Gremmels. On 2 October 1947 he wrote to Schmitt asking for a meeting.

*μεταβολή, τροπή, φορά …* —

*φθοραὶ τοίνυν ἐξ ἀνάγκης τότε μέγισται συμβαίνουσι τῶν τε ἄλλων ζῴων, καὶ δὴ καὶ τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένος ὀλίγον τι περιλείπεται: περὶ δὲ τούτους ἄλλα τε παθήματα πολλὰ καὶ θαυμαστά.*

“The greatest destructions then necessarily occur among the other animals as well, and only a small remnant of the human race survives. And among these survivors many other strange and remarkable things then occur.”

Plato, *Statesman*, 270d; translation by Friedrich Schleiermacher.

*μεταβολή* — Change.

*ἐναντία* — Movement in the opposite direction.

**9 November 1947**

Baumgartner’s speech — The Bavarian politician Joseph Baumgartner (1904–1964) supported Bavarian independence.

*qui accuse s’excuse* — A reversal of the familiar saying *qui s’excuse, s’accuse*: “whoever excuses himself accuses himself.”

Hermann Hefele — (1885–1936), Romance-language scholar. Schmitt is referring to Hermann Hefele, *Niccolo Machiavelli* (Colemans kleine Biographien, 14), Lübeck 1933.

Kelsen’s presumption — See Hans Kelsen, *Wer soll der Hüter der Verfassung sein?*, Berlin 1931.

**12 November 1947**

Kassner’s revealing remarks — Rudolf Kassner, “Faust oder der Barockmensch,” in *Europäische Revue* 18, 1942, pp. 199–213.

“Desire of power that ceaseth only in death” — “So that in the first place I put for a general inclination of all mankind a perpetual and restless desire of power after power, that ceaseth only in death.” Thomas Hobbes, *Leviathan*, Part I, chapter 11.

**13 November 1947**

To Ernst Jünger — See *BW EJ*, pp. 213 ff., with slight differences.

Joy is an acceleration of the circulation of the blood — Thomas Hobbes, *Leviathan*, Part I, chapter 6.

“as many pulsations as possible” — From Walter Pater’s 1868 essay “Poems by William Morris,” in *Pre-Raphaelitism. A Collection of Critical Essays*, edited by James Sambook, Chicago 1974, pp. 105–117.

**16 November 1947**

Ed. Meyer — Schmitt is referring to Eduard Meyer, *Caesars Monarchie und das Principat des Pompejus. Innere Geschichte Roms von 66 bis 44 v. Chr.*, Stuttgart/Berlin 1918.

James Burnham — J. Burnham, *The Managerial Revolution: What Is Happening in the World*, New York 1941, and later editions.

**17 November 1947**

Max Stirner, p. 244 — Max Stirner, *Der Einzige und sein Eigentum*, Part II: “I,” chapter 4, “The Owner,” section A, “My Power.” Schmitt quotes the end of this chapter inaccurately.

**18 November 1947**

Kaegi — Werner Kaegi, “Probleme des Rechtsstaats,” in *Universitas* 2, 1947, pp. 909–913.

Hobbes — Thomas Hobbes, “An Answer to Bishop Bramhall’s Book Called *The Catching of the Leviathan*,” in *The English Works of Thomas Hobbes*, edited by William Molesworth, vol. IV, p. 322.

**19 November 1947**

Remarks by Franz von Baader —

“The animal, wholly immersed in time, perceives time just as little as the person wholly rapt in eternity. The perception of time can therefore belong only to man in his present amphibious existence—and even more strongly to Satan beneath him.”

Baader to Adolph Wagner, 10 September 1817, in Fr. von Baader, *Sämtliche Werke*, vol. 15, Leipzig 1857, p. 326.

**21 November 1947**

Marie Stewens — (1899–1981), secondary-school teacher in Witten and sister-in-law of Peterheinrich Kirchhoff. See *Schmittiana* IV, 1994, pp. 272–284.

Robert Mohl — (1799–1875), professor of political science and politician. See Robert von Mohl, “Die Staatsromane. Ein Beitrag zur Literaturgeschichte der Staatswissenschaften,” in *Zeitschrift für die gesamte Staatswissenschaft* 2, 1845, pp. 24–74; and *Geschichte der Staatswissenschaften*, vol. 1, Erlangen 1855, Part III, pp. 167–214: “Staatsromane.”

Kleinwächter — Friedrich Kleinwächter, *Die Staatsromane. Ein Beitrag zur Lehre vom Communismus und Socialismus*, Vienna 1891.

Ernst Bloch — Schmitt is referring to Ernst Bloch, *Freiheit und Ordnung. Abriss der Sozial-Utopien*, New York 1946; later also included in E. Bloch, *Das Prinzip Hoffnung*, Frankfurt am Main 1959, pp. 547–729. See below, note to p. 234.

Thomas More, who invented the word “Utopia” — Thomas More, *Libellus vere aureus nec minus salutaris quam festivus de optimo reipublicae statu, deque nova insula Utopia*, Leuven 1516.

Pierre Linn — (1897–1966), French banker and philosopher, and an early translator of Schmitt into French, including *Political Romanticism* in 1928.

**22 November 1947**

“Nothing is more to me than myself” — Final sentence of the introduction to Max Stirner, *Der Einzige und sein Eigentum*.

**24 November 1947**

Veit — Otto Veit, “Die geistesgeschichtliche Situation des Naturrechts,” in *Merkur*, 1947, pp. 390–405.

Donoso Cortés had already understood this — See Juan Donoso Cortés, *Über die Diktatur. Drei Reden aus den Jahren 1849/50*, edited, translated from Spanish, and annotated by Günter Maschke, Vienna and elsewhere, 1996.

**25 November 1947**

Letter from Popitz — Johannes Popitz wrote:

“[…] Above all, many thanks for sending me *The Concept of the Political*! We must talk about it. My impression is that you have achieved here the best thing I have yet read by you—and I have read a great deal that was excellent.”

RW 265 no. 11161.

“Donoso Cortés, tanned into table-leather and cut down into cheap novel-trim” — “Table-leather” is a malicious play on the name of Peter Tischleder (1891–1947), professor of Catholic moral theology and Christian social teaching in Münster, and from 1946 in Mainz. Schmitt regarded him as having a ponderous, “Tischleder-like” style. He was also the doctoral supervisor of Josef Westemeyer; see above, note to p. 11.

The writer Elisabeth Langgässer (1899–1950) discusses Donoso in the second book of her novel *Das unauslöschliche Siegel* (1946 and later editions). According to the Donoso specialist Günter Maschke, she treats him quite appropriately, contrary to Schmitt’s remark.

“the ascetic restraint of the scholarly academic” — Max Weber, *Politik als Beruf*, Munich/Leipzig 1919, p. 25. Schmitt used the second edition of 1926, which has identical pagination.

**26 November 1947**

Winckelmann — Johannes Winckelmann (1900–1985), jurist and editor of Max Weber’s works, who had known Schmitt since 1938. See Stefan Breuer, “Klassiker der Karlsruher Republik. Johannes Winckelmann etabliert nach 1945 Max Weber,” in *Zeitschrift für Ideengeschichte* IX, 2015, no. 2, pp. 89–104.

**27 November 1947**

“spat out again by Leviathan three times” — See above, note to p. 7.

“the Russian major” — After Soviet troops captured Schlachtensee at the end of April 1945, Schmitt was questioned by a Russian officer.

Carl Tobias — An allusion to the apocryphal Old Testament Book of Tobit. Tobias is the son of a blind father whose sight is restored through him (Tobit 11). It is unclear who used the name as a pseudonym.

**28 November 1947**

*Conjuratio …* — “Conspiracy.”

When the Roman Republic was in danger, the Senate declared a state of emergency and empowered the consuls with the formula:

*Videant consules ne quid detrimenti res publica capiat.*

“Let the consuls see to it that the state suffers no harm.”

The consuls then addressed the citizens with the words:

*Qui rem publicam salvam esse velit, me sequatur.*

“Whoever wishes the state to be saved, let him follow me.”

Altheim — Franz Altheim, *Lex sacrata. Die Anfänge der plebeischen Organisation* (Albae vigiliae, 1), Amsterdam 1940.

Plutarch — *Plutarchi vitae parallelae. Recogn. Cl. Lindskog et K. Ziegler*, vol. 3, fasc. 2, including the *Lives of Galba and Otho* and fragments of lost lives, 2nd ed., Leipzig 1973.

“If this night …” — See Max Weber, *Politik als Beruf*, Munich/Leipzig 1919, p. 66. Correct wording: “… has apparently blossomed so luxuriantly now.”

KDF — *Kraft durch Freude* (“Strength Through Joy”), the Nazi organization responsible for organizing leisure activities.

“Now there will …” — Max Weber, *Politik als Beruf*, Munich/Leipzig 1919, p. 56, not p. 57.

“Whoever wishes to act according to the ethics of the Gospel …” — Correctly:

“Whoever wishes to act according to the ethics of the Gospel should refrain from strikes—for they are coercion—and should join the yellow trade unions. Above all, however, he should not speak of ‘revolution.’ For that ethic surely does not mean to teach that civil war in particular is the only legitimate war.”

Max Weber, *Politik als Beruf*, Munich/Leipzig 1919, p. 55, not p. 57.

**29 November 1947**

Hans Barth and his essay on Leviathan — H. Barth, “Wirklichkeit und Ideologie des totalen Staates,” in *Neue Schweizer Rundschau* NF 6, 1938, pp. 449–458.

Also: “Vom totalen Staat und seinen ideologischen Voraussetzungen,” in the same journal, pp. 614–627 and 673–682, including discussion of E. R. Huber.

Also: “Über die Entstehung der Ideologie vom totalen Staat,” in *Neue Zürcher Zeitung*, 1938; reprinted in H. Barth, *Denken in der Zeit. Philosophisch-politische Beiträge in der Neuen Zürcher Zeitung 1932–1964*, with an introduction by Hermann Lübbe, Zurich 1988, pp. 200–209.

“the refined, righteous tone of the comb-makers” — See Gottfried Keller, *Die drei gerechten Kammacher* (“The Three Righteous Comb-Makers”).

Fritz Ernst in *Corona* VII — F. Ernst, “Johannes von Müller. Zürcher Rede,” in *Corona* 7, 1937, pp. 109–126; the quotation appears on p. 123.

Schmitt apparently saw a parallel with his own life in Müller’s decision to enter the service of Jérôme Napoléon, King of Westphalia, as a councillor of state.

**30 November 1947**

Letter from Barion dated 11 November 1947 — The long letter, RW 265 no. 694/1, concerns Rudolph Sohm. Before turning to Sohm, Barion describes the difficulties he was having in being reinstated in his professorship at Bonn.

**1 December 1947**

Aldous Huxley — In the epilogue to his book, Huxley explains the Shakespeare quotation from which the title of his novel comes. This is presumably what Schmitt means by “gloss.”

**2 December 1947**

Annie Kraus — See below, note to p. 155.

Mr. Dr. R. — Possibly Eduard Rosenbaum.

Baader … answered prayer — Franz von Baader, *Vorlesungen über religiöse Philosophie* I/1, Munich 1827, pp. 87 ff.

**3 December 1947**

*Minima non curat praetor, maxima non curat praetor* — “The praetor does not concern himself with small matters; the praetor does not concern himself with great matters either.”

The first sentence comes from Roman law. Schmitt added the second himself.

**5 December 1947**

Kierkegaard, *The Concept of Anxiety* — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Søren Kierkegaard, *Gesammelte Werke*, with an afterword by Christoph Schrempf, translated by Wolfgang Pfleiderer and Christoph Schrempf, Part 5: *Der Begriff der Angst*, Jena 1912.

Chapter 3: “Anxiety as a Consequence of That Sin Which Consists in the Absence of Consciousness of Sin,” pp. 77–107; section 2: “Anxiety Dialectically Defined in Relation to Fate,” pp. 93–100.

Zeller — Schmitt is probably referring to Eduard Zeller, *Geschichte der deutschen Philosophie seit Leibniz* (= *Geschichte der Wissenschaften in Deutschland*, published by the Historical Commission of the Royal Academy of Sciences, 13), 2nd ed., Munich 1875.

**8 December 1947**

*Une armée dont on se sert …* — In Ernst Jünger’s translation:

“An army that is used for oppression must first itself be subdued. The hammer must endure as many blows as the anvil.”

E. Jünger, *Sämtliche Werke* 14, Stuttgart 1978, p. 273.

**10 December 1947**

Gerhard Nebel’s essay — In G. Nebel, *Von den Elementen. Essays*, Wuppertal 1947, pp. 9–31. The date of composition is given there as 1940, not “1941.”

**11 December 1947**

*postiche* — Fake; not genuine.

“O happiness of the gnat” — See Rilke, Eighth *Duino Elegy*.

Ebeling’s thesis — See Gerhard Ebeling, *Kirchengeschichte als Geschichte der Auslegung der Heiligen Schrift*, Tübingen 1947.

**13 December 1947**

*Ils ont outragé l’esprit* — “They have insulted the spirit.” The sentence comes from the French version of Paul’s Letter to the Hebrews, chapter 10, verse 29.

**16 December 1947**

“old Huxley had already imagined …” —

“If the fundamental proposition of evolution is true—namely that the whole world, animate and inanimate, is the result of the mutual interaction, according to definite laws, of the forces possessed by the molecules from which the primordial nebula of the universe was composed—then it is no less certain that the present world existed potentially in that cosmic vapor, and that an intelligence sufficient to know the properties of the molecules of that vapor could, for example, have predicted the state of the fauna of Great Britain in 1868 with as much certainty as one can say what will happen to the vapor of one’s breath on a cold winter’s day.”

Schmitt quotes Huxley through Bergson: Henri Bergson, *L’évolution créatrice* (Bibliothèque de philosophie contemporaine), Paris 1913, pp. 41–42.

**17 December 1947**

the office of G. & K. — The office of the Graewe & Kaiser company in Plettenberg-Eiringhausen, where Schmitt’s father worked as an accountant.

**18 December 1947**

“Even the most sublime ideas …” — Probably modeled on:

“The most civilized peoples are as close to barbarism as the most highly polished iron is to rust.”

In Ernst Jünger’s German translation: “The most civilized peoples are no farther removed from barbarism than the brightest iron is from rust.”

E. Jünger, *Sämtliche Werke* 14, Stuttgart 1978, p. 257.

*au début de la vie* —

“Philosophy, being the fruit of long meditation and the result of an entire life, cannot and should never be presented to the people, who are always at the beginning of life.”

In Ernst Jünger’s translation: “Philosophy, as the late-ripened fruit of the mind and the autumn of life, must not be offered to the people, who always remain in childhood.”

E. Jünger, *Sämtliche Werke* 14, Stuttgart 1978, p. 257.

**19 December 1947**

Saint-Martin — Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin (1743–1803), mystical and theosophical writer and translator of Jakob Böhme into French.

René Guénon — (1886–1951), esoteric philosopher.

*κατέχων* — The *Katéchon*, “the restrainer,” appears both in a personal form (*κατέχων*) and in a neuter form (*κατέχον*).

The reference is to 2 Thessalonians 2:6–7:

*καὶ νῦν τὸ κατέχον οἴδατε, εἰς τὸ ἀποκαλυφθῆναι αὐτὸν ἐν τῷ ἑαυτοῦ καιρῷ. τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται τῆς ἀνομίας· μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται.*

Luther:

“And you know what still holds him back, until he is revealed at his appointed time. For the mystery of evil is already at work; only the one who now holds it back must first be removed.”

In medieval theology, the “mystery of evil” was interpreted as the Antichrist, who appears at the end of time in the Book of Revelation.

The *Katéchon* was a central theme for Schmitt, and not only in his later years. On 20 October 1974 he wrote to Hans Blumenberg:

“For more than forty years I have been collecting material on the problem of *katécwn*, or *katécon* (Thess. 2:2, 6).”

See *BW Blumenberg*, p. 120, with notes on pp. 122–123.

In fact, Schmitt’s interest probably went back even further, to the middle of the 1920s, and was likely encouraged by Erik Peterson.

The material Schmitt collected on the subject survives among his papers, RW 265, nos. 20022, 20023, 20024, 20026, 20172, and 21149.

On the *Katéchon*, see also *Nomos*, pp. 28 ff.

Schmitt rejected the translation “one who delays” or simply “restrainer” when discussing the term with Sander and Julien Freund. See Carl Schmitt/Hans-Dietrich Sander, *Werkstatt-Discorsi. Briefwechsel 1967–1981*, edited by Erik Lehnert and Günter Maschke, Schnellroda 2008, p. 65, note 15:

“the word ‘Katechon’ does not mean to delay; it means rather ‘to hold down.’”

On 24 January 1980 Walter Warnach wrote to Herbert Nette about Schmitt’s understanding of the *Katéchon*. From a final conversation with Schmitt the previous autumn, Warnach understood that Schmitt’s concern was

“to protect Christianity from every suspicion of eschatologism and, accordingly, to anchor the medieval Empire and its mission in the world as firmly as possible in Scripture.”

Nette papers, Deutsches Literaturarchiv Marbach, HS 948460.

Adso — (c. 920–992), Benedictine abbot and author of a work on the Antichrist: Adso of Montier-en-Der, *De ortu et tempore Antichristi*, in *Corpus Christianorum. Continuatio Mediaevalis* 45, Turnhout 1976.

Haimo of Halberstadt (Migne X. 117, col. 779) — Haimo of Halberstadt, died 853, bishop. The commentary on Revelation to which Schmitt refers, printed in J. P. Migne’s *Patrologia Latina*, is now attributed instead to the Benedictine monk Haimo of Auxerre.

**20 December 1947**

“Delusion, everywhere delusion” — From Hans Sachs’s monologue on delusion in Richard Wagner’s *Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg*. See Carl Schmitt, “Richard Wagner und eine neue ‘Lehre vom Wahn’,” in *Bayreuther Blätter. Deutsche Zeitschrift im Geiste Richard Wagners* 35, 1912, pp. 239–241.

Mrs. Winckelmann — Freda Winckelmann, wife of Johannes Winckelmann.

**21 December 1947**

Père dom Deschamps — Léger-Marie Deschamps (1716–1774), Benedictine. His work *Le Vrai Système ou le Mot de l’énigme métaphysique et morale*, discovered only in 1862, made him appear as a precursor of Hegel.

Claude-Nicolas Ledoux — (1736–1806), French architect and one of the leading representatives of Revolutionary architecture.

Laberthonnière — Lucien Laberthonnière (1860–1932), Catholic theologian. See 6 December 1949.

Erich Voegelin — Eric Voegelin (1901–1985), political scientist and philosopher.

In connection with Graetz’s remark, Schmitt is referring to E. Voegelin, *Rasse und Staat*, Tübingen 1933; and in connection with the reference to Goethe, to E. Voegelin, *Die Rassenidee in der Geistesgeschichte von Ray bis Carus*, Berlin 1933. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 25790.

See also Schmitt’s correspondence with Voegelin in *Schmittiana* NF II, 2014, pp. 183–199.

Schubert — Gotthilf Heinrich von Schubert (1780–1860), natural scientist and philosopher of nature.

**22 December 1947**

“Prometheus work” — No source can be identified; possibly an unrealized project by Nebel.

“So meaning, the more it searches for itself …” — Final stanza of the poem “Klage über der Schöpfung” by Konrad Weiß; Weiß, pp. 407–408.

Gilles — Werner Gilles (1894–1961), painter and friend of Carl and Duška Schmitt. For a time he lived in the Schmitt household at Kaiserswerther Str. 17 in Berlin.

**23 December 1947**

Wehberg — Hans Wehberg (1885–1962), pacifist scholar of international law and author of a commentary on the Covenant of the League of Nations, first published in 1921.

Hegel — G. F. W. Hegel, *Über die wissenschaftlichen Behandlungsarten des Naturrechts, seine Stelle in der praktischen Philosophie, und sein Verhältnis zu den positiven Rechtswissenschaften*, in *Jenaer kritische Schriften (II)*, newly edited by Hans Brockard and Hartmut Buchner, Hamburg 1983, pp. 90–178.

Also Hegel, “Hamanns Schriften,” in *Sämtliche Werke*, vol. XI: *Berliner Schriften*, Hamburg 1956, pp. 221–294.

Bilfinger — Carl Bilfinger (1887–1958), jurist. Thirty-eight letters and eight postcards survive among Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 nos. 1346–1393 and 18598.

*Mentimur regnare Iovem …* — This and the following quotations are from *Pharsalia* VII, 442 ff. Schmitt substituted “Germania” for “Arabes Medique Eoaque.”

The passage reads:

*Felices Arabes Medique Eoaque tellus,
Quam sub perpetuis tenuerunt fata tyrannis.
Ex populis qui regna ferunt sors ultima nostra est,
Quos servire pudet. Sunt nobis nulla profecto
Numina: cum caeco rapiantur saecula casu,
Mentimur regnare Jovem.*

“Happy are the Arabs and Medes, happy the East, whom fate has kept permanently under the rule of tyrants! Of all peoples forced to endure tyranny, ours is truly the worst fate, because we are ashamed to be slaves. No, for us there are no gods. Since the ages are swept along by blind chance, we lie when we say that Jupiter rules.”

*Reditura numquam libertas?* —

*Quod fugiens civile nefas redituraque numquam
Libertas ultra Tigrim Rhenumque recessit.*

“… freedom, fleeing the horrors of civil war and never to return, withdrew beyond the Rhine and the Tigris.”

Ibid., lines 432–433.

**24 December 1947**

*Bella pares superis facient civilia divos* —

*Mortalia nulli
Sunt curate deo. Cladis tamen huius habemus
Vindicatam, quantam terris dare numina fas est:
Bella pares superis facient civilia divos.*

“No god cares for the fate of mortals. Yet the gods have paid the penalty for this disaster, as far as gods can make amends to men: civil war will make the deified dead equal to the gods above.”

Ibid., lines 454 ff.

**25 December 1947**

H. Bung — Hubertus Bung (1908–1981), jurist and pupil of Schmitt.

Confusion with my namesake in Tübingen — Carlo Schmid.

The first letter from Herbert Lemmel—see above, note to p. 4—to Schmitt reached him in 1948 on a Russian postcard addressed to:

“Professor Carl Schmidt, French Zone, Tübingen am Neckar (Württemberg).”

RW 265 no. 8725/1.

It was therefore delivered in Tübingen to Württemberg councillor of state and professor Karl Schmid, who at that time had not yet begun calling himself “Carlo.” Schmid forwarded it to Plettenberg with a covering letter on stationery headed “Staatsrat Prof. Dr. Karl Schmid,” RW 265 no. 8725/2:

“Dear Professor Schmitt,

I assume that the writer of the enclosed letter was trying to reach you rather than me, and I am therefore sending his letter on to you.

With best wishes,

Yours sincerely,
Schmid.”

Schmitt and Schmid knew one another personally from meetings at the Academy for German Law and from a wartime journey Schmitt made to France, during which they met in Lille, where Schmid was serving as a military judge.

See Schmitt’s letter to Nette of 29 June 1980, Deutsches Literaturarchiv Marbach, Nette papers, HS 948460.

**27 December 1947**

the fish by Gilles, the Leviathan by Nay, the magnificent diamond by Nay — Paintings by Werner Gilles and Ernst Wilhelm Nay (1902–1968) which Schmitt owned and particularly loved.

The complete letter is published in *BW GJ*, pp. 99–101.

Jünger — Friedrich Georg Jünger, *Griechische Götter. Apollon, Pan, Dionysos*, Frankfurt am Main 1943. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 22251.

*Non intelligor ulli* — In a letter written during his exile on the Black Sea, Ovid complains:

*Barbarus hic ego sum, quia non intelligor ulli.*

“Here I am the barbarian, because no one understands me.”

Charles Péguy — (1873–1914), French writer and representative of the Catholic revival.

**28 December 1947**

“the highly educated Swiss” — Jacob Burckhardt. See below, notes to pp. 105 and 272.

**29 December 1947**

“like that Serenissimus” — During the Berlin uprising of 1848, the Prussian king Friedrich Wilhelm IV is said to have shouted to the rebels:

“But they are not allowed to do that.”

**31 December 1947**

to Nette — A draft of the letter dated 26 December 1947 survives among Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 29474.

**1 January 1948**

*omine auctus* — “Magnified by the omen.”

J. K. — Josef Kohler (1849–1919), professor of civil law, philosophy of law, and criminal law at Berlin’s Friedrich Wilhelm University.

Schmitt attended Kohler’s lectures in 1907, during his first semester. Decades later he described him in his notes “1907 Berlin.” See *Schmittiana* I, 1988, pp. 15–16.

**2 January 1948**

*You Can’t Go Home Again* — Title of a novel by Thomas Wolfe.

**5 January 1948**

Samuel Butler, *Erewhon* — Samuel Butler, *Erewhon; or, Over the Range*, London 1872 and later editions. German edition: *Erewhon oder jenseits der Berge*, Frankfurt am Main 1994, pp. 123 ff.

**6 January 1948**

To R. Smend — Letter published in *BW Smend*, p. 121.

**7 January 1948**

reply from my childhood friend Kluxen — This letter is missing from the surviving Kluxen correspondence among Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 nos. 7909–7928.

Fritz Brust — (1884–?), probably a fellow student. In 1909 he received his doctorate in Strasbourg with the dissertation *Die Ästhetik der Musik in neueren Kunsttheorien und das Problem ihrer Allgemeingültigkeit*.

*καὶ ἡ θάλασσα οὐκ ἔστιν ἔτι* — “And the sea is no more.” Revelation 21:1, Greek New Testament.

*Sors de l’enfance* — A quotation from Jean-Jacques Rousseau, *La Nouvelle Héloïse*, Part V. The first letter begins:

“Leave childhood behind, my friend, wake up; do not surrender your whole life to the long sleep of reason. The years are passing; you have only enough left to become wise.”

Schmitt had already quoted this in 1922 in “Schatten Gottes.” See *Tb 1921–24*, p. 416.

**8 January 1948**

W. Weber’s legal opinion — Werner Weber, *Die Rechtslage des Johannishospitals in Leipzig* (legal opinion), Leipzig 1948.

Joseph Kaiser’s dissertation — Joseph H. Kaiser, *Die politische Klausel der Konkordate*, doctoral dissertation in law, Tübingen 1947.

**11 January 1948**

Saint Séverin, the saint of 8 January — The feast day of Saint Severinus of Noricum is not 8 January but 19 January. The eighth of January was the date of his death, in the year 482. He therefore did not live around the year 500.

Severinus’s political and spiritual work in the Danube frontier region, which Rome had long since abandoned, attracted considerable attention in his own time.

Lavelle — Louis Lavelle (1883–1951), *La présence totale*, Paris 1934; German translation: *Die Gegenwart und das Ganze. Entwurf einer Philosophie des Seins und der Teilhabe*, Düsseldorf 1952.

R. Capitant — René Capitant (1901–1970), French jurist, political scientist, and politician; member of the Resistance and minister in de Gaulle’s government in exile. He had known Schmitt in Berlin since 1931.

*petite dentelle de Vénise* — Fine lacework from Burano, the island in the Venetian lagoon.

**12 January 1948**

“I have defied the Escaveçades of fate …” — This and the following sentences paraphrase Schmitt’s “Song of the Sixty-Year-Old” at the end of ECS. See also *Gedichte*, pp. 5–7.

*Nam potenti et fido amico plus praesidii habet …* — Correctly:

*Nam potenti et fido amico niti plus praesidii habet …*

“For relying on a powerful and faithful friend gives a person greater protection than most arts and intrigues.”

Francis Bacon, *De dignitate et augmentis scientiarum*, in *The Works of F. Bacon*, edited by James Spedding, Robert Leslie Ellis, and Douglas Denon Heath, vol. II, London 1857, p. 463.

**13 January 1948**

“The servant glides …” — Quotations from *Erewhon*. See above, note to p. 57.

**15 January 1948**
