Bourdin — Paul Bourdin (1900–1955), editor-in-chief of *Die Welt* and commentator for the weekly newspaper *Die Zeit*.

**22 December 1953**

“Statement by Lorenz von Stein” — Schmitt refers to Lorenz von Stein, *Geschichte der sozialen Bewegung in Frankreich von 1789 bis auf unsere Tage*, ed. Gottfried Salomon, Munich 1921, vol. 2, p. 11; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 25087. See C. Schmitt, “Die Stellung Lorenz von Steins in der Geschichte des 19. Jahrhunderts.” In: SGN, pp. 156–65.

**26 December 1953**

“Federal Constitutional Court judgment of 17 December 1953” — The judgment held that all civil-service employment relationships had ended on 8 May 1945.

*Le Pal* — Title of a weekly newspaper written entirely by Léon Bloy, of which four issues appeared in 1885. A fifth issue was assembled in 1935 from texts Bloy had intended for it. A new annotated complete edition appeared in 1979: L. Bloy, *Le Pal*, notes and prefaces by Daniel Habrekorn, complete edition revised and corrected against the originals, Vanves 1979.

*Das Brandmal* — Emmy Hennings, *Das Brandmal. Ein Tagebuch*, Berlin 1920; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 22103. Emmy Hennings was the wife of Hugo Ball.

*temerataque jura relinquo* — “Here I leave peace behind, and violated law.” *Pharsalia*, I, 225. The words are spoken by Caesar after crossing the Rubicon. Schmitt quoted the line repeatedly; see Dirk Blasius, *Carl Schmitt. Preußischer Staatsrat in Hitlers Reich*, Göttingen 2001, pp. 69–70; *Gespräch*, pp. 171–72; BW EJ, p. 446. As late as the end of 1983, he used it as a dedication to Christian Meier; see *Zeitschrift für Ideengeschichte*, IV/3, 2010, p. 104.

“Carry your incomprehended heart to the dead” — Friedrich Schiller, *Demetrius*, Act 1:

> Go down in silence, and carry to the dead
> your undiscovered, incomprehended heart.

“Do not let yourself be invited and then disinvited again” — Hans Schomerus, director of the Evangelical Academy in Herrenalb, had invited Schmitt to a conference on “Conservatives and Reactionaries” scheduled for 7–10 May 1953 and asked him to give a lecture on “The Antichrist and Creation.” The invitation went back to a discussion Schmitt had had with Wilhelm Stapel in 1942 about the *katechon*.

Schomerus also asked him to speak at a conference on the island of Mainau from 16–18 May on the theme “A New Approach to Shakespeare.”

Schmitt immediately accepted, but wanted the title of the first lecture changed to “The Antichrist and What Holds Him Back,” and the title of the second to “Hamlet, God’s Player.”

After protests from Adolf Arndt, Gustav Heinemann, Walter Strauss, and others, Regional Bishop Julius Bender ordered that Schmitt be disinvited.

On 5 May, Schmitt received a telegram from Schomerus:

> “Both lectures prohibited by bishop.”

See Schomerus’s letters to Schmitt, RW 265 nos. 14493–14498; Schmitt’s letters to Schomerus, RW 265 nos. 13505–13506; BW Forsthoff, pp. 396–97.

**12 March 1954**

*tutela praesens* — “present protection.” Refers to Horace, *Carmina* IV, 14.43. In: idem, *Sämtliche Werke. Lateinisch und deutsch*, 10th ed., Munich and Zurich 1985, p. 206.

For Schmitt, *tutela praesens* was an essential part of political representation:

> “Representation is nothing if it is not *tutela praesens*.”

*Leviathan*, p. 53.

“Bonald said” —

> *Dieu existe avant la société des hommes intelligents, et la création n’a fait que le produire à l’univers. Donc Dieu existe avant l’homme; donc Dieu est cause, et l’homme est effet.*

> “God exists before the society of intelligent human beings, and creation merely brought him forth into the universe. Therefore God exists before man; therefore God is the cause, and man the effect.”

L. G. A. de Bonald, *Oeuvres complètes*, published by Migne, vol. 1, Paris 1859, col. 481.

*tacito rumore Mosella sc. nondum canalisata* — “the Moselle flowing with a quiet murmur — namely, the Moselle before it had been canalized.”

With *tacito rumore Mosella*, Schmitt, whose ancestors came from the Moselle region, quotes the poem *Mosella* by the late Roman poet Decimus Magnus Ausonius. See ECS, p. 10.

When plans to canalize the Moselle were being considered in the 1950s, Schmitt added the qualification. For example, in a letter to E. Jünger dated 30 December 1955, he wrote:

> “In the ‘Conversation with Spranger’ in *Ex Captivitate Salus* it should read: *tacito rumore Mosella sc. nondum canalisata*. I am therefore your uncanalizable Moselle man.”

BW EJ, pp. 288–89.

**15 March 1954**

“They harp away at the devastation …” — Possibly a parody of Rilke’s poem “Das jüngste Gericht.”

**16 March 1954**

“Aldous Huxley recommends that we …” — *Der Spiegel*, no. 10, 3 March 1954, reviewed Aldous Huxley’s book *The Doors of Perception*, in which Huxley describes his experience with mescaline, under the title “Ersatz für Alkohol” — “A Substitute for Alcohol.”

**1 June 1954 — newspaper clipping**

“Encyclical 1930” — Correctly: 1939; see above, note to p. 274.

*Laicus taceat in et extra ecclesiam …* — “The layman shall remain silent both inside and outside the Church, unless he is cheering the competent ecclesiastical superior.” An allusion to 1 Corinthians 14:34.

**9 June 1954**

“The convert, Mr. Hausenstein” — Wilhelm Hausenstein converted to Catholicism in 1940. Schmitt was generally suspicious of converts:

> “[…] I cannot stand converts.”

*Gespräch*, p. 56. See also above, pp. 99–100, on Helmut Rumpf, and below, p. 330, on Simone Weil and Edith Stein.

**9 July 1954**

“I have founded my cause on nothing” — Opening line of Goethe’s poem “Vanitas! Vanitatum vanitas!”, written in 1806 as a parody of a hymn by Adam Reußner. See J. W. Goethe, *Gedichte. Vollständige Ausgabe*, Stuttgart, n.d. [c. 1959], p. 98.

*Ne joco quidem* — “I am certainly not joking.”

Anton Kuh — (1890–1941), Austrian writer and feuilletonist. Schmitt is probably referring to A. Kuh, *Juden und Deutsche. Ein Résumé*, Berlin 1921, reprint Hamburg 2012, in which Kuh describes the Jews as marked by a “guilt of lineage.”

**15 July 1954**

“But I know my Oppenheimers” — A large and widely branched German-Jewish family. Schmitt probably means above all the liberal economist Franz Oppenheimer (1864–1943), who was hostile to the state. See BdP, p. 75; BW Mohler, p. 343; BW Forsthoff, pp. 205, 458.

Heinz Weitzel — (1902–1990), lawyer at the Hengeler-Müller firm, in which several members of the Oppenheimer family had worked until 1933. Weitzel had known Schmitt since the proceedings concerning the nationalization of the Buderus works; see BW Forsthoff, pp. 212, 462.

**26 July 1954**

“for 25 August 1930” — The thirtieth anniversary of Nietzsche’s death.

**1 August 1954**

“We jump from one ice floe to another” — Schmitt wrote in 1922 in *Der Schatten Gottes*:

> “I live in a raging current, on a melting ice floe. Perhaps I can save myself onto the next one and, by jumping from one to another, keep myself above water for a while. But no shore is in sight, no shore.”

*Tb 1921–24*, pp. 406–7.

Schmitt wrote in 1930 in “Staatsethik und pluralistischer Staat”:

> “Perhaps there are a few agile and mobile individuals who manage the trick of keeping themselves free beside the many powerful social groups, as one jumps from one ice floe to another. But this acrobatic kind of freedom cannot be demanded from the mass of ordinary citizens as a normal ethical duty.”

PuB, p. 157.

Werner Schütz — (1900–1975), jurist and CDU politician, Minister of Education and Cultural Affairs in North Rhine-Westphalia from 1954 to 1956 and again from 1958 to 1962.

**30 August 1954**

*Un sot trouve toujours un plus sot …* — “A fool always finds a greater fool …” Nicolas Boileau-Despréaux, *L’Art poétique*, Canto I. In: idem, *Oeuvres de Boileau Despréaux à l’usage des collèges royaux et des écoles secondaires*, Tours 1838, p. 167.

**12 September 1954**

“the question as it stood in the spring of 1933” — In his book *Der christliche Epimetheus*, Konrad Weiß discusses in 1933 what he calls the “pairing of a conservative German spirit with the actual current of the new German party movement”:

> “The more a person, in the certainty of a fruitful and wide-ranging contemplation, feels history resting within itself, the less hurried and compliant he will be in action.
>
> “And yet the age now stands within an antithesis, in the most tangible division imaginable, defined at this moment by inner tension and by contrary meanings opposed to the more ‘objective’ tendencies and emphases on values. From within this division, one is led to ask, at a higher level: what will now contribute more to meaning and to the inner image — the more conservative political style, or the fanatical and limitless commitment thrown wholly onto a single point?
>
> “What once determined the growth of the inner image: the maturity of a world-form that knows what it is and finds expression within conservatism, or the future approaching through the speechlessness of barbarians who act under a continual pressure of necessity?”

K. Weiß, *Der christliche Epimetheus*, Potsdam 1933, p. 92.

**1 November 1954**

“Meanwhile, however, Mr. L. has triumphed” — Karl Löwenstein.

**14 November 1954**

“I read in a diary entry of 3 February 1941: I am Benito Cereno” — Gretha Jünger reports on 2 February 1941 on conversations with Schmitt about Benito Cereno. G. von Jeinsen [= G. Jünger], *Die Palette*, Hamburg 1949, pp. 46–47.

**12 December 1954**

*L’initié tue l’initiateur* — “The initiate kills the initiator.” See above, p. 112.

On 30 November 1954 Schmitt sent his “Gespräch über die Macht” to Nicolaus Sombart and inscribed this sentence from Ballanche as a dedication.

As Sombart’s relationship with Schmitt became increasingly critical in the 1960s, Schmitt repeatedly returned to the sentence and saw in it an explanation for Nicolaus Sombart’s behavior toward him. See BW Sombart, pp. 64–65, note 150, and p. 127.

*lingua occidistis* — This does not occur in the Good Friday liturgy. It comes instead from St. Augustine’s commentary on the Psalms:

> *Et vos, o Iudaei, occidistis. Unde occidistis? Gladio linguae.*

> “And you, O Jews, have killed. With what did you kill? With the sword of the tongue.”

See also *Tb 1930–34*, p. 421.

“It takes only one Jew” — Correctly:

> “It is certainly difficult to remain patient; but one must remember that it takes only one beggar Jew to mock a God on the cross.”

Goethe, letter to Carl Ludwig von Knebel, 12 January 1814. In: Goethe, *Werke*, Weimar edition, section IV, vol. 24, p. 99.

“Desecration and slaughter by Carl Linfert on NWDR” — On 22 November 1954, Nordwestdeutscher Rundfunk repeated Schmitt’s “Gespräch über die Macht,” which Hessischer Rundfunk had already broadcast on 22 June, now under the title “Macht — so gefährlich wie immer, so verdächtig wie nie” — “Power — As Dangerous as Ever, As Suspect as Never Before.”

Carl Linfert (1900–1981), head of NWDR’s late-night educational programming, introduced the broadcast with a very cautious disclaimer. Schmitt commented on this to Mohler:

> “The NWDR broadcast of my conversation was introduced by Carl Linfert, with endless apologies, as though something were about to follow that God had forbidden.”

BW Mohler, p. 183. Schmitt made a similar remark in a letter to Rolf Hinder; see *Schmittiana* V, 1996, p. 173.

See also G. Giesler’s afterword, p. 80, in C. Schmitt, *Gespräch über die Macht und den Zugang zum Machthaber*, Stuttgart 2008, and Monika Boll, *Nachtprogramm. Intellektuelle Gründungsdebatten in der frühen Bundesrepublik*, Münster 2004, p. 103, note 39.

*Memor approbii* — “I keep the applause in my memory.”

**30 January 1955**

*homicidae <fuistis>, et manent* — Vulgate, Acts 7:52: “You were murderers.” The early Christian preacher and first martyr Stephen accuses the Jews of murdering the prophets. The addition *et manent* — “and they remain so” — is not in the Bible and was added by Schmitt.

The biblical passages that follow contain the parable of the workers in the vineyard who kill the vineyard owner’s son in order to seize the inheritance.

*Quid timidi estis! Et facta est tranquillitas magna* — Vulgate, Matthew 8:26:

> *et dicit eis quid timidi estis modicae fidei tunc surgens imperavit ventis et mari et facta est tranquillitas magna.*

> “And he said to them: Why are you afraid, you of little faith? Then he rose and commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm.”

**14 February 1955**

“Tarnbruder John” — Otto John (1909–1997), first president of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, from 1950 to 1954. On 20 July 1954 he went to East Germany, probably under duress, and criticized the Federal Republic for the growing influence of former National Socialists.

In 1955 he escaped back to West Berlin, was charged with treason, and sentenced to four years in prison. He was later pardoned. According to current historical understanding, he was innocent.

**19 March 1955**

*Ne simus faciles in nominibus* — See above, note to p. 15.

*Νόμος Basileus* — For an explanation of the concept, see *Nomos*, pp. 42 ff.

**20 March 1955**

“The stump-and-style spirit of Mr. Böhm” — Franz Böhm wrote in the letter mentioned:

> “An end to denazification? Good. I would never have started it in the first place.
>
> “But anyone who understands ‘an end to denazification’ to mean the rehabilitation and restoration of the Nazis, their ways of thinking, and their political methods will have to accept that there is a gulf between him and the other Germans greater than the gulf separating us from even the most foreign inhabitants of any country on this planet — indeed, even from enemies of Germany who think justly.
>
> “German is not a biological concept but a spiritual one. It includes sinners and dubious characters of every kind, including criminals. But it does not include people who concern themselves with integrating National Socialism, in any form, into our historical and political tradition …”

In: *Frankfurter Hefte* 10, 1955, p. 167.

**3 April 1955**

“Kojève, *Introduction*” — Schmitt is referring to Alexandre Kojève, *Introduction à la lecture de Hegel. Leçons sur la phénoménologie de l’esprit professées de 1933 à 1939 à l’École des hautes-études*, collected and published by Raymond Queneau, Paris 1947; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 24734.

“he took his own life” — Schmitt gives no page reference, but he is probably referring to the following passage:

> The individual “experiences the double meaning contained in what it did, namely that it took its life; it took its own life, but in doing so it rather seized death.”

G. W. F. Hegel, *Phänomenologie des Geistes*, *Sämtliche Werke*, ed. H. Glockner, vol. 2, p. 282.

“So eating and drinking can be called a form of knowing” — H.-R. Müller-Schwefe, “Erkenntnis und Wort Gottes.” In: *Freundschaftliche Begegnungen. Festschrift für Ernst Jünger zum 60. Geburtstag*, ed. Armin Mohler, Frankfurt am Main 1955, pp. 56–74; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 23095.

“Taking, dividing, pasturing” — See C. Schmitt, “Nehmen / Teilen / Weiden. Ein Versuch die Grundfragen jeder Sozial- und Wirtschaftsordnung vom Nomos her richtig zu stellen.” In: VA, pp. 489–504; first published in 1953.

“Gelimer’s laughter” — Gelimer, the last king of the Vandals, was decisively defeated in 533 by the Byzantine general Belisarius, bringing the Vandals’ historical existence to an end. Gelimer responded to the destruction of his kingdom with grim laughter.

Schmitt identified with this reaction as the laughter of a defeated man to such an extent that he gave Book V of the *Glossarium* the heading “Gelimer.” See the appendix; see also above, p. 371. See BW EJ, pp. 353, 454–55; Reinhard Mehring, “Das Lachen der Besiegten. Das Lachen Gelimers.” In: *Zeitschrift für Ideengeschichte* 4, 2012, no. 1, pp. 32–45; Martin Tielke, “Habent sua fata libelli et balli.” In: *Sinn und Form* 64, 2012, pp. 466–67.

“see my diary entry of 6 April 1933” —

> “… at 7:45 by taxi to Popitz for the press reception. Saw Hitler and Goebbels. Saw both clearly. Great excitement. Hitler like the greedy bull in the arena. Shaken by that look.”

*Tb 1930–34*, p. 279. See also *Gespräch*, p. 105.

H. Recknagel — The commercial lawyer Heinz Recknagel asked Schmitt for the work because the German consul in Malmö, Dr. Meyer, had advised him to read it so that he could better understand the policies of the Soviet Union, where Recknagel had contacts. See his letter to Schmitt of 8 December 1958; RW 265 no. 11334.

**10 April 1955**

*Cor ne edito* — “Do not eat your heart out”; a proverb meaning: “Don’t worry.” *anthropophagus cordis mei* — “The devourer of my own heart.”

**16 April 1955**

to E. Forsthoff — Not in *BW Forsthoff*!

**17 April 1955**

to Kojève, 9 May 1955 — In: *Schmittiana* VI, 1998, p. 101. Kojève, his letter of 2 May 1955 — In: *Schmittiana* VI, 1998, p. 100. Jews who recognized the grotesque insolence of this E. K. — See Kurt Hiller, “Der Fall Erich Kaufmann.” In: idem, *Köpfe und Tröpfe*, Hamburg 1948, pp. 74–80.

During Kempner’s interrogation of Schmitt, Schmitt’s mention of E. Kaufmann was a tactical chess move. In the Wilhelmstrasse Trial, Kempner later called Kaufmann as a witness and tried to discredit him as a nationalist and militarist; see *Carl Schmitt – Antworten in Nürnberg*. Edited and annotated by Helmut Quaritsch, Berlin 2000, pp. 42 ff.

**9 May 1955**

Farewell song of the old Moselle man — Under the title “Gesang des alten Mosellaners 1957” (“Song of the Old Moselle Man, 1957”), Schmitt also sent this poem to A. Kojève (see *Schmittiana* VI, 1998, p. 123) and to A. Mohler (*BW Mohler*, p. 232). See also the note above on p. 305.

Törwang — A village in Upper Bavaria where E. Forsthoff had a holiday home and where Schmitt visited him in May 1955.

**5 June 1955**

In Göttingen, manly professors have … — When the right-wing nationalist Leonard Schlüter, representing the FDP in the Lower Saxony state government, was appointed Minister of Education and Cultural Affairs at the end of May 1955, the University of Göttingen mounted a major protest. As a result, Schlüter submitted his resignation on 9 June. See Heinz-Georg Marten, *Der niedersächsische Ministersturz. Proteste und Widerstand der Georg-August-Universität Göttingen gegen den Kultusminister Schlüter im Jahre 1955*, Göttingen 1987. See also *Schmittiana* VI, 1998, pp. 108 f.; *BW Forsthoff*, pp. 502 f.; *BW Mohler*, p. 200.

**9 June 1955**

“It is for it …” — Correctly:

> “As it thus grasps itself, it is as though the world were only now coming into being for it. Before this, it does not understand the world; it desires it and works upon it, withdraws from it into itself, and destroys it for itself, while also destroying itself as consciousness—as consciousness of the world as essence, and as consciousness of its nothingness. Only here, after the grave of its truth has been lost, and after the destruction of its reality has itself been destroyed … does it discover the world as its new real world.”

G. F. W. Hegel, *Werke*. Edited by Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 3, Frankfurt am Main 1970, p. 179.

yesterday I wrote to Kojève — Correctly: on 7 June; see *Schmittiana* VI, 1998, pp. 108 ff.

**11 June 1955**

to Wirsing — Giselher Wirsing (1907–1975), journalist. In the 1920s he belonged to the Tat circle around Hans Zehrer and, until 1945, served as an editor of various periodicals. In 1948 he was a co-founder of the weekly newspaper *Christ und Welt*, which he edited as editor-in-chief from 1954 to 1970. During the 1950s, Wirsing was an important supporter of Schmitt in the press. See Kai Burkhardt (ed.), *Carl Schmitt und die Öffentlichkeit. Briefwechsel mit Journalisten, Publizisten und Verlegern aus den Jahren 1923 bis 1983*, Berlin 2013.

**9 August 1955**

when the jurist Sir Edward Coke told the king … —

> “…when Coke said before the king, that ‘his Majesty was defended by the laws,’ James, in anger, told him he spoke foolishly, and he said he was not defended by the laws, but by God (alluding to his ‘divine right’).”

Isaac Disraeli, *The Literary Character or, The History of Men of Genius. Drawn from Their Own Feelings and Confessions. Literary Miscellanies; and an Inquiry into the Character of James the First*. A new ed. (*The Works of Isaac Disraeli*, [4]), London etc. 1859, p. 423.

**15 August 1955**

Adolf Caspary — (1898–1953), jurist, emigrated to the United States in 1942. Schmitt had contact with him in 1932 (see *Tb 1930–34*, p. 184) and refers approvingly above, p. 63, to Caspary’s 1927 book *Die Maschinenutopie*.

Leo Strauss — (1899–1973), political philosopher. On his relationship with Schmitt, see Heinrich Meier, *Carl Schmitt, Leo Strauss und „Der Begriff des Politischen“. Zu einem Dialog unter Abwesenden*, 3rd ed., Stuttgart/Weimar 2013.

Walter Benjamin — (1892–1940), philosopher, literary critic, and translator. See Susanne Heil, *„Gefährliche Beziehung“. Walter Benjamin und Carl Schmitt*, Stuttgart/Weimar 1996; Michael Rumpf (ed.), “Briefwechsel Michael Rumpf – Carl Schmitt.” In: *Schmittiana NF* II, 2014, pp. 275–285.

under the impact of the words “sacrifice for life …” — Schmitt repeatedly worked through Benjamin’s book on German tragic drama with great intensity; see Reinhard Mehring, “Geist ist das Vermögen, Diktatur auszuüben. Carl Schmitts Marginalien zu Walter Benjamin.” In: idem, *Kriegstechniker des Begriffs. Biographische Studien zu Carl Schmitt*, Tübingen 2014, pp. 132–152; Jürgen Thaler, “Genial. Carl Schmitt liest Walter Benjamin.” In: Marcel Atze/Volker Kaukoreit (eds.), *Lesespuren – Spurenlesen oder Wie kommt die Handschrift ins Buch? Von sprechenden und stummen Annotationen*, Vienna 2011, pp. 246–251.

**23 August 1955**

Pleasure conceives and gives birth to sin — 1 John 2:16; see above, p. 315.

**1 September 1955**

Michel Mourre, *Lamennais* p. 141 — Michel Mourre, *Lamennais ou l’hérésie des temps modernes*, Paris 1955.

Have I not done exactly the same myself with Adam Müller — In: *PR*.

**14 September 1955**

The world in which Prof. Wilhelm Grewe’s little light shines — Grewe, who from 1950 onward advised Adenauer in negotiations with the victorious powers of the Second World War, took part in the 1955 trip to Moscow. There he was less willing than Adenauer to make concessions to the Soviets. He is regarded as the originator of the Hallstein Doctrine.

The full-blooded Moju can do that better — This refers to Moritz Julius Bonn, who took part in the negotiations over the Treaty of Versailles as a member of the German delegation in 1919 and was appointed adviser to the Reich Chancellor on reparations in 1920.

**15 September 1955**

Johann Jacob Reiske — (1716–1774), German scholar of Greek, Arabic, and Byzantine studies. In his works, Wilamowitz-Moellendorff repeatedly drew attention to Reiske’s philological achievements, which went unrecognized for many years.

**15 September 1955**

Come along, Cohn — From Theodor Fontane’s poem “An meinem Fünfundsiebzigsten” (“On My Seventy-Fifth Birthday”), which ends:

> I was something to everyone,
> They all read me,
> They had all known me for ages,
> And that is the main thing … “come along, Cohn.”

**21 September 1955**

the anti-Roman feeling of the historian Fritz Kern — Kern (1884–1950) became Schmitt’s colleague at the University of Bonn in 1922. On 5 May 1923 Schmitt wrote about him in his diary: “I dislike him; a Protestant professor.” (*Tb 1921–24*, p. 192). Kern converted to Catholicism in 1949.

**30 September 1955**

“That is the true taking of land” —

> “Again and again, from the tangled outlines of the Littorale, the Saracen tower emerged, gradually growing smaller as the perspective changed, a pale shape amid the solitude of rock and sea. At every bend I was glad to see it again, the guardian of a southern territory that had become for me a piece of spiritual homeland. That is the true taking of land.”

E. Jünger, *Sämtliche Werke*, vol. 6, p. 315.

**4 October 1955**

Konrad Beyerle — (1872–1933), jurist and politician, co-author of the Weimar Constitution. Article 153 of the Weimar Constitution—corresponding to Article 14 of the German Basic Law—guaranteed property, but also stated:

> “Property entails obligations. Its use should also serve the common good.”

This led to a debate lasting several years over the expropriation of the former princely houses. A popular initiative supported expropriation in 1926, but the referendum that followed did not. The attempted expropriation of the princes therefore failed.

**5 October 1955**

My cousin André — André Steinlein (1891–1964), son of the younger brother of Schmitt’s mother, whom Schmitt had known since their school days. On 16 December 1954, Schmitt wrote to Nicolaus Sombart about his ambivalent relationship with him:

> “…But I still have to coordinate matters with my Lorraine cousin, an aging *bon vivant* who, after a typically bourgeois life as a notary, has retreated into a rural backwater on the Seille. Yet, from old habit—we have somehow kept running into one another ever since our youth—I am very fond of him; if only because the old saying applies to him in a typical way: *il n’y a pas de notaire qui n’ait rêvé de sultan*—there is no notary who has not dreamed of being a sultan.”

(*BW Sombart*, pp. 67 f.)

**6 October 1955**

Hear the Nobel Prize prophet — This refers to Max Born (1882–1970), who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1954. Schmitt is quoting M. Born, “Das entscheidende Motiv. Eine Erwiderung.” In: *Merkur*, 1955, no. 92, p. 999.

**14 October 1955**

Alfons Adams — (1899–1973), philosopher, brother of Paul Adams.

Good Friday of the spirit — See G. F. W. Hegel, *Glauben und Wissen*. In: idem, *Werke*, ed. Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 2, p. 432. Hegel’s spelling of *Karfreitag* has been modernized here.

Mount of Olives of world history — See Konrad Weiß, *Zum geschichtlichen Gethsemane*, Mainz 1919, reprint Bigge n.d. [1945], pp. 185 ff.

κληρο-νόμος — “the heir.”

*Vigens disciplina, Fides moribunda* — “The discipline [of the Church] flourishing, faith dying.” *Vigens ecclesiae disciplina* is a term from canon law.

**26 October 1955**

Wilhelm Wackernagel says — W. Wackernagel (1806–1869), Germanist and art historian, professor in Basel from 1835. Schmitt is referring to Wilhelm Wackernagel, *Über die dramatische Poesie*, Basel 1838. See Carl Schmitt, *Hamlet oder Hekuba*, 2nd ed., Stuttgart 1993, p. 51, with note 21 on pp. 72 f. (first published 1956).

report on Adolf Grabowsky — A. Grabowsky (1880–1969), geopolitician, lecturer at the *Deutsche Hochschule für Politik* from 1921 to 1933, published *Gott und der Zauberer. Ein Mythos*, Berlin 1912. Schmitt’s report on it is in his papers, RW 265 no. 19394.

Pierre Leyris — (1907–2001), translator and literary critic. Schmitt means: H. Melville, *Benito Cereno* (*Biblioteca Zig Zag*, 19), Santiago de Chile 1944. On pp. 130–142 appears P. Leyris, “Reflexiones sobre ‘Benito Cereno’.” Leyris had already published an annotated French translation of *Benito Cereno*, with a preface, in 1937.

**28 October 1955**

May 1953 in Herrenalb — See the note above on p. 304.

It took that article in the *Linksrheinischer Merkur* — Eduard Rosenbaum, “Carl Schmitt vor den Toren.” In: *Rheinischer Merkur* no. 48, 25 November 1950.

Again and again I fell for the deception — Schmitt is quoting himself here: *ECS*, p. 88; see also the entries above for 11 February 1948 and 11 August 1950.

**6 November 1955**

Friedrich Glum — F. Glum, *Philosophen im Spiegel und Zerrspiegel. Deutschlands Weg in den Nationalismus und Nationalsozialismus*, Munich 1954.

Rüdiger Altmann — (1922–2000), jurist, political writer, and political adviser. At the end of the war he studied under Schmitt, later under Wolfgang Abendroth. Schmitt quotes the essay “Was heißt christliche Demokratie?” by Friedrich Grund, probably a pseudonym for Rüdiger Altmann. In: *Civis. Zeitschrift für christlich-demokratische Politik* 2, 1955, no. 11, pp. 57–58. The sentence:

> “In fact, today there is no substantive ethic in the Western cultural sphere other than the Christian one”

appears on p. 57.

**10 November 1955**

Karl Korn — K. Korn, “Kyklos. Zu F. G. Jüngers neuen Gedichten.” In: *Berliner Hefte für geistiges Leben* 3, 1948, pp. 42–55.

*La nullité protège mieux. L’ambiguité protège mieux* — “Nothingness protects better. Ambiguity protects better.” A variation on Rivarol’s frequently quoted maxim, *L’obscurité protège mieux*—“Obscurity protects better.” See the note above on p. 158.

With *The Origin of Species* in 1859 — Charles Darwin, *On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favored Races in the Struggle for Life*, London 1859.

The secret of eating bread … —

> “…those who affirm the truth and certainty of the reality of sensory objects [can] be told that they must be sent back to the lowest school of wisdom, namely the ancient Eleusinian mysteries of Ceres and Bacchus, and must first learn the secret of eating bread and drinking wine…”

G. W. F. Hegel, *Werke*. Edited by Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 3, Frankfurt am Main 1970, p. 91.

Brothers of the gently living flesh — Thomas Müntzer called Luther “the soft-living flesh of Wittenberg.”

It is the hump … — See above, p. 131.

**11 November 1955**

And powers of delusion … — Theodor Däubler, “Hymne an Sizilien.” In: idem, *Dichtungen und Schriften*. Edited by Friedhelm Kemp, Munich 1956, p. 86.

Peter Schneider — (1920–2002), Swiss jurist, assistant to Carlo Schmid. In 1955 he completed his postdoctoral qualification with the study *Ausnahmezustand und Norm. Eine Studie zur Rechtslehre von Carl Schmitt*, Stuttgart 1957. Schmitt first learned of Schneider in 1953 through A. Mohler; see *BW Mohler* (index) and *BW Huber*, pp. 374 ff.

**16 November 1955**

Simone Weil, Karl Epting — See the note above on p. 299.

**17 November 1955**

The poor celibate bureaucracy — Schmitt coined the term “celibate bureaucracy” in 1923; see *RK*, p. 6; *Gespräch*, p. 57.

**18 November 1955**

Edith Stein, who had herself baptized and became impenetrable within the religious order — E. Stein (1891–1942), philosopher and women’s rights advocate. She converted from Judaism to Catholicism in 1922 and entered the strict Carmelite order. She was murdered at Auschwitz and canonized in 1998.

concept of the chosen one — See the note above on p. 208.

**23 November 1955**

Caux — Swiss resort town, known from 1946 onward as an international conference center for Moral Re-Armament.

**24 November 1955**

Above my cap … — Parody of Goethe; see the note above on p. 170.

Rolf Schroers — (1919–1981), writer; see van Laak, pp. 251–255.

article by Baron von der Heydte in *Hochland* — Friedrich August von der Heydte, “Heil aus der Gefangenschaft? Carl Schmitt und die Lage der europäischen Rechtswissenschaft.” In: *Hochland* 43, 1950/51, pp. 288–294; see also the note above on p. 210.

**28 November 1955**

Julian Huxley — (1887–1975), English biologist and researcher of animal behavior. Schmitt is referring to J. Huxley, *Entfaltung des Lebens* (*Fischer Bücherei*, 61), Frankfurt am Main/Hamburg 1954. A copy containing annotations is in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 26715.

all the Walter Ottos and all the Schadewaldts — Walter F. Otto (1874–1958), classical scholar; Wolfgang Schadewaldt (1900–1974), classical scholar. Both studied the continuing influence of Greek mythology and religion.

**4 December 1955**

in an article in *Junge Wirtschaft* — Winfried Martini, “Ein gefährliches Provisorium.” In: *Junge Wirtschaft. Zeitschrift für fortschrittliches Unternehmertum*, 1955, no. 11, pp. 404–405.

**19 December 1955**

a poisonous Morgenthau type — This refers to Franz Borkenau (1900–1957), Marxist sociologist and philosopher of history. Schmitt is referring to F. Borkenau, “Spengler – Weitergedacht. Eine Antwort an seine Kritiker.” In: *Der Monat* 8, 1955, pp. 46–55. The quotation beginning “The malice …” appears on p. 48.

… *non canalisata, non canalisabilis* — “…not channeled, not capable of being channeled”; see the note above on p. 305.

*miching mallecho. It means mischief* — See the note above on p. 271.

We Christian folk now have joy — Opening line of a Christmas hymn by Kaspar Füger (1521–1592), also used as an organ chorale by J. S. Bach.

**26 December 1955**

to Sombart, to Jünger — Schmitt’s letter of 26 December 1955 to Nicolaus Sombart ends with the sentence:

> “I wish you and your wife happiness and good health in the New Year and remain, on this side and beyond every boundary of age and market, your eternally unchannelable Moselle man.”

(*BW Sombart*, p. 85). Similar wording in *BW EJ*, p. 289.

**4 January 1956**

lecture by Hermann Heimpel — The historian Heimpel (1901–1988), professor at the Reich University of Strasbourg from 1941 to 1944 and a friend of E. R. Huber, spoke on NDR—not NWDR—at 6:25 p.m. on 1 January 1956 under the title “Was verlangt das neue Jahr?” (“What Does the New Year Demand?”).

No longer the Jews … — The 1906 Catechism of the Catholic Church stated that Jesus was condemned to death because Pilate “cowardly gave in to the threatening pressure of the people of Jerusalem.” In the 1955 catechism the wording became:

> “The Son of God was rejected by the leaders of the chosen people.”

(*Kath. Katechismus der Bistümer Deutschlands*, Freiburg 1955, p. 53). In the revised catechism of 2005, this became “some leaders.”

Sovereign is he who decides on the state of exception. — Schmitt formulated this not in 1921 but in 1922, in *Political Theology*. The problem of the exception had, however, already been discussed systematically in 1921 in Carl Schmitt, *Die Diktatur. Von den Anfängen des modernen Souveränitätsgedankens bis zum proletarischen Klassenkampf*, 6th ed., Berlin 1994, pp. XVII f. and passim.

Exceptions do not count — Not a literal quotation; see Hans Freyer, *Theorie des gegenwärtigen Zeitalters*, Stuttgart 1955, pp. 157 ff.

about the conversation with Hans Freyer after Wiesbaden — On 6 January 1956, a colloquium on Hans Freyer’s *Theorie des gegenwärtigen Zeitalters* was held in Wiesbaden.

the passage from 1921 … —

> “The formal feature [of a justification of dictatorship] lies in the authorization by a supreme authority that is legally capable of suspending the law and authorizing a dictatorship—that is, permitting a concrete exception whose content, compared with the other case of a concrete exception, the granting of a pardon, is enormous. Abstractly speaking, the problem of dictatorship would be the problem of the concrete exception, a problem that has so far received little systematic treatment in general legal theory.”

C. Schmitt, *Die Diktatur*, 6th ed., Berlin 1994, p. XVIII.

**1 February 1956**

Küster — Otto Küster (1907–1989), jurist.

W. Strauss — Walter Strauss (1900–1976). As State Secretary in the Federal Ministry of Justice, he was the driving force behind the withdrawal of Schmitt’s invitation to the Evangelical Academy of Baden conference in Herrenalb in May 1953; see the note above on p. 304.

**2 February 1956**

Banquet of the slaughtered Leviathan — See *Leviathan*, p. 18.

**4 February 1956**

Dombois — Hans Adolf Dombois (1907–1997), theologian and jurist, a student of Smend. In 1950 he published a book on denazification that Schmitt studied intensively: Hans Dombois, *Politische Gerichtsbarkeit. Der Irrweg der Entnazifizierung und die Frage des Verfassungsschutzes. Mit e. Nachw. von Hermann Ehlers*, Gütersloh [1950]. The copy held at the Institute for Political Science and Sociology at the University of Bonn contains the dedication:

> “Respectfully dedicated to Prof. Dr. Schmitt with gratitude, Hemer 14/5/1953, Dr. Dombois.”

Klaus Ritter — (born 1918). Schmitt is referring to K. Ritter, *Zwischen Naturrecht und Rechtspositivismus. Eine erkenntnistheoret. Auseinandersetzung mit den neueren Versuchen zur Wiederherstellung e. Rechtsmetaphysik. Mit e. Vorw. von Hans Dombois*, Witten 1956.

Emil Wiener — Not identified.

Coing — Helmut Coing (1912–2000), jurist, Rector of the University of Frankfurt in 1955/56.

**16 February 1956**

Ernst Jünger (6 March 1956) — *BW EJ*, pp. 295 f.

Neesse — Gottfried Neeße (1911–1987), National Socialist jurist specializing in civil-service law and a colleague of Schmitt at Berlin University. He dedicated the following work to Schmitt: *Geheimnis mitten im Licht: Das ist Naxos. Carl Schmitt zum 80. Geburtstag*, n.p. 1968. Typescript, RW 265 no. 27664.

Peter Diederichs — (1904–1990), publisher. In 1949 he re-established in Cologne the Diederichs publishing house his father had run in Leipzig. Schmitt’s *Hamlet oder Hekuba* appeared there in 1956.

Millions of heads and one record — A variation on the poem “Himmel und Hölle” by Franz von Paula Huber, which says:

> Millions of souls, one thought,
> Millions of hearts and one beat!

Schlagintweit — Several brothers who published accounts of their travels and research in the nineteenth century.

**1 March 1956**

Three premiums, three premiums … — After the folk and soldiers’ song:

> Three lilies, three lilies,
> I planted on my grave;
> Then came a proud horseman
> And broke them off.

On the “three premiums attached to the legal possession of power,” see *LuL*, pp. 32 f., with the later note in *VA*, p. 348. Schmitt also used this “political surplus value” attached to the legal possession of power to explain his own conduct in 1933; see *Gespräch*, pp. 68 ff.

On *obéissance préalable*—“prior obedience”—see the note above on p. 25; on the “application of general clauses,” see C. Schmitt, *Über die drei Arten des rechtswissenschaftlichen Denkens*, 3rd ed., Berlin 2006, pp. 48 f.

**16 March 1956**

*jus primae noctis* — “The right of the first night.” In the period of serfdom, the lord exercising judicial authority was said to have the right to spend the first night with a bride. Whether, and to what extent, this was ever actually practiced is unclear.

**30 March 1956**

Whoever does not work shall not eat — The saying comes from Paul (2 Thess. 3:10) and appears in Article 12 of the Constitution of the Soviet Union of 5 December 1936.

**1 April 1956**

*Caduca culmina vagi saeculi contemnens* — Correctly: *caduca vagi contemnens culmina saecli*, “despising the decaying heights of this restless age”; from the *Carmen paschale* of the Christian Latin poet Caelius Sedulius, fifth century.

Novalis: The Jew must perish —

> “The fundamental difference between the Old and New Testaments. Why Palestine and the Jews were chosen for the founding of the Christian religion. Just as the Jews perished through it, so the French in the present Revolution.”

Novalis, *Teplitzer Fragmente*. In: idem, *Schriften*. Edited by Paul Kluckhohn and Richard Samuel, vol. 2, Stuttgart etc. 1981, p. 616.

*Positionen und Begriffe*, p. 113, note — *PuB*, p. 128, note 2.

It lives on as a ghost … — See the note above on p. 207.

They have Niehans-style fresh cells injected into themselves — This refers to Pope Pius XII; see above, p. 297.

see Lucan (*sed victa Catoni*) — *Pharsalia*, I, 128; see also the note above on p. 79.

**2 April 1956**

Henri Lévy-Bruhl — H. Lévy-Bruhl (1884–1964), sociologist of law and professor of Roman law at the University of Paris.

**7 April 1956**

Pascal’s “human condition” (fr. 139) — Schmitt is using Brunschvicg’s numbering. The fragment says:

> “all the unhappiness of men comes from one thing: their inability to remain quietly alone in their room.”

B. Pascal, *Über die Religion und über einige andere Gegenstände (Pensées)*. Translated and edited by Ewald Wasmuth, 8th ed., Heidelberg 1978, p. 77.

Hobbes’s sociology of competition — Schmitt is referring to Chapter 13 of *Leviathan*.

**13 May 1956**

pp. 511/12 *PhdG* — See G. W. F. Hegel, *Werke*. Edited by Eva Moldenhauer and Karl Markus Michel, vol. 3, p. 571.

**18 May 1956**

Hans Graß — (1909–1994), Protestant theologian.

**29 May 1956**

Mr. von Sedlmayer — Hans Sedlmayr, *Verlust der Mitte. Die bildende Kunst des 19. und 20. Jahrh. als Symbol der Zeit*, Salzburg 1948.

**31 May 1956**

Ernst Bloch: the fascist Carl Schmitt … —

> “The way the universal plays with individuals is called here not only cunning but mystification or cheating […] This is a final echo of the capitalist complex of cunning, which, not without reason—namely, in complete harmony with every reactionary fraud—the fascist Carl Schmitt was the first to point out […]”

E. Bloch, *Subjekt – Objekt. Erläuterungen zu Hegel*. Expanded edition, Frankfurt am Main 1971, pp. 235 f.

According to Günter Maschke, Bloch said during a lecture in 1965:

> “That dog Carl Schmitt—I repeat: that dog Carl Schmitt.”

Ernst Bloch (1885–1977), whom Schmitt probably knew from their shared work for the journal *Summa*, had still written positively before 1933 about the author of *Political Romanticism*; see *BW Feuchtwanger*, p. 35.

In a diary entry of 8 May 1945, Schmitt wrote of Bloch:

> “First, in 1917 in Munich at the General Command, his book *Spirit of Utopia*. Then I saw him at Feuchtwanger’s. He spoke about my *Political Romanticism* and saw everything accurately, including the fact that I am a born victim for literary plunder.”

(RW 265 no. 19586, sheet 27.)

and is made a professor for it — In 1948, Bloch, then sixty-four years old, was offered the chair of philosophy in Leipzig. Against the resistance of the faculty, the Ministry of Public Education installed him as professor and director of the Institute of Philosophy.

**6 July 1956**

my copy into the hands of Karl Löwith — See M. Tielke, “Die Bibliothek Carl Schmitts.” In: *Schmittiana NF* I, 2011, p. 269.

*taedium fugae* — “weariness of flight”; see Schmitt’s letter to E. Jünger of 11 June 1948:

> “I suffer from *taedium fugae*, and I am heartily tired of the hunt whose quarry I have now been for years.”

*BW EJ*, p. 228.

*Évidemment, ce ne sont pas seulement nos actes qui nous suivent* — “Obviously, it is not only our actions that follow us.” See the note above on p. 202.

Unwillingly and only faithfully — See the note above on p. 19.

**10 July 1956**

I am terrified by my power … — From Arthur Schnitzler, *Der Puppenspieler*. In: idem, *Gesammelte Werke*, section II, vol. 3, Berlin 1922, p. 267.

Great Wurstel — *Zum großen Wurstel*, a play by Arthur Schnitzler.

**11 July 1956**

Joh. Adams — Johannes Adams, son of Alfons Adams; see above, p. 325.

L. Ilschner — Author of the following book: Liselotte Ilschner, *Rembrandt als Erzieher und seine Bedeutung. Studie über d. kulturelle Struktur d. neunziger Jahre*, Danzig [1928]. Ilschner also worked on Shakespeare; four of her letters survive in Schmitt’s papers.

Germany is Hamlet — Quotation from Ferdinand Freiligrath’s 1848 poem “Hamlet”; see C. Schmitt, *Hamlet oder Hekuba. Der Einbruch der Zeit in das Spiel*, 2nd ed., Stuttgart 1993, p. 11.

**12 July 1956**

Heller’s interjection — See the note above on p. 274.

**16 July 1956**

E. Jünger counts himself among the Order of the Shandians —

> “And so, under worthy circumstances, I entered the secret Order of the Shandians, to which I have remained faithful to this day.”

E. Jünger, *Sämtliche Werke*, vol. 9, p. 38. This refers to Laurence Sterne’s *The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman*.

Rameau’s Nephew — The nephew of Jean-Philippe Rameau, composer and author of an influential theory of harmony, was the failed artist Jean-François Rameau. Denis Diderot’s posthumous work *Le neveu de Rameau* was translated into German by Goethe in 1805 and published for the first time in that translation.

**17 August 1956**

as Kommerell says — Max Kommerell, *Lessing und Aristoteles. Unters. über die Theorie der Tragödie*, Frankfurt am Main 1984, p. 32.

parable of the forged rings — See Carl Schmitt, “Die vollendete Reformation. Zu neuen Leviathan-Interpretationen.” In: *Leviathan*, p. [163].

**25 August 1956**

Habermas at the conference of the “Bund” — A conference entitled “Kulturkonsum und Konsumkultur” was held in Wuppertal in 1955, at which Jürgen Habermas discussed with Arnold Gehlen and Günther Anders; see *Bericht über die Tagung „Kulturkonsum und Konsumkultur“*, Wuppertal 1955.

I had jokingly defined — Schmitt probably means his preface to the second edition of *Political Romanticism*, where he writes:

> “For what has art meant socially since Romanticism? Either it ended in *l’art pour l’art*, in the polarity between snobbery and bohemia, or it became a matter of private producers of art supplying private consumers interested in art.”

*PR*, p. 21.

**26 September 1956**

threw me into what they called automatic arrest — Incorrect; see the note above on p. 201.

**4 October 1956**

Why don’t you ask Mr. Kranzbühler — Otto Kranzbühler (1907–2004), naval judge, defense counsel for Dönitz and Flick at the Nuremberg trials.

**9 November 1956**

the conversation with Nicolaus — N. Sombart. Nothing more can be established about this conversation, but on 20 June 1973 Schmitt wrote to N. Sombart:

> “I would very much like to know what you think of the ‘Lincolnization’ of *Benito Cereno* carried out by Marianne Kesting—now a professor in Bielefeld.”

(*BW Sombart*, pp. 118 f.)

**5 December 1956**

Listen and suffer — See the note above on p. 227.

End of 1956

Humanity needed it, Hegel says —

> “Then, against that overwhelming superiority in armament, another technical means was discovered—gunpowder. Humanity needed it, and immediately it was there.”

G. F. W. Hegel, *Vorlesungen über die Philosophie der Geschichte*. In: idem, *Werke*. Edited by Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 12, Frankfurt am Main 1970, p. 481. See *Nomos*, p. 299.

**17 January 1957**

lecture by Kojève — Alexandre Kojève (1902–1968), Russian philosopher and Hegel scholar, gave a lecture to the Rhine-Ruhr Club in Düsseldorf on 16 January 1957 entitled “Kolonialismus in europäischer Sicht” (“Colonialism from a European Perspective”). See *Schmittiana* VI, 1998, which also prints the text of the lecture and the incomplete correspondence between Schmitt and Kojève.

**18 January 1957**

Konrad Kaletsch told me about the incident … — K. Kaletsch (1898–1978), cousin of Friedrich Flick and, from 1924 onward, a member of the Flick Group’s executive board, ultimately as a personally liable partner. He had known Schmitt since the summer of 1945, when he commissioned an expert opinion from Schmitt concerning Flick; see *Angriffskrieg*, pp. 127 ff.

Kaletsch was charged at Nuremberg together with Friedrich Flick but was acquitted. While Flick was imprisoned, Kaletsch conducted negotiations with the Allies over plans for seizure and liquidation. The Maxhütte works, which belonged to the Flick Group, were initially partly expropriated after 1945. After long negotiations, Flick recovered full ownership in 1955; see Norbert Frei, *Flick. Der Konzern, die Familie, die Macht*, Munich 2009, pp. 478–504.

The “incident” was described in *Der Spiegel* on 27 January 1957:

> “The ceremonial reception given by the Bavarian state government at the end of an inspection tour by the investment committee of the Coal and Steel Community Parliament, at Nuremberg’s Grand Hotel, was marred by a protocol blunder. Before dinner, the French delegate—former Minister of Justice and current Popular Republican member of the French National Assembly, Professor de Menthon—refused to take the seat assigned to him beside the industrial magnate Friedrich Flick. Shortly before, the committee had visited Flick’s major Bavarian plant, the Maximilianshütte in Sulzbach-Rosenberg. Bavarian Economics Minister Bezold (FDP) tried in vain to talk Professor de Menthon out of his resentment toward Flick, who had been the principal defendant in the Nuremberg trial named after him. In the end, the Frenchman exchanged seats with a German colleague on the committee. De Menthon had served as the chief French prosecutor at the International Military Tribunal in Nuremberg.”

(*Spiegel*, 27 January 1957).

François de Menthon (1900–1984) was the chief French prosecutor at the Nuremberg trials. Jean Armengaud, French general, had been air attaché in Warsaw in 1939 and appeared as a witness at the Nuremberg trials.

**21 January 1957**

in my essay “Die Buribunken” — In: *Summa*, 1918, 4, pp. 89–106; reprinted in *Tb 1915*, pp. 453–471.

**3 February 1957**

Kojève avoided … every reference to current affairs — The following paragraphs are largely identical to Schmitt’s letter to Nicolaus Sombart of 3 February 1957 (*BW Sombart*, pp. 96 ff.). Sombart had intended to attend Kojève’s lecture but cancelled at the last moment.

**3 February 1957**

the chapter “Plotnoi” in Mutius’s *Katorgan* — Bernhard von Mutius (1913–1979), Schmitt’s assistant at Berlin University in 1934/35. From 1949 he worked in the East German Foreign Ministry. In 1950 he was arrested for espionage and sentenced to forced labor in Vorkuta. In 1955 he was released as part of the freeing of German prisoners of war secured by Adenauer.

Under a pseudonym he published a book about his time in the Soviet labor camp: Bernhard Roeder, *Der Katorgan*, Cologne/Berlin 1956; the chapter “Der Plotnoi” appears on pp. 83–98. A presentation copy is in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 26443.

Schmitt wrote to Forsthoff on 15 February 1956:

> “Mutius … is coming tomorrow for a few days.”

*BW Forsthoff*, p. 121.

Mutius is also discussed at length in Schmitt’s letters to N. Sombart, who had known him since the early 1930s and later became his colleague and friend at the Council of Europe in Strasbourg. In 1979 Sombart delivered the funeral address for him; typescript in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 21820.

Nicolaus asked about the patriot — See Nicolaus Sombart, “Patriotismus im Welt-Bürgerkrieg.” In: *Der Zeitgenosse und sein Vaterland. Eine Vortragsreihe des Bayerischen Rundfunks*. Edited by Gerhard Szczesny, Munich 1957, pp. 31–51.

I answered him — Letter of 3 February 1957 (*BW Sombart*, pp. 96 ff.).

**28 February 1957**

“Those were never your bells …” — From the poem “Venus Religio” by Richard Dehmel (1863–1920), in: R. Dehmel, *Die Verwandlung der Venus*, Berlin 1907, p. 59.

**17 March 1957**

Peter Schneider’s book — See the note above on p. 329.

**23 March 1957**

πολλὰ τὰ δεινά — πολλὰ τὰ δεινά κοὐδὲν ἀνθρώπου δεινότερον πέλει.

> “Many powerful things exist, but nothing is more powerful than man.”

Sophocles, *Antigone*, 332 f.

**30 March 1957**

Meanwhile Hans Zehrer is trumpeting … — H. Zehrer, “Wer hat die Macht?” In: *Die Welt*, 30 March 1957.

**10 April 1957**

killing of Wallenstein in 1634 (according to Pekař) — Josef Pekař, *Wallenstein 1630–1634. Tragödie einer Verschwörung*, Berlin 1937.

“Even the murder of the monarch …” — Quoted in abbreviated form. Kant writes:

> “Among all the horrors of a revolution brought about by rebellion, even the murder of the monarch is not the worst. For one can still imagine that the people kill him out of fear that, if he remains alive, he may recover his power and make them suffer the punishment they deserve. In that case it would not be an act of punitive justice, but merely one of self-preservation. It is the formal execution that fills a soul steeped in the idea of human rights with a horror that is felt again and again whenever one thinks of such a scene, as in the fate of Charles I or Louis XVI. […] But how are we to explain this feeling, which is not aesthetic […] but moral—a feeling produced by the complete reversal of every concept of law? It is regarded as a crime that remains forever and can never be erased (*crimen immortale, inexpiabile*)…”

Kant, *Werke in zehn Bänden*. Edited by Wilhelm Weischedel, vol. 7, Darmstadt 1968, pp. 440 f.

my expert opinion on the *scelus infandum* — This refers to *Angriffskrieg*, p. 16; see also the notes above on pp. 66 and 219.

**13 April 1957**

The land of socialist construction — Correctly:

> “By contrast, the land of socialist construction has committed all its enormous power to ensuring—and must unfailingly use it to ensure—that power over human beings comes to an end. […] So that instead of the so-called constitutional state, which because of its rotten class content has become completely a state of injustice, no state at all will any longer be necessary.”

Ernst Bloch, *Das Prinzip Hoffnung*, Frankfurt am Main 1959, p. 1061.

*Tantam fidem non inveni nisi in Israel!* — Correctly: *audiens autem Iesus miratus est et sequentibus se dixit amen dico vobis non inveni tantam fidem in Israel*; Vulgate, Matthew 8:10. Luther translates:

> “When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him: Truly I tell you, I have found no such faith in anyone in Israel.”

*Tantam justificationem per finem non inveni apud Jesuitas!* — Schmitt’s alteration of the preceding quotation:

> “Such a justification by the final goal I have not found even among the Jesuits.”

**24 April 1957**

*Quid pectora pulsas? …* —

> “Why do you beat your breast and groan? Why do you shed useless tears and refuse to admit that you willingly obey criminal orders?”

*Pharsalia*, IV, 182–184.

**28 April 1957**

*trahimur sub nomine pacis* — “Peace is being used as a pretext to enslave us.” *Pharsalia*, IV, 222.

**22 May 1957**

Dachau Trial, April/May 1957 — In the issue mentioned, *Der Spiegel*, under the title “Der Furcht so fern, dem Tod so nah,” reports on the 1957 proceedings before the Munich jury court and the Osnabrück Regional Court against the SS leaders Dietrich, Lippert, von Woyrsch, and Müller-Altenau for their participation in the Röhm murders. The article emphasizes the Reichswehr’s interest in eliminating the SA.

Potempa Trial — During the night of 9–10 August 1932, SA men murdered the worker Konrad Pietrzuch in the Silesian village of Potempa. On the same day, 9 August, the Reich government had issued an emergency decree against political terrorism providing for the death penalty. As a result, the five murderers were sentenced to death in a rapid trial on 22 August.

A large National Socialist propaganda campaign against the “blood verdict” followed, after which the Reich President felt compelled to commute the death sentences to life imprisonment. After the Nazi seizure of power, the perpetrators were released in March 1933.

Robert Graves — Schmitt is referring to Graves’s edition of Lucan: Marcus Annaeus Lucanus, *Pharsalia. Dramatic Episodes of the Civil Wars*. Translated by Robert Graves (*The Penguin Classics*, 66), Harmondsworth 1956. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 23823.

He is rhetorical; Th. Hobbes already knew that — The reference to Hobbes concerns his comment in the preface to his translation of the *Odyssey*:

> “Lucan shews himself openly in the Pompeyan Faction, inveighing against Caesar throughout his Poem, like Cicero against Cataline [sic!] or Marc Antony, and is therefore justly reckon’d by Quintilian as a Rhetorician rather than a Poet.”

Quoted from “Preface to Homer’s Odysses, translated by Tho. Hobbes of Malmsbury.” In: *Critical Essays of the Seventeenth Century*, ed. J. E. Spingarn, vol. II, 1650–1685, Oxford 1908, p. 73. See also David Norbrook, *Writing the English Republic. Poetry, Rhetoric and Politics 1627–1660*, Cambridge 2000, chapter 1, “Lucan and the Poetry of Civil War,” pp. 23–62.

*si scelus est plus te nobis debere fatere …* — Correctly:

*Si scelus est, plus te nobis debere fateris, / Quod scelus hoc non ipse facis.*

> “If it is a crime, you admit that you owe us all the more because you are not committing this crime yourself.”

essay whose boldness—indeed, audacity—no one understood at the time — See Wolfgang Schuller’s afterword in *Tb 1930–34*, pp. 461 ff.

press chief Du Prel — Maximilian Du Prel (1904–1945), jurist and National Socialist politician, was in 1934 “Reich Office Director of the NSDAP Reich Press Office.”

Funck-Brentano — Frantz Funck-Brentano (1862–1947), French writer and historian. The work mentioned, however, appeared not in 1907 but in 1912: F. Funck-Brentano, *L’ancienne France. Le roi*, Paris 1912.

**1 June 1957**

Roegele — Otto B. Roegele (1920–2005), editor-in-chief of the *Rheinischer Merkur*, its publisher from 1963 onward, and professor of newspaper studies in Munich. Schmitt’s two-page letter to Warnach was written on 29 May 1957. Published in *Vorber.*

Calvo Serer — Rafael Calvo Serer (1916–1988), Spanish philosopher of history, invited Schmitt to Spain during the 1950s.

**10 June 1957**

I wrote to Peter Schneider — Letter in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 13493.

What am I still doing in this world? / Do you see the lightning falling there? — Quotation from the poem “Das Gewitter” by Gustav Benjamin Schwab (1792–1850).

conversation with George Schwab — G. D. Schwab (born 1931), American political scientist and translator of Schmitt. His doctorate at Columbia University in New York was initially blocked in 1962 by Otto Kirchheimer’s vote and could only proceed after Kirchheimer’s death in 1965. The dissertation appeared in 1970 as G. Schwab, *The Challenge of the Exception. An Introduction to the Political Ideas of Carl Schmitt Between 1921–1936*, Berlin 1970. During the 1950s, Schwab visited Schmitt several times.

**30 July 1957**

we laughed at Adorno’s revealing remark — Hegel’s thought contained:

> “something of the grand peasant cunning that has learned for so long to bow before the powerful and adapt itself to their needs that it can finally wrest power away from them.”

T. W. Adorno, *Drei Studien zu Hegel*. In: idem, *Gesammelte Schriften*. Edited by Rolf Tiedemann, vol. 5, 3rd ed., Frankfurt am Main 1990, p. 287.

**17 August 1957**

Wonderful, by contrast, was Hans Freyer in his reply to Arnold Gehlen’s birthday speech — Gehlen described the birthday celebration and his disagreement with Schmitt in a letter to Helmut Schelsky dated 3 August 1957:

> “Freyer’s birthday was pleasant; honorary doctorate from Münster. The Grand Cross of Merit will probably follow. My lecture—the thesis was that Freyer had shown, though without explicitly saying so, that in the future history would cease to provide the interpretation of the present and sociology would take its place—was well received, but not by C. S., who has now, of all things, discovered HEGEL and wants to impose him on everyone. He got terribly on my nerves. I found him more venomous, resentful, and arrogant than ever before, constantly forcing his ‘discoveries’ on everyone. Even *Hamlet* was really nothing more than an inflated trifle.”

University and State Library Münster, Papers of Schelsky, box 23, 030.

Papalekas — Johannes Chr. Papalekas (1924–1996), sociologist, then working at the Social Research Center in Dortmund. He completed his postdoctoral qualification under Hans Freyer and later became professor in Münster and Bochum. Schmitt met him at the time of Kojève’s lecture in Düsseldorf in January 1957; see his letter to Sombart of 3 February 1957 (*BW Sombart*, pp. 96 ff.).

**13 September 1957**

*Ubi nihil vales …* — See the note above on p. 14.

As Michel Mourre did then in Notre Dame — At Easter 1950, Mourre, wearing a Dominican habit, climbed into the pulpit of Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris during Mass and announced to the congregation: “God is dead.” See his autobiography *Malgré le blasphème*, Paris 1951; German: *Gott ist tot*, Vienna/Munich 1954; *BW Mohler*, p. 181 and passim.

Georg Lukács in the same tragicomic situation — Lukács served in 1956 as Minister of Education in Imre Nagy’s government and was arrested after the suppression of the Budapest uprising. From then on he was under official disgrace.

**6 October 1957**

the note at the end of my expert opinion — *Angriffskrieg*, pp. 80 f.

precedent — An allusion to Anglo-American case law.

Hugo Ball criticized my *Political Romanticism* … — Hugo Ball, “Carl Schmitts Politische Theologie.” In: *Hochland* 21, 1924, p. 466.

**28 October 1957**

Three grim prophecies — Based on an epigram by Schiller and Goethe:

> In vain, Germans, you hope to shape yourselves into a nation;
> Instead, if you can, shape yourselves more freely into human beings.

Friedrich Schiller, *Sämtliche Werke in 5 Bänden*. Edited by P.-A. Alt, A. Meier, and W. Riedel, vol. 1, Munich 2004, p. 267.

**29 October 1957**

that I spoke of the “proletarian consciousness of having been cheated” — Possibly a reference to *PuB*, pp. 129 f.:

> “The fascist ethos, too, proceeds from that feeling of having been cheated which can be found everywhere from the nineteenth century onward, which is by no means merely a proletarian emotion, and which after the World War found stronger expression in the Latin countries than in Germany.”

Bloch’s remarks have not been identified.

**31 December 1957**

So good old Werner Becker expects … — W. Becker (1904–1981), jurist and theologian, a student of Schmitt in Bonn who earned his doctorate under him with a dissertation on Hobbes; see W. Becker, *Briefe an Carl Schmitt*. Edited and annotated by Piet Tommissen, Berlin 1998, pp. 10 ff.

Schmitt is probably referring to W. Becker, *Die Wirklichkeit der Kirche und das Ärgernis*, Leipzig 1957. Two copies are in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 nos. 26637 and 26681.

*pecca fortiter* — Luther wrote to Melanchthon on 1 August 1521:

*Esto peccator et pecca fortiter, sed fortius fide et gaude in Christo, qui victor est peccati, mortis et mundi.*

> “Be a sinner and sin boldly, but be still stronger in faith and in your joy in Christ, who is the victor over sin, death, and the world.”

M. Luther, *D. Martin Luthers Werke* (Weimar edition), section 4, vol. 2, p. 372.

**6 April 1958**

*Et ta Race est 89* — The French “Jacobin” historian Jules Michelet (1798–1874) wrote:

> “From India down to ’89 there flows a torrent of light, the river of Right and Reason. You are high antiquity. And your race is ’89.”

J. Michelet, *Bible de l’humanité*, Paris 1864, p. 485.

**25 May 1958**

Aubrey Beardsley seems to have been right — Schmitt is referring here to Franz Blei, who described an encounter with Beardsley and quoted him as saying:

> “Every one of us. Nothing but Hamlets. The Protestant ending.”

F. Blei, *Zeitgenössische Bildnisse*, Amsterdam 1940, p. 194.

trial of Böhme — In the 1958 “Ulm Einsatzgruppen Trial,” former SS Sturmbannführer Hans-Joachim Böhme (1909–1960), together with other defendants, was sentenced to fifteen years in prison for assisting in 3,907 instances of collective murder committed in Lithuania in 1941.

Pflimlin — Pierre Eugène Jean Pflimlin (1907–2000), French jurist and politician, briefly Prime Minister of France in 1958.

Kühlmann — Richard von Kühlmann (1873–1948), German diplomat and industrialist, State Secretary of the Foreign Office from 1917 to 1918.

*par nobile fratrum* — “A noble pair of brothers,” used ironically to mean “a fine pair indeed”; quotation from the satires of Horace.

**1 June 1958**

C. F. von Weizsäcker’s account — Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker, *Die gegenwärtigen Aussichten einer Begrenzung der Gefahr eines Atomkrieges*, Hamburg 1958.

Poor Delano — In Herman Melville’s story *Benito Cereno*, the American captain Amasa Delano visits a Spanish slave ship lying at anchor without realizing that its captain, Benito Cereno, is being held hostage by the slaves who have mutinied.

**3 June 1958**

who therefore calls himself Carlo — An allusion to Carlo Schmid, with whom Schmitt was occasionally confused and who was still calling himself “Karl” in 1948; see the note above on p. 52.

Otto Weininger’s hatred of the Viennese waltz — See O. Weininger, *Über die letzten Dinge*, 4th ed., Vienna/Leipzig 1918, p. 99. See also the note above on p. 253.

**5 June 1958**

a pension under Article 131 — Article 131 of the Basic Law provided that the pension and employment status of civil servants who were not reinstated after 1945 was to be regulated by federal law. This was done on 11 May 1951 in such a way that everyone who had not been classified as a major offender or offender could once again be employed as a civil servant or become eligible for a pension. Schmitt thereby became entitled to receive his pension.

July 1958, Christian Courtois’s book — Chr. Courtois, *Les Vandales et l’Afrique*, Paris 1955.

Gelimer’s laughter and Daniel’s smile — On Gelimer, see above, p. 312. For Schmitt, Gelimer’s opposite was the Romanesque statue at the portal of Santiago Cathedral showing the prophet Daniel laughing over the lions that could do him no harm. See *BW Forsthoff*, pp. 161 f., 540 (illustration); *BW d’Ors*, p. 191; *Schmittiana NF* I, 2011, p. 243.

*JZ* for the seventieth birthday — Hans Huber, “Einige Bemerkungen über die Rechts- und Staatslehre von Carl Schmitt. Zu Peter Schneiders Buch ‘Ausnahmezustand und Norm’.” In: *Juristenzeitung* 13, 1958, pp. 341–343.

1959 *JZ* — Adolf Schüle, “Eine Festschrift.” In: *Juristenzeitung* 14, 1959, pp. 729–731. See also the resulting letters-to-the-editor debate in *Deutsche Zeitung* of 24 February, 22 March, and 23 March 1960.

1962 *NZZ* — H. F. Pfenninger, “Carl Schmitt und der ‘Partisan’ Rousseau.” In: *Neue Zürcher Zeitung*, 27 July 1962.

**22 August 1958**

*indocilis privata loqui* — “Unable to speak like an ordinary mortal.”

*Et mortem sentire juvat* — “It is a comfort to feel death approaching.” *Pharsalia*, IV, 570.

**25 August 1958**

*princeps reliogissimus Sisebut* — Correctly: *religiosissimus*, “the most devout King Sisebut.” Sisebut (died 621) was king of the Visigoths.

*Lecto de la validez* and the *validez del Lecto* — “Reading validity” and “the validity of the reading.”

Vitoria later dealt with it in exactly the same way — In his *Relecciones de Indis*, Francisco de Vitoria rejects forced baptism.

*Coactus voluit* — *Etsi coactus tamen voluit*, “although compelled, he nevertheless willed it.” A formula of Roman contract law according to which agreements entered into under compulsion were still valid, although their validity could be challenged.

Innocent III and his decretal *Maiores* — Innocent III, pope from 1198 to 1216, ruled that a forced baptism was invalid.

Canon 57 of the Fourth Council of Toledo and Gratian’s gloss, C 5 D. XLV — The Fourth Council of Toledo, held in 633 under the presidency of Isidore of Seville, condemned the forced baptisms of Jews ordered by King Sisebut. This was incorporated into the *Decretum Gratiani*, Chapter V, Distinction XLV.

*À corsaire, corsaire et demi* — A French proverb meaning that an aggressive person must be met by someone even more aggressive.

*Secundum occasionem et veritatem coactus sive condicionaliter, sive absolute voluit* — “According to the circumstances and the truth of the matter, though compelled, he willed it either conditionally or absolutely.”

Quevedo’s *Sueños* — Schmitt is referring to Francisco de Quevedo, *Los sueños*, Buenos Aires 1952. A copy with annotations is in his papers, RW 265 no. 22688; German: *Die Träume*, Frankfurt am Main 1980. Also: idem, *La hora de todos y la fortuna con seso*, Madrid 1987.

The latter work, published posthumously, incorporated “La isla de los Monopantos.” On its relationship to the *Protocols of the Elders of Zion*, see J. A. van Praag, “Los ‘Protocolos de los Sabios de Sión’ y la ‘Isla de los Monopantos’.” In: *Bulletin Hispanique* 51, 1949, pp. 169–173.

**26 August 1958**

Through gentleness—practice this duty … — Schmitt is remembering lines from a hymnbook here; see *BW EJ*, p. 354.

**9 September 1958**

as Ernst Jünger said against me — *BW EJ*, p. 247. See also above, pp. 222 f.

**21 September 1958**

Pribićević — Svetozar P. (1875–1936), Croatian-Serbian politician who initially supported a united Yugoslavia, but from 1927 onward adopted the opposite position and went into exile in 1931.

Sava told me — Sava Kličkovič (1916–1990), Serbian, a student of Schmitt in Berlin from 1936 and awarded his doctorate in 1940. See Christian Tilitzki, “Carl Schmitt – Staatsrechtler in Berlin. Einblicke in seinen Wirkungskreis anhand der Fakultätsakten 1934–1944.” In: *Etappe* 7, 1991, pp. 95 f. Schmitt remained on friendly terms with Kličković and his family throughout his life. An extensive correspondence survives in his papers.

**22 September 1958**

It is most dangerous with Bonald — Louis-Gabriel-Ambroise, vicomte de Bonald (1754–1840), French counter-revolutionary philosopher who “sociologized the idea of God” (R. Spaemann).

**27 September 1958**

Crooke — Possibly a reference to John Crook, *Consilium Principis. Imperial Councils and Counsellors from Augustus to Diocletian*, Cambridge 1955.

Jünger’s new diary — E. Jünger, *Jahre der Okkupation*, Stuttgart 1958. On Niekisch, see the note above on p. 79.

**10 October 1958**

ready or not to go, he must stand before his judge — F. Schiller, *Wilhelm Tell*, end of Act IV.

**30 October 1958**

Henry Morgenthau — (1891–1967), U.S. Secretary of the Treasury from 1934 to 1945, originator of the “Morgenthau Plan,” which proposed turning Germany into an agricultural state.

“out of regard …” — After initially accepting the Nobel Prize, Boris Pasternak declined it on 29 October 1958 under massive pressure, explaining that he did so:

> “out of regard for the society in which I live.”

See *Die Zeit*, 30 October 1958.

**9 November 1958**

ERP funds — From 1948 onward, funds from the European Recovery Program, based on the Marshall Plan, were made available to support economic reconstruction.

Montherlant’s *Maître de Santiago* — Henry de Montherlant, *Le Maître de Santiago*, play, 1947; German: *Der Ordensmeister*, 1948.

Hans-Joachim Arndt — (1923–2004), political scientist, a member of the Heidelberg circle of Schmitt’s informal students; see van Laak, passim.

*leyenda negra* — Faced with the accusation that they were a brutal people, Spaniards answered with the term *leyenda negra*—“Black Legend”—coined in the late nineteenth century, which presented the accusation as anti-Spanish propaganda.

*sublime néant* — In Montherlant’s *Le Maître de Santiago*, the character Alvaro wavers between God and the “sublime nothingness.”

**11 November 1958**

journalist Cassandra — The cover story in the issue of *Der Spiegel* mentioned here concerns the English journalist William Neil Connor (1909–1967), who wrote columns for the *Daily Mirror* for more than thirty years under the pseudonym Cassandra. In the interview with *Der Spiegel*, he emphasizes his contempt for everything German.

*if the Germans are not what he says they are—what is he?* — A variation on *The Education of Henry Adams*; see the note above on p. 136.

**12 November 1958**

Erich Strauss — Schmitt occasionally published poems under the pseudonym Erich Strauss; see *Gedichte*.

**16 November 1958**

In 1932 I found the decisive word — This refers to *LuL*.

**7 December 1958**

I wrote to Jünger that I already feel embarrassed enough —

> “Niekisch belongs to the victors of the Second World War, and he already made my wife feel that in 1946. As far as I am concerned, he can go on winning and write history as a victor. I will not answer the lies he spreads about conversations with me. It is embarrassing enough for me that I ever entered into a conversation with him at all, when thirty years later I am presented with this kind of ‘report’ by him about that conversation.”

*BW EJ*, pp. 356 f. See also the note above on p. 79.

*Steppenverhöre* — Allusion to Werner Helwig, *Das Steppenverhör. Roman*, Düsseldorf/Cologne 1957.

*doceo, sed frustra* — “I teach, but in vain”; see the note above on p. 180.

Haecker’s afterword of 1918 — This refers to Haecker’s afterword to his 1917 edition of Kierkegaard’s *Begriff des Auserwählten*, which was also published separately by Hegner in Hellerau in 1918; now in idem, *Essays*, Munich 1958, pp. 9–87. See the note above on p. 110.

preacher’s tabs exchanged for a rosary — This refers to Haecker’s conversion from Protestantism to Catholicism.

Novalis believed —

> “The Last Day will not be a single day, but simply that period which is also called the thousand-year kingdom.”

Novalis, *Religiöse Schriften*, Bremen 2012, p. 124.

**8 December 1958**

“abyss of mendacity of degenerate Furche pietists” — T. Haecker, *Essays*, Munich 1958, p. 81. “Furche pietists” refers to authors associated with the Furche publishing house, founded in 1916, which had an explicitly Christian program.

You can no longer think of anything to say about Hitler — An allusion to the anti-Hitler writer Karl Kraus, who remarked in 1933:

> “As for Hitler, nothing occurs to me.”

**28 December 1958**

The story of the three men — W. Helwig, *Das Steppenverhör*; see the note above on p. 377.

letter from October 1923 — A letter from Feuchtwanger to Schmitt, not from October but from 18 June 1923; in: *BW Feuchtwanger*, pp. 35 f.

**30 December 1958**

“jument ruant étalon” — The Baldung Grien engraving is correctly titled: “Étalon et la jument Kicking avec des chevaux sauvages.”

**31 December 1958**

Our venerable head of state … — Federal President Heuss’s speech was printed in the *FAZ* of 17 December 1958. A copy with underlining and stenographic notes survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 20830. See also *BW Mohler*, pp. 293 f.

*Obiter dictum* and *obiter factum* — “Something said in passing” and “something done in passing.” In legal practice, an *obiter dictum* is an opinion expressed by a judge apart from the judgment itself.

the reading of Odo Marquard’s study — Schmitt is referring to Odo Marquard, *Skeptische Methode im Blick auf Kant* (*Symposion*, 4), Freiburg im Breisgau/Munich 1958. A copy containing many annotations and inserted newspaper clippings survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 27763.

I do not compare the victims; I compare only the judges — A reversal of a sentence by Lucien Laberthonnière; see the note above on p. 214.

Rafo Konforti — A character in Ivo Andrić’s novel *Das Fräulein*, which appeared in German in 1958.

chorus in Nestroy’s farce *Judith* — Correctly:

> “We Hebrews have miracles enough in our history;
> We can do without miracles of bravery.”

*Quid sum miser tunc dicturus? / Quem jutorem rogaturus?* — Correctly: *Quid sum miser tunc dicturus? / Quem patronum rogaturus?*

> “What shall I, poor wretch, say then?
> What advocate shall I ask for?”

Quotation from the hymn *Dies irae*. Schmitt replaces *patronum*—“advocate”—with *jutorem*—“helper.”

my thesis about the transformation of the subject matter of a trial — See above, p. 42. Schmitt published nothing further on this. Compare his remark from 1958:

> “A fundamental scholarly investigation is needed into the question of how far the means and methods of a judicial process alter the very object that the process is supposed to examine.”

*VA*, p. 109.

*judex homini lupus* — “The judge is a wolf to man.”

*J’en appelle de ta justice à ta réalité* — Actually: *J’en appelle de ta justice à ta gloire*, meaning: “I appeal from Your justice to Your glory.” Léon Bloy, *Das Heil und die Armut. Mit Beiträgen von Georges Bernanos, Raïssa Maritain und Karl Pfleger*, Heidelberg, 1953, p. 374. In his diary, Léon Bloy records that Ernest Hello said this sentence to him (entry of 13 August 1892). He later uses it in his description of the Last Judgment in Chapter 28 of his book *Le Salut par les Juifs*. Schmitt names Hello as his source; cf. *RK*, pp. 55–56.

## Commentary on the Appendix

**My tables** — Shakespeare, *Hamlet*, Act I, Scene 5: “My tables, — meet it is I set it down.” Schlegel translates this into German as: “Writing tablet, here! I must write it down.”

**μὴ μνησικακεῖν** — not to keep the wrongs one has suffered in mind; not to bear a grudge.

**Αμνηστία** — amnesty.

**JW Jan. 1933** — Dr. Ernst Wichards, Regional Court Councillor at the Prussian Ministry of Justice, “Das Reichsgesetz über Straffreiheit vom 20. Dezember 1932.” In: *Juristische Wochenschrift*, issue 1, 62nd year (1932), appendix.

**Duguit** — Léon Duguit/Henry Monnier, *Les constitutions et les principales lois politiques de la France depuis 1789. Collationnées sur les Textes Offic., précédées de Notices Histor. et suivies d’une Table Analyt. détaillée*, Paris, 1898.

**Jean de Saint-Thomas** — Schmitt quotes him from Charles Journet, *L’Église du Verbe incarné*, Paris, 1941 and later editions. In the Fribourg 1962 edition, the passage that Schmitt quotes somewhat inaccurately appears on pp. 875–876.

**Bellarmin** — Roberto Bellarmino, *De Summo Pontifice*, Ingolstadt [1587].

**Billot** — Ludovico Billot, *Tractatus de ecclesia Christi sive continuatio theologiae de verbo incarnato*, Rome, 1909.

**Ed. Meyer** — Eduard Meyer, *Caesars Monarchie und das Principat des Pompejus. Innere Geschichte Roms von 66 bis 44 v. Chr.*, Stuttgart/Berlin, 1918 and later editions.

**pomerium** — “the strip of open ground left free along the city wall, both inside and outside it, marked off by stones and defining the limits of the city’s auspices; the open space around the wall” (Georges, Latin-German dictionary).

**Procul e [correctly: a] muris …** — “Then, outside the walls and some distance away, a detachment appeared. It was not advancing in scattered little groups, but in an ordered formation, as if marching against an enemy of equal strength. They advance at a run …”

**Michelet, la loi; the Vistula as a border** — See the note above on p. 20.

**1901. Education of Henry Adams** — See the note above on p. 136.

**Niekisch published a book, *East-West*** — Ernst Niekisch, *Ost-West. Unsystematische Betrachtungen*, Berlin, 1947.

**Borgese** — Giuseppe Antonio Borgese, “Russland – Versuch einer Umwertung.” In: *Frankfurter Hefte* 2, 1947, pp. 750–765.

**Ortega** — José Ortega y Gasset, “Über die Vereinigten Staaten.” In: *Europäische Revue* 9, 1933, pp. 353–360.

**ex abundantia** — “out of abundance”; “from an overflow.”

**Just** — Arthur W. Just, “Russische Gegenwart.” In: *Europäische Revue* 8, 1932, pp. 94–103; also by the same author, “Russische Gegenwart. Der zweite Fünfjahresplan.” In: *Europäische Revue* 8, 1932, pp. 303–313.

**Karl Renner** — (1870–1950), Austrian lawyer and politician. Schmitt is referring to K. Renner, “Die soziale Funktion der Rechtsinstitute.” In: *Marx-Studien* 1, 1904, pp. 65–192; later also published several times as a separate work.

**“easy prey to the power of the moment”** — “Man, living and feeling, is easy prey to the power of the moment.” Friedrich Schiller, *The Maid of Orleans*, III, 4.

**Yes, he fishes for pearls …** — From the poem “Der Dichter – Dichters Glück” by Annette von Droste-Hülshoff.

**Gustav Klemm** — Gustav Friedrich Klemm (1802–1867), cultural historian and librarian. He regarded inequality among human races as the driving force of world history, an idea later taken up by German nationalist and racialist circles. Klemm’s principal work is the ten-volume *Allgemeine Culturgeschichte der Menschheit*.

**Fauchille** — Paul Auguste Joseph Fauchille (1858–1926), French lawyer. Schmitt is referring to Paul Fauchille, *Traité de droit international public*, 8th edition, completely revised, expanded, and brought up to date from Henry Bonfils’s *Manuel de droit international public*, Vols. I.1–3 and II, Paris, 1922–1926. See also *Nomos*, p. 235, n. 2.

**Verdross** — This refers to Alfred Verdross’s article “Amnestie” in Karl Strupp, ed., *Wörterbuch des Völkerrechts und der Diplomatie. Begonnen von Julius Hatschek. Fortges. und hrsg. von Karl Strupp*, Vols. 1–3, Berlin and elsewhere, 1924–1929. See also *Nomos*, p. 235, n. 2.

**Grotius III 10, §§ 3–4** — Schmitt is referring to Hugo Grotius, *De jure belli ac pacis libri tres*.

**Gudelin: in amnestia …** — “The substance of peace consists in amnesty; without it, there is no peace.” Schmitt took this quotation from the lawyer Peter Gudelin (1550–1619) from the following book: Heinrich Rogge, *Nationale Friedenspolitik. Handbuch des Friedensproblems und seiner Wissenschaft auf der Grundlage systematischer Völkerrechtspolitik*, Berlin, 1934, p. 55. Ernst Forsthoff drew Schmitt’s attention to the passage on 17 October 1951; cf. *BW Forsthoff*, p. 80.

**Art. 120 of the Jacobin Constitution of 1793** — The article reads in the original: “It gives asylum to foreigners banished from their homeland for the cause of liberty. — It refuses asylum to tyrants.”

**JW 1933** — Hans Kasche, “Das politische Verbrechen in den deutschen Auslieferungsverträgen.” In: *Juristische Wochenschrift*, issues 29/30, 62nd year (1933), pp. 1639–1640.

**Lauterpacht** — Lassa Oppenheim, *Disputes, War and Neutrality*, Part 2 of *International Law*, edited by Hersch Lauterpacht, 6th ed., London and elsewhere, 1940.

**Itinerarium acroamaticum …** — “An entertaining guide to the roads of hell. A book of instruction on how, through proper conduct of one’s life, to keep out of Leviathan’s way.” Probably inspired by Theodor Däubler, *Lucidarium in arte musicae des Ricciotto Canudo aus Gioja del Colle*, Hellerau, 1917.

**De nobis ipsis silemus** — See the note above on p. 83.

**I already know those dear Germans** — See the note above on p. 129.

**exul in patria** — See the note above on p. 7.

**inuar uigandun** — From the Merseburg Incantations:

*insprine haptandun*
*inuar uigandun*

Break free from the bonds,
escape from the enemies.

**I endure, watchful …** — A line written in 1908 by Schmitt’s friend Franz Kluxen. Schmitt wrote it down from memory in 1948 together with several other lines by Kluxen; cf. *RW* 265, no. 21288.

**Gelimer’s laughter** — See the note above on p. 312.

**Durando saecula vincit** — *Multa virum volvens durando saecula vincit.* “After passing through many generations of men, it conquers the centuries by enduring.” Publius Vergilius Maro, *Georgics*, Book II, line 295; German translation by Johann Heinrich Voß.

**Adam, where are you?** — Genesis 3:9.

**Quo usque tandem?** — *Quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?* “How much longer, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?” Marcus Tullius Cicero, *First Catilinarian Oration*.

Hölderlin’s echo begins again like numinous humming; we thought we had reached something firm and classical in <Hölderlin>. But that is not true. God is elemental—nonsense. There is another possibility too. Hölderlin <…>. Jünger is decisionist. Command. But he does not know where to go from there. He cannot bring himself to decide to become Roman Catholic. The English language the same.”
